<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:profile-is-upset}
For every task $P$, $\mathsf{Prof}(P)$ is an upset of $\mathcal Q$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:canonical-upset-decomposition}
For every $U\in\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$,
\(
  U=\bigcup_{X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)}\mathord{\uparrow} X,
\)
and $\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is the unique antichain giving an irredundant
representation of $U$ by principal upsets.
Consequently, antichains and upsets are in bijection.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-certificate}
Let $P$ be a task and $U\in\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$. Then $\mathsf{Prof}(P)=U$
if and only if
\[
\begin{aligned}
  P&\in\mathsf{Sol}(X)
    &&\text{for every }X\in\operatorname{Min}(U),\\
  P&\notin\mathsf{Sol}(Y)
    &&\text{for every }Y\in\operatorname{Max}(\mathcal Q\setminus U).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:disjunction-easy-direction}
For every finite family,
\(
  \bigcup_{i\in I}\mathsf{Prof}(P_i)
  \subseteq
  \mathsf{Prof}\left(\bigvee_{i\in I}P_i\right).
\)
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:basic-inclusions}
For every scheduler $K$ and model $M$,
\[
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^K\ge\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^K\ge\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^K,\qquad
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^K\ge\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^K\ge\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^K,
\]
and
\(
  M^F\ge M^R\ge M^S,\;
  M^S\ge M^{A_{LC}}\ge M^A,\;
  M^S\ge M^{A_{CM}}\ge M^{A_M}\ge M^A.
\)
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:atomicity-equivalences}
\(
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_{LC}},\quad
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^A\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_{LC}},\quad\\
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M}\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_{CM}},\quad
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_{CM}}.
\)
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:equ-FCOMF-by-FSTAF}
For exactly two robots under the assumptions above,
\(
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^F\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F.
\)
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:six-bounds}
Under the assumptions of this paper, the following hold.
\renewcommand{\textcolor{lipicsGray}{\sffamily\bfseries\upshape(\theenumi)}}{\textcolor{lipicsGray}{\sffamily\bfseries\upshape(\theenumi)}}
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{lem:six-cge-star-bounds}
  $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)$ and
  $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^R)$.
\item\label{lem:six-sro-bounds}
  $\mathrm{SRO}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R)$ and
  $\mathrm{SRO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)\cup\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S)$.
\item\label{lem:six-mcv-bounds}
  $\mathrm{MCv}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S)$ and
  $\mathrm{MCv}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A)\cup\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
\item\label{lem:six-cfsm-bounds}
  $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A)$ and
  $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)\cup\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
\item\label{lem:six-vss-bounds}
  $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A)$ and
  $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)\cup\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R)$.
\item\label{lem:six-dmsd-bounds}
  $\textnormal{\text{DMSD}}\xspace\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M})$ and
  $\textnormal{\text{DMSD}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Items~(1)--(6) are proved in
Appendices~\ref{app:epgs}, \ref{app:sro}, \ref{app:mcv},
\ref{app:cfs}, \ref{app:vss} and~\ref{app:dmsd}, respectively.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:six-signature-landscape}
Write $\sigma(\mu)=\{P\in\mathcal B_6: P\in\mathsf{Sol}(\mu)\}$. The settings
under consideration form exactly thirteen computational equivalence
classes, represented by the rows of
Table~\ref{tab:six-separator-signatures}, and for any two
representatives $\mu,\nu$,
\[
  \mu\ge\nu
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \sigma(\mu)\supseteq\sigma(\nu).
\]
The certificate is given in Appendix~\ref{app:signature-order-certificate}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:six-principal-separators}
The tasks in \( \mathcal B_6\)
are principal, with
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathsf{Prof}(\mathrm{EPG}^{*})&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F,
  &\mathsf{Prof}(\mathrm{SRO})&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R,\\
  \mathsf{Prof}(\mathrm{MCv})&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S,
  &\mathsf{Prof}(\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace)&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A,\\
  \mathsf{Prof}(\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace)&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A,
  &\mathsf{Prof}(\textnormal{\text{DMSD}}\xspace)&=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}.
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For each task, the positive and maximal negative bounds stated above,
together with upward closure of solvability, determine exactly the
corresponding principal upset.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:min-separators}
Any family of tasks separating all thirteen classes of
$\mathcal Q$ contains at least six tasks. Hence
$\mathcal B_6$ is minimum.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The quotient contains the chain
\[
  \ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^A<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R<\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R<\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^R<\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F.
\]
Along a chain, the solvability set of each task is an upper interval
and hence can create at most one cut. Distinguishing the seven
elements therefore requires at least six tasks.
Table~\ref{tab:six-separator-signatures} shows that $\mathcal B_6$ achieves this
bound.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:unique-principal-separators}
The unique minimum family of principal upsets separating all elements
of $\mathcal Q$ is
\(
 \{
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F,\,
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R,\,
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S,\,
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A,\,
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A,\,
 \mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}
 \}.
\)

Equivalently, the profiles of the six tasks in $\mathcal B_6$
form the unique minimum principal separating family.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:ospo-bounds}
Under the assumptions of this paper,
\(
  \mathrm{OSPO}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R),
\)
whereas
\(
  \mathrm{OSPO}
  \notin
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)
  \cup
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S)
  \cup
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S).
\)
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The solvability algorithm in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R$ and the three impossibility
arguments are given in Appendix~\ref{app:osp}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:s-rdv-bounds}
Under the assumptions of this paper,
\(
  \mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S),
\)
whereas
\(
  \mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}
  \notin
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)
  \cup
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R)
  \cup
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A).
\)
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The solvability algorithm in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S$ and the three impossibility
arguments are given in
Appendix~\ref{app:s-rdv-bounds}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:principal-task-basis}
Let $\mathcal B=\{B_X:X\in\mathcal Q\}$ be the family specified in
Table~\ref{tab:PP13}. Under the model assumptions and observation
convention of this paper, every task $B_X$ has initial-instance space
$\mathcal I_\star$ and satisfies
\(
  \mathsf{Prof}(B_X)=\mathord{\uparrow} X.
\)
Consequently, $\mathcal B$ is a principal task basis consisting of
thirteen tasks and extending the six-task separating family
$\mathcal B_6$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If $X\in\mathcal X_6$, the identity $\mathsf{Prof}(B_X)=\mathord{\uparrow} X$ is exactly
one of the six statements of
Theorem~\ref{thm:six-principal-separators}.

If $X\in\mathcal X_7$, the task-specific results referenced in
Table~\ref{tab:PP13}, including
Corollary~\ref{cor:epg_profile}, establish solvability at $X$ and
impossibility at every class in $\mathcal N_X$. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-certificate} gives
$\mathsf{Prof}(B_X)=\mathord{\uparrow} X$. This also covers $X=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^A$, where
$\mathcal N_X=\varnothing$.

Since $\mathcal Q=\mathcal X_6\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal X_7$ and
all tasks use $\mathcal I_\star$, the conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:solo-drift}
Let $\rho$ be an admissible execution with joint-stop sequence $(C_i)_{i\ge0}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If one of the two robots completes no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ between the joint stop
  realizing $C_i$ and the one realizing $C_{i+1}$, then
  \(
    \tfrac12(a_{i+1}+b_{i+1})\neq\tfrac12(a_i+b_i).
  \)
\item Let $K\in\{R,S,A_{LC},A_M,A\}$. For every algorithm there is a fair
  execution in which the $\ensuremath{\mathit{LCM}}\xspace$ cycles of the two robots are pairwise disjoint
  in time. In such an execution either no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, in which
  case $(C_i)$ has the single term $C_0$ and the perpetuity condition fails, or
  $\tfrac12(a_1+b_1)\neq c_0$ and the expansion condition fails at $i=0$.
  In both cases $\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}$ fails, and so does
  $\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:cf-expansion-exchange}
For every deterministic algorithm in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R$, there is an admissible
fair execution that violates $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$,
$\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}$, and $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$ simultaneously.
In particular, for each
$E\in\{\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV},\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\}$,
\[
  \mathrm{EPG}^{*}\vee E\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R).
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Use coordinates on the initial line with $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $d>0$,
so the outer points are $0,3d$ and $c_0=3d/2$. Activate $a,b$
alternately, completing each cycle before the next one starts; this is
an admissible fair $R$ execution with an empty fully synchronous prefix.
Under normalized observations, the two robots traverse the same private
state sequence until the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$.

If no such ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs, all three tasks fail their progress requirements.
Otherwise $a$ performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ alone, changing the center
of gravity at the next joint stop and violating $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$.
The shared exchange phase requires one of $(3d,2d),(d,0),(3d,0)$ with
cumulative nonzero-move counts $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$, respectively.
Thus this first solo ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ must land at $3d$: any other landing
would require another nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ to reach an admissible
exchange configuration, exceeding its allowed count.

If $a$ lands at $3d$, then $b$, at its next activation, has the same
private state as $a$ had before that ${\mathit{Move}}$ and receives the same normalized
input. Hence it performs the same normalized displacement, which in its
current physical frame is twice its current distance to the peer,
and therefore lands at $2d+2d=4d$. This lies outside the segment $[0,3d]$ required
by $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ and outside the allowed endpoint set $\{0,d,2d,3d\}$ of $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$.
In either case both exchange tasks fail irreversibly. Continue with fair
alternating activations; all three violations persist.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:cf-sro-exchange-family}
For every deterministic algorithm in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S$ there is an admissible fair
execution that violates $\mathrm{SRO}$ and both tasks in $\mathcal E$
simultaneously. Consequently
$\mathrm{SRO}\vee E\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S)$ for every $E\in\mathcal E$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We first recall the geometric obstruction. SRO permits a clockwise
$90^\circ$ rotation of the segment, or a clockwise $45^\circ$ rotation
with scale $1/\sqrt2$. With the peer fixed at $(0,0)$ and the moving
robot initially at $(-1,0)$, the four possible two-step choices place
the moving robot at one of
\(
  (1,0),\; (1/2,1/2),\; (0,1/2).
\)
All lie outside the square with the initial segment as diagonal,
contrary to SRO's containment condition. Thus two consecutive solo
nonzero moves defeat SRO (Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves}).

Use the same initial positions and normalized observations as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:cf-expansion-exchange}. If the initial state orbit
contains no nonzero output, a fair alternating execution never moves
and violates all three tasks. Otherwise activate $a$ alone until its
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$; $S$ permits any finite number of solo activations.
If $a$ lands at $3d$, the segment reverses without changing length,
violating SRO. Activating $b$ through its preceding zero-output states
then reproduces the move to $4d$, violating both exchange tasks.

For any other landing, both exchange tasks have already failed.
Unless SRO also fails immediately, the robots remain distinct.
If $a$ has another nonzero output, execute it with $b$ fixed and apply
the two-move obstruction. Otherwise let $b$ perform its corresponding
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. Either this violates SRO, or both robots now follow
the same zero-output state suffix. Fair alternating activations then
leave the configuration stationary forever, violating SRO's perpetuity.
In the finite-violation cases, append a fair alternating suffix.
Appendix~\ref{app:cf-sro-family} gives the complete argument.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-common-failure}
Let $A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)$. Suppose that, for every $Y\in\mathcal N_A$
and every deterministic algorithm $\mathcal A$ in $Y$, there are an
initial instance $\iota\in\mathcal I_\star$ and an admissible fair
execution $\rho$ of $\mathcal A$ from $\iota$ such that
\(
  \rho\not\models\Phi_{B_X}
  \;\text{for every }X\in A,
\)
where $\Phi_{B_X}$ denotes the temporal predicate of the principal
task $B_X$ of Table~\ref{tab:PP13}.
We then say that $\{B_X:X\in A\}$ has the \emph{common-failure
property} in $Y$. Under this hypothesis, $\mathsf{Prof}(B_A)=U_A$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If $Z\in U_A$, then $Z$ solves some $B_X$ with $X\in A$, and the same
algorithm solves $B_A$.

Conversely, the assumed executions show that $B_A\notin\mathsf{Sol}(Y)$
for every $Y\in\mathcal N_A$. Every $Z\notin U_A$ lies below some
such $Y$, by finiteness of $\mathcal Q$. If $B_A$ were solvable in
$Z$, it would also be solvable in $Y$, a contradiction. Hence
$\mathsf{Prof}(B_A)\subseteq U_A$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:all-common-failure-boundaries}
For every $A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)$ with $2\le |A|\le3$ and every
$Y\in\mathcal N_A$, the family $\{B_X:X\in A\}$ has the common-failure
property in $Y$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The five two-task rows of Table~\ref{tab:cf-family-coverage} exhaust the
twenty-four two-element antichains and the three remaining rows exhaust the
sixteen three-element ones. Table~\ref{tab:PP13-join2} and
Table~\ref{tab:PP13-join3} name, for each listed $Y\in\mathcal N_A$, the
construction that violates every predicate of $A$ on one admissible fair
execution.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:exact-disjunctive-basis}
The principal task basis $\mathcal B=\{B_X:X\in\mathcal Q\}$ is an
exact disjunctive basis. For every $A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)$,
\(
  \mathsf{Prof}\left(\bigvee_{X\in A}B_X\right)
  =\bigcup_{X\in A}\mathord{\uparrow} X.
\)
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For $A=\varnothing$, both sides are empty by the convention for the
empty disjunction. For $|A|=1$, the claim is
Theorem~\ref{thm:principal-task-basis}. For $2\le |A|\le3$, apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:all-common-failure-boundaries} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure}. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:width-three} these cases exhaust all antichains.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:profile-realization}
For every nonempty upset $U\in\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$, define
\(
  B_U\coloneqq\bigvee_{X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)}B_X.
\)
Then $\mathsf{Prof}(B_U)=U$, and $\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is the unique irredundant set of
principal generators of $U$; the expression above is therefore the
canonical disjunctive normal form of $U$ at the profile level. With
$B_\varnothing=(\mathcal I_\star,\mathsf{false})$ the same identity
holds for $U=\varnothing$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
$\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is an antichain, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-disjunctive-basis} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-upset-decomposition} give
$\mathsf{Prof}(B_U)=\bigcup_{X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)}\mathord{\uparrow} X=U$. If
$U=\bigcup_{X\in S}\mathord{\uparrow} X$ irredundantly, then every $Y\in\operatorname{Min}(U)$
lies in some $\mathord{\uparrow} X$ with $X\in S\subseteq U$, and minimality
forces $X=Y$; any further generator lies above a minimal element and is
redundant. Hence $S=\operatorname{Min}(U)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:minimum-profile-basis}
Let $\mathcal G\subseteq\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$ be a family whose unions
generate every element of $\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$. Then
$\mathord{\uparrow} X\in\mathcal G$ for every $X\in\mathcal Q$. Consequently
$\{\mathord{\uparrow} X:X\in\mathcal Q\}$ is the unique least union-generating
family of profiles, of cardinality thirteen.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $\mathord{\uparrow} X=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal G_X}G$ with
$\mathcal G_X\subseteq\mathcal G$. Some $G\in\mathcal G_X$ contains $X$,
and being an upset it contains $\mathord{\uparrow} X$; the displayed equality
gives the reverse inclusion, so $G=\mathord{\uparrow} X$. Conversely the
principal upsets generate every upset by canonical decomposition, and
they are distinct.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:minimum-exact-task-basis}
Any task family $\mathcal D$ supplying an exact
representation\footnote{A finite disjunction from $\mathcal D$ is an
\emph{exact representation} of $U$ when the selected subfamily
$\mathcal D_U\subseteq\mathcal D$ satisfies
$\mathsf{Prof}(\bigvee_{P\in\mathcal D_U}P)
 =\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal D_U}\mathsf{Prof}(P)=U$; the empty disjunction is
allowed, and only the representations used to generate the profiles
need be exact.} of every upset of $\mathcal Q$ contains at least
thirteen tasks. The family $\mathcal B$ attains this bound, and if
$|\mathcal D|=13$ its task profiles are exactly
$\{\mathord{\uparrow} X:X\in\mathcal Q\}$, each occurring once.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The profiles $\{\mathsf{Prof}(P):P\in\mathcal D\}$ generate every upset by
union, so Theorem~\ref{thm:minimum-profile-basis} forces all thirteen
principal upsets to occur; $\mathcal B$ attains the bound by
Theorem~\ref{thm:profile-realization}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $X\in\mathsf{Prof}(P)$ and $X\preceq Y$. Then
\[
  P\in\mathsf{Sol}(X)\subseteq\mathsf{Sol}(Y),
\]
and hence $Y\in\mathsf{Prof}(P)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{Q}$ is finite, every element of $U$ lies
above a minimal element of $U$.
Thus $U=\bigcup_{X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)}\mathord{\uparrow} X$.
Conversely, let $A$ be an antichain with
$U=\bigcup_{X\in A}\mathord{\uparrow} X$. Every element of $A$ is minimal
in $U$, since $A$ is an antichain, and every minimal element of $U$
lies above, hence equals, some element of $A$. Thus $\operatorname{Min}(U)=A$.
The representation is irredundant because each
$X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)$ belongs to no other principal upset
in the union.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Necessity is immediate. For sufficiency, every $Z\in U$ lies above
some $X\in\operatorname{Min}(U)$, since $\mathcal Q$ is finite. Thus $P\in\mathsf{Sol}(Z)$
by Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-is-upset}. Every $Z\notin U$ lies
below some $Y\in\operatorname{Max}(\mathcal Q\setminus U)$. If $P$ were solvable in
$Z$, it would also be solvable in $Y$, since $Z\le Y$, contradicting
the assumed impossibility at $Y$. Hence $\mathsf{Prof}(P)=U$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
If a model class solves $P_j$, the same algorithm always satisfies
$\Phi_j$ and therefore always satisfies $\bigvee_{i\in I}\Phi_i$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The cross-model inclusions follow by ignoring capabilities:
a $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace$ robot can execute an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ or $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ algorithm,
and either intermediate model can execute an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ algorithm.

The scheduler inclusions follow by restricting admissible
executions. If every schedule and timing choice permitted
by $K_1$ is also permitted by $K_2$, then any algorithm
correct under $K_2$ remains correct under $K_1$.
Thus,
\(
  \mathsf{Sol}(M,K_2)\subseteq\mathsf{Sol}(M,K_1).
\)
Applying this observation to the scheduler restrictions
in the model definitions proves the stated inclusions.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
These equivalences follow directly from the observation capabilities
of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ and from the definitions of the corresponding
atomic scheduler classes.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:fsynch-no-cost-simulation}
\label{lemma:no-cost-sim}
Let $\mathcal A$ be a deterministic two-robot $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F$ algorithm with
a palette $C$ of $k$ colors and a designated initial color $c_0$.
There are algorithms $\mathcal A_S$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F$ and $\mathcal A_C$ in
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^F$, both using the palette $C$, such that, for every initial
geometric configuration $I$ and every execution $\rho$ of either
simulator from $I$, there is an admissible execution $\widehat\rho$
of $\mathcal A$ from $I$ with
\(
  \pi_{\mathrm{geom}}(\rho)
  =\pi_{\mathrm{geom}}(\widehat\rho).
\)
The matching execution has the same round boundaries and movement
timings. Each simulator round implements exactly one round of
$\mathcal A$, without auxiliary colors or initialization rounds.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Write
\[
  \mathcal A(p,c_r,c_{\bar r})=(q,c').
\]
Fix $e=(0,1)$. For $p\neq0$, let $N_p$ be the
orientation-preserving similarity mapping $p$ to $e$,
and let $N_0=\mathrm{id}$.

\paragraph*{Construction.}
Both simulators start with $c_0$. In each round, a robot with peer position $p$ reads the available color $c$: its own color in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F$, or its peer's color in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^F$.
It computes
\[
  (q,c')=\mathcal A(N_{p}(p),c,c),
\]
sets its state or external light to $c'$, and moves to $N_{p}^{-1}(q)$ in its actual local coordinates.
This uses only permitted observations and the palette $C$; $N_p$ is computed from the current snapshot and
 is not stored between rounds.

 \paragraph*{Correctness.}
Fix an arbitrary execution $\rho$ of either simulator.
We construct a matching execution $\widehat{\rho}$ of the
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F$ algorithm $\mathcal A$ by induction over rounds.

At the beginning of round $j$, we maintain the following invariant:
the corresponding robots in $\rho$ and $\widehat{\rho}$ occupy the
same positions, and the two robots have a common color $c_j$.
The invariant holds initially by the designated common initial color.

Let $\psi_{r,j}$ be the map from global coordinates to robot $r$'s
actual local coordinates at its Look in round $j$, and let
$p_{r,j}$ be the observed peer position in these coordinates.
In the corresponding execution of $\mathcal A$, choose the virtual
local coordinate system
\[
  \widehat{\psi}_{r,j}
  =
  N_{p_{r,j}}\circ\psi_{r,j}.
\]
Because $N_{p_{r,j}}$ is an orientation-preserving similarity,
$\widehat{\psi}_{r,j}$ is admissible under variable disorientation
and preserves chirality.

By the induction hypothesis, the geometric configuration and the
two colors at the beginning of the round coincide in the two
executions. Hence, under the virtual coordinate system,
each source robot receives exactly the normalized input used by
the simulator. In particular, when the robots are at distinct
positions, both receive
\[
  (e,c_j,c_j),
\]
whereas at coincidence both receive
\[
  (0,c_j,c_j).
\]
Therefore, determinism of $\mathcal A$ implies that both corresponding
computations produce the same next color $c_{j+1}$.

Let $q_j$ be the destination computed by $\mathcal A$ in the
normalized coordinates. The global destination of robot $r$ in
$\widehat{\rho}$ is
\[
  \widehat{\psi}_{r,j}^{-1}(q_j)
  =
  \psi_{r,j}^{-1}
  \bigl(
    N_{p_{r,j}}^{-1}(q_j)
  \bigr),
\]
which is exactly the destination used by the simulator.

We now choose the same round boundaries, phase timings, and progress
along each rigid movement segment in $\widehat{\rho}$ as in $\rho$.
Thus the two executions have identical geometric trajectories
throughout round $j$, and the common-color invariant is preserved
for round $j+1$.

Induction over all rounds therefore yields an admissible infinite
execution $\widehat{\rho}$ of $\mathcal A$ satisfying
\[
  \pi_{\mathrm{geom}}(\rho)
  =
  \pi_{\mathrm{geom}}(\widehat{\rho}).
\]
Moreover, each simulator round implements exactly one round of
$\mathcal A$, and no auxiliary colors or initialization rounds are
introduced. Hence the simulator uses the same palette and preserves
the round and movement timings claimed in the theorem.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The quantitative simulation theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:fsynch-no-cost-simulation})
 shows that every
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F$ algorithm can be simulated in both $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^F$,
preserving the geometric execution.
Hence
\[
  \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F)\subseteq\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F)
  \cap\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^F).
\]
The reverse inclusions follow immediately because $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$
are submodels of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:sro}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions. Let $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ be the set
of times at which neither robot is inside a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operation,
list the configurations at the times of $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ in chronological order,
and remove consecutive repetitions; call the resulting sequence
$C_0,C_1,C_2,\dots$ with $C_i=(a_i,b_i)$. Put $d_i:=b_i-a_i$, let
$Q_i$ be the square with diagonal $a_ib_i$, interior included, and set
$Q_{-1}:=\mathbb R^2$. Let $R_\phi$ denote the counterclockwise
rotation by $\phi$. The first condition (perpetuity) requires the
sequence $(C_i)$ to be infinite. The second condition (rotation)
requires that for every $i$ the vector $d_{i+1}$ be the clockwise
$90^\circ$ rotation of $d_i$ ($\mathbf{C1}$), or its clockwise
$45^\circ$ rotation scaled by $1/\sqrt2$ ($\mathbf{C2}$), and that
$a_{i+1},b_{i+1}\in Q_{i-1}$ ($\mathbf{C3}$).
\begin{align*}
\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}\equiv\big[\ &\{\,(C_i)_{i\ge0}\ \text{is infinite}\,\}\\
 &\text{and}\ \{\,\forall i\ge0:\
 \bigl(d_{i+1}=R_{-90^\circ}d_i\ \text{or}\
 d_{i+1}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i\bigr)\\
 &\qquad\wedge\bigl(a_{i+1},b_{i+1}\in Q_{i-1}\bigr)\,\}\ \big]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:sro-not-fc-s}
$\mathrm{SRO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry the same color. If
$\lambda_\gamma=0$ for every color $\gamma$ occurring in that common
sequence, this fair execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, the
configuration never changes, the sequence $(C_i)$ reduces to $C_0$
alone, and the first condition fails. Otherwise let $\gamma$ be the
first color with $\lambda_\gamma>0$ and truncate the prefix at the
round in which both robots carry $\gamma$; the configuration is still
the initial one.

Now activate $a$ alone twice in a row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}; under
$\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ the robot that is not activated has no pending operation), and
write $C_i$ for the configuration at the beginning of this interval. The
visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot is the color of its peer, and $b$ is
not activated, so that color is constant; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the displacement rule of $a$ is the
single pair $(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$, and $\lambda_\gamma>0$
makes every activation a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. If $c_1(\gamma)=0$ and $a$
reaches the position of $b$, then $d=0$ in that configuration and
neither $\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$ can hold, so the second
condition fails. Otherwise $d>0$ is preserved. For the first move to
satisfy the second condition it must satisfy the rotation condition,
and with the peer at rest only two displacements do so, one of type
$\mathbf{C1}$ and one of type $\mathbf{C2}$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves}). The rule being single, the second
move is of the same type, and among the four computations of that
lemma the two relevant ones both give $a_{i+2}\notin Q_i$, so
$\mathbf{C3}$ fails.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:sro-not-fs-s}
$\mathrm{SRO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ the robot that is not activated has no pending operation,
so the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:solo} hold at every round
boundary. The visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot is its own color, so in
the normalized frame of Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) the color sequence of
each robot is $c_0,g(c_0),g^2(c_0),\dots$ independently of the
schedule, and it is eventually periodic with preperiod $p$ and period
$q$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB2}). The displacement of each activation is
likewise determined by the color through
$(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$.

\emph{The periodic part contains a color with $\lambda_\gamma>0$.}
Activating $a$ alone $p+2q$ times (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}) makes $a$
perform at least two nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations while $b$ stays at rest;
write $C_i$ for the configuration at the beginning of this interval.
Zero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations do not advance the sequence $(C_i)$, so these
correspond to two consecutive terms of $(C_i)$. If at some point
$c_1(\gamma)=0$ and $a$ reaches the position of $b$, then $d=0$ in
that configuration and neither $\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$ can
hold, so the second condition fails. Otherwise $d>0$ is preserved and
the same robot performs two consecutive nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations with
its peer at rest, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the rotation
condition and $\mathbf{C3}$ cannot both be satisfied and the second
condition fails.

Suppose now that the periodic part contains no color with
$\lambda_\gamma>0$.
                     
After the preperiod the color sequence stays in
the periodic part, where $\lambda_\gamma=0$, so each robot performs at
most $p$ nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations whatever the schedule. Hence the
configuration changes at only finitely many times, the sequence
$(C_i)$ is finite, and the first condition fails.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:sro-in-ob-r}
$\mathrm{SRO}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Each robot moves to the point obtained by rotating its own position
clockwise by $90^\circ$ about the midpoint of the two robots. If both
robots are activated simultaneously, the segment is rotated by
$90^\circ$ and $\mathbf{C1}$ holds; if only one robot is activated,
the segment is scaled by $1/\sqrt2$ and rotated by $45^\circ$, and
$\mathbf{C2}$ holds.

An $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ execution is either fully synchronous throughout,
which is the case treated in~\cite[Lemma~22]{FSW19}, or a finite
fully synchronous prefix followed by alternating singleton
activations (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}).
Fully synchronous rounds preserve the square.
If such a round is followed by a singleton round,
both new positions lie in the same square.
For two consecutive alternating singleton rounds, consider the
square immediately before the first round: the first mover
reaches one of its vertices, and the second reaches its centre.
Thus $a_{i+1},b_{i+1}\in Q_{i-1}$ for every $i\ge1$;
the case $i=0$ is vacuous since $Q_{-1}=\mathbb{R}^2$.
Hence $\mathbf{C3}$ holds as well.

The destination is determined by the midpoint and the rotation
alone and requires no unit of length, so it is computable
in each robot's own local frame.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:mcv}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions, and we write
$d(t):=\|a(t)-b(t)\|$. The first condition (convergence) requires the
two robots to converge to a common point $l$. The second condition
(monotonicity) requires their distance never to increase.
\[
  \Phi_{\mathrm{MCv}}
  \equiv
  \bigl[\ \{\,\exists l\in\mathbb R^2:\
    \lim_{t\to\infty}a(t)=\lim_{t\to\infty}b(t)=l\,\}
  \ \text{and}\
    \{\,\forall t,t'\ge0:\ t\le t'\Rightarrow d(t')\le d(t)\,\}\ \bigr]
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:mcv_not_fc_a}
$\mathrm{MCv}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Run fully synchronous cycles with normalized frames.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}, the two robots carry the same color
at every round boundary.
If every output along this execution is zero, the resulting
fair, time-divergent execution keeps the robots at their
distinct initial positions, violating convergence.
 
Otherwise, stop the zero-Move prefix just before the first
round with a nonzero output.
Let $\gamma$ be the common color at this point, so that
$\lambda_\gamma>0$, and put $c:=c_1(\gamma)$.
 
Let $b$ perform its ${\mathit{Look}}$, and delay its ${\mathit{Comp}}$.
This finite delay is permitted under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:suspend}.
The saved snapshot determines the nonzero displacement
\[
  v=\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}(w_{\mathrm{old}}),
\]
where $w_{\mathrm{old}}$ is the vector from $b$ to $a$
at that ${\mathit{Look}}$.
Although $b$ has not yet performed its ${\mathit{Comp}}$, determinism
ensures that it will compute this displacement from the
saved snapshot when its ${\mathit{Comp}}$ is eventually performed.
 
Throughout the delay, both the position and the visible
color $\gamma$ of $b$ remain unchanged.
Since an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot does not read its own color, we may
therefore activate $a$ for any prescribed finite number
of complete cycles, using normalized frames and the same
nonzero displacement rule
$(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$ in each cycle.
 
If $c>1$, a single such Move increases the distance
between its starting and ending times, violating monotonicity.
If $c=1$, the starting and ending positions of this nonzero
Move are distinct points at the same distance from the
stationary robot $b$.
The midpoint of the movement segment is strictly closer
to $b$ than either endpoint.
Thus the distance increases between the time $a$ passes
that midpoint and the completion of its Move, again
violating monotonicity.
 
It remains to consider $0\le c<1$.
Choose a finite $k\ge1$ such that, after $k$ complete
cycles of $a$,
\[
  \|w_k\|=c^k\|w_{\mathrm{old}}\|<\frac{\|v\|}{2},
\]
where $w_k$ is the vector from $b$ to $a$ at that time.
For $c=0$, take $k=1$; otherwise every cycle starts
with distinct robot positions, so the normalized rule
can be applied repeatedly.
 
Keep $a$ stationary and let $b$ complete its ${\mathit{Comp}}$
using the saved snapshot, update its color, and perform
the resulting Move with displacement $v$.
The distance immediately before that Move is $\|w_k\|$,
whereas at its completion it satisfies
\[
  \|w_k-v\|
  \ge \|v\|-\|w_k\|
  > \|w_k\|.
\]
Hence monotonicity fails.
 
In every finite-violation case, complete any pending cycle
and append an arbitrary admissible fair, time-divergent
continuation.
The violation persists, so no such algorithm solves
$\mathrm{MCv}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:mcv_not_fs_am}
$\mathrm{MCv}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
We prove the following stronger statement: from any configuration
with distinct robot positions, a common internal color, and no
pending operation, there is an admissible fair, time-divergent
continuation violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{MCv}}$.

Use normalized frames whenever the robots are distinct.
At a configuration with common color $s$, write
\[
  z_s=\lambda_s e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_s},
  \qquad c_s=|1-z_s|.
\]
We advance the common color by activating $a$ and then $b$,
one complete cycle at a time, except in the special case
specified below.

If $z_s=0$, both cycles are zero moves and both robots reach
color $g(s)$.

If $c_s=0$, then $z_s=1$. Instead, let both robots Look and
Compute before either moves, and let them execute their moves
simultaneously with equal fractional progress. They exchange
positions, so their distance becomes zero and then positive
again. Monotonicity fails.

If $z_s\ne0$ and $c_s\ge1$, a solo move of $a$ already violates
monotonicity. For $c_s>1$ its landing distance is larger than
its starting distance. For $c_s=1$, the endpoints are distinct
points at the same distance from the stationary peer; the
interior of the movement segment contains points strictly
closer to that peer, so the distance increases before landing.

It remains to consider $0<c_s<1$. Execute the two singleton
cycles. If either move increases the distance at any time,
monotonicity has already failed. Otherwise both robots finish
at distinct positions with common color $g(s)$.

Continue in this way through the transient and one period of
the common normalized color orbit. Unless a violation has
already occurred, every nonzero rule in the period has
$0<c_s<1$. If every rule in the period is zero, an infinite
fair continuation leaves the robots at distinct fixed
positions, so convergence fails.

Otherwise, the product $\Gamma$ of the solo distance ratios
over one period satisfies $0<\Gamma<1$. Advance both robots
to a common periodic color with a nonzero rule. Let $b$ Look
and Compute a nonzero displacement $v$, and delay its Move
until after a prescribed finite number of complete cycles
of $a$. This is admissible under $A_M$ by Corollary~E.6.
During the delay, $b$ remains fixed, while the private color
of $a$ follows its periodic orbit. Consequently, after
sufficiently many periods the vector $w$ from $b$ to $a$
satisfies $\|w\|<\|v\|/2$.

Keep $a$ stationary and let $b$ complete its pending Move.
The distance increases, since
\[
  \|w-v\|\ge\|v\|-\|w\|>\|w\|.
\]
After every finite violation, complete any pending cycle
and append an arbitrary fair, time-divergent continuation.
The construction uses neither the designated initial color
nor the original positions, provided that its starting
configuration satisfies the three stated conditions.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:mcv_in_ob_s}
$\mathrm{MCv}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Each robot moves to the midpoint of the two observed positions. Under
$\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ every round is atomic, so it suffices to follow the
configuration at the round boundaries. If only one robot is activated
in a round, it lands at the midpoint and the distance is halved; if
both are activated, they land on the same midpoint and the distance
becomes $0$. In either case the distance never increases, so the
monotonicity condition holds, and $d$ is at least halved in every
round, so $d(t)\to0$.
 
Moreover each landing point lies on the segment joining the two current
positions, so the segments $[a(t),b(t)]$ form a nested family of
compact sets whose diameters tend to $0$. Their intersection is a
single point $l$, and both robots converge to it, which is the
convergence condition.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:het}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions. Let $v_0,\dots,v_5$ be
the vertices of the regular hexagon having $a(0)$ and $b(0)$ as
opposite vertices, labelled counterclockwise from $v_0=a(0)$ and
$v_3=b(0)$, the indices being read modulo $6$. The cycles of the two
robots are
\[
  w_a:=(v_0,v_{-1},v_0,v_1),
  \qquad
  w_b:=(v_3,v_2,v_3,v_4).
\]
The first condition (perpetuity) requires each robot to perform
infinitely many nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations. The second condition (edge
traversal) requires each robot $r$, at every time at which it is not
moving, to stand at the vertex of its own cycle indexed by the number
$m_r(t)$ of nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations it has performed so far.
\begin{align*}
\Phi_{\mathrm{HET}}\equiv\big[\
  &\{\,\forall r\in\{a,b\}:\ \mathrm{moves}(r)=\infty\,\}\\
  &\text{and}\
  \{\,\forall r\in\{a,b\},\ \forall t\ge0:\
     \lnot\operatorname{Move}_r(t)\Rightarrow
     r(t)=w_r\bigl(m_r(t)\bmod4\bigr)\,\}\ \big]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:het_not_ob_f}
$\mathrm{HET}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ algorithm and consider the fully
synchronous execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}, in which the two
robots apply one and the same pair $(\lambda,\theta)$ in every round.
If $\lambda=0$ then $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$ and the perpetuity condition fails.

Assume $\lambda>0$. If either robot ever leaves its prescribed cycle,
the edge-traversal condition fails. Otherwise, normalizing the
circumradius of the hexagon to $1$, the configuration at the beginning
of round~$1$ is $(v_0,v_3)$ and at the beginning of round~$2$ it is
$(v_{-1},v_2)$. In round~$1$ the robot $a$ sees its peer at
$v_3-v_0$, of length $2$, and must perform the displacement
$v_{-1}-v_0$, of length $1$, so the required pair is
$(\lambda,\theta)=(1/2,+60^\circ)$. In round~$2$ it sees its peer at
$v_2-v_{-1}$, again of length $2$, and must perform the displacement
$v_0-v_{-1}$, of length $1$, so the required pair is
$(1/2,-60^\circ)$; the same two pairs are required of $b$ by the
symmetry of the two cycles. The two rounds therefore demand opposite
rotations relative to the peer, which a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$
cannot deliver, so the edge-traversal condition fails in one of the two
rounds.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:het_not_fs_r}
$\mathrm{HET}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R)$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The adversary chooses the alternating singleton activation
$\{a\},\{b\},\{a\},\dots$ with an empty fully synchronous prefix
(Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}).

\emph{First stage.} The configuration is unchanged until the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. The hexagon and the two cycles of
Definition~\ref{def:het} are carried onto each other by the rotation by
$\pi$ about the midpoint combined with exchanging $a$ and $b$, and this
rotation preserves chirality. The local input of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot is the
pair consisting of the relative position of the peer and its own state,
and does not contain the state of the peer, so in the normalized frame
of Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) both local inputs have the form
$(e,\text{own state})$ and are isomorphic. The two robots start from the
same initial state $s_0$, so $a$ in round $2k-1$ and $b$ in round $2k$
both pass from $s_{k-1}$ to $s_k$. If no state occurring in
$s_0,s_1,\dots$ produces a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, then $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$ and the
perpetuity condition fails. Let $j$ be the least index that produces a
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$; then $a$ performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in round $2j+1$,
from state $s_j$.

\emph{Second stage.} If the landing point of $a$ is not $v_{-1}$, the
edge-traversal condition $a(t)=w_a(1)=v_{-1}$ fails at the time
$m_a=1$. So assume $a$ lands at $v_{-1}$. Writing $R$ for the
circumradius of the hexagon, the edge length is $R$ and the diagonal
length is $2R$, so the constant of Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) is
\[
  \lambda_{s_j}=\frac{\|v_{-1}-v_0\|}{\|v_3-v_0\|}=\frac12 .
\]

\emph{Third stage.} The robot $b$, activated in round $2j+2$, has not
yet moved and is in state $s_j$. The robots have no common unit of
length, so in the normalized frame the local input of $b$ is the same
$(e,s_j)$ as that of $a$ in the second stage: the change of the
observed distance from $2R$ to $\|v_{-1}-v_3\|=\sqrt3\,R$ does not
appear in the local input. Hence $b$ applies the same
$\lambda_{s_j}=\tfrac12$ to its own peer vector $v_{-1}-v_3$, and the
length of its displacement is $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}R$. The landing point
required of $b$ by the edge-traversal condition is $w_b(1)=v_2$, with
$\|v_2-v_3\|=R$. Since $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}R\neq R$, the robot $b$ cannot
land at $v_2$ and the edge-traversal condition fails.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:het_not_fc_s}
$\mathrm{HET}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry the same color. If
$\lambda_\gamma=0$ for every color $\gamma$ occurring in that common
sequence, this fair execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$ and the perpetuity condition fails. Otherwise let
$\gamma$ be the first color with $\lambda_\gamma>0$ and truncate the
prefix at the round in which both robots carry $\gamma$; no nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ has occurred, so the configuration is still the initial one.

Now activate $a$ alone repeatedly (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}; under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
the robot that is not activated has no pending operation). The visible
state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot is the color of its peer, and $b$ is not
activated, so that color stays $\gamma$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the displacement rule of $a$ is the
single pair $(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$, and $\lambda_\gamma>0$
makes every activation a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. The cycle
$w_a=(v_0,v_{-1},v_0,v_1)$ requires the two successive steps
$v_0\to v_{-1}$ and $v_{-1}\to v_0$. With $b$ standing still at $v_3$,
the first of them approaches the peer, since
$\|v_{-1}-v_3\|=\sqrt3\,R<2R=\|v_0-v_3\|$, and the second retreats from
it. By Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule} a single pair
$(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$ cannot realize both, so the
edge-traversal condition fails.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:het_in_lu_r}
$\mathrm{HET}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^R)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Each robot records its position in its own cycle with a light of four
colors. Since a $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace$ robot sees both lights, it learns from the color
of its peer which vertex the peer currently occupies, so even under the
alternating singleton activations of an $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ execution it can
reconstruct the hexagon from the observed relative position and move to
the next vertex of its cycle. The destination is determined by the
relative position of the peer and by chirality alone and requires no
unit of length, so it is computable in each robot's own local frame.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:zcc}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions. The first condition
(convergence) requires the two robots to converge to a point $l$. The
second condition (collision freedom) requires each robot never to go,
as seen from its own initial position, farther than its peer. The third
condition (zig-zag) requires, with $f_r(t):=\|r(t)-r(0)\|$, that for
each robot $r$ there be times $0=t_{-1}<t_0<t_1<\cdots$ at which $f_r$
takes maxima $f_r(t_{2i})$ and minima $f_r(t_{2i+1})$ alternately, the
minima increasing.
\begin{align*}
\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}\equiv{}
 &\bigl[\,\{\,\exists l\in\mathbb R^2:\
   \lim_{t\to\infty}a(t)=\lim_{t\to\infty}b(t)=l\,\}\\
 &\quad\text{and}\ \{\,\forall r\in\{a,b\},\ \forall t\ge0:\
     f_r(t)\le\|\bar r(t)-r(0)\|\,\}\\
 &\quad\text{and}\ \{\,\forall r\in\{a,b\},\
   \exists\,0=t_{-1}<t_0<t_1<\cdots,\\
 &\quad\phantom{\text{and}\ \{\,}\forall i\ge0:\
   f_r(t_{2i-1})<f_r(t_{2i+1})<f_r(t_{2i})\,\}\,\bigr]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:zcc_not_ob_f}
$\mathrm{ZCC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
An $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F$ robot applies the same rule in every round, so it cannot
switch between the two directions that the zig-zag condition demands.
Consider the fully synchronous execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1},
let $m$ be the midpoint and $v:=a(0)-m$. The difference vector is
mapped in every round by the same similarity $I-2\lambda R_\theta$, of
ratio $c_2$ and rotation angle $\varphi$, and the midpoint is invariant
(Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii)), so $a(k)-m=c_2^{\,k}R_\varphi^{\,k}v$ and
$b(k)-m=-(a(k)-m)$.

If $\lambda=0$ the robots never move and $f_r\equiv0$.

If $c_2=0$ the two robots coincide at $m$ at the end of round~$1$, and
by Lemma~\ref{lem:keep-coincident} the coincidence is maintained. While
they coincide the observed peer position is $0$. If the local output is
then zero, the robots never move again and $f_r$ is constant from
round~$1$ on. Otherwise the adversary chooses their common global
displacement (Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(2)); choosing in every round one and
the same direction $w$ with $\langle w,v\rangle<0$ makes
$f_a(t)=\|a(t)-a(0)\|$ strictly increasing from round~$1$ on.

In both cases the restriction of $f_a$ to a tail is monotone, so the
zig-zag condition fails by the criterion stated after
Definition~\ref{def:zcc}.

Assume $\lambda\neq0$ and $c_2\neq0$. If
$\varphi\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(iii)
applied to the nonzero angle $\varphi$ there is $k\ge1$ with
$\cos(k\varphi)\le-\tfrac12<0$, whence
$\langle v,a(k)-m\rangle=c_2^{\,k}\cos(k\varphi)\|v\|^2<0$. Since
$b(k)-m=-(a(k)-m)$ and $a(0)=m+v$,
\[
  \|a(k)-a(0)\|^2-\|b(k)-a(0)\|^2
  =-4\,\langle v,a(k)-m\rangle>0 ,
\]
so at the end of round $k$ we have $f_a>\|b(k)-a(0)\|$ and the
collision-freedom condition fails. This is a safety violation at a
finite time.

If $\varphi\equiv0$, then $R_\varphi=I$ and $a(k)=m+c_2^{\,k}v$, so all
the positions of $a$ lie on the ray from $m$ through $a(0)$ and advance
monotonically along it, towards $m$ when $c_2<1$ and away from $a(0)$
when $c_2>1$; the value $c_2=1$ would force $\lambda=0$. Since
movements are rigid along segments, $f_a(t)=|\,c_2^{\,\cdot}-1\,|\,\|v\|$
interpolates monotonically within each round, so $f_a$ is monotone on
the whole execution and the zig-zag condition fails by the same
criterion. This is a liveness violation, witnessed by the infinite
fully synchronous execution itself.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}
$\mathrm{ZCC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
We prove a continuation property that will also be used in the
common-failure arguments. Fix the original initial positions
$a_0,b_0$. Suppose that a finite prefix ends with no pending
operation and with the robots lying in $[a_0,b_0]$ in their
original order. Their current colors need not be equal.
There is a fair, time-divergent continuation violating
$\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, with $a_0,b_0$ kept fixed.
 
First consider a configuration in which the robots coincide.
Activate them alternately, one complete cycle at a time.
If every output is zero, both positions remain constant forever,
so the zig-zag condition fails by the criterion stated after
Definition~\ref{def:zcc}. Otherwise, at the first nonzero
output, choose the local frame so that the moving robot increases
its distance from its own original initial position; this is
possible by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(2).
Its peer remains at the common position, so the collision-freedom
inequality is violated. Append an arbitrary fair tail.
We call this construction the \emph{coincidence continuation}.
 
Now suppose that the robots are distinct. Use alternating
singleton activations as the default schedule, with normalized
frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$. For the currently activated robot $r$, put
\[
  \sigma=1-\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}.
\]
If $\sigma\in(0,1]$, let the cycle complete and continue with the
default schedule. Such a cycle either leaves $r$ stationary or
moves it towards its peer without reaching it. Thus both robots
remain in the initial segment in their original order.
 
At the first output with $\sigma\notin(0,1]$, freeze the peer
and repeatedly activate $r$. Its peer's color is fixed, so the
same normalized rule is used until a coincidence occurs.
If $\sigma=0$, the first cycle reaches the peer and the
coincidence continuation above applies.
 
Assume $\sigma\ne0$, and write
$\sigma=c e^{\mathrm{i}\psi}$.
At the start of this repetition, let $\bar r$ denote the peer and
\[
  L=\|\bar r-r(0)\|,\qquad h=\|\bar r-r\|.
\]
The maintained order gives $L\ge h>0$. After $j$ repetitions,
\[
  \|r_j-r(0)\|^2
  =L^2+c^{2j}h^2-2Lc^j h\cos(j\psi).
\]
If $\psi\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, some finite $j$ satisfies
$\cos(j\psi)\le0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(iii)), so this quantity
exceeds $L^2$.
If $\psi\equiv0$, then necessarily $c>1$, and for sufficiently
large finite $j$ we again have $\|r_j-r(0)\|>L$.
In either case the stationary peer remains at distance $L$
from $r(0)$, so the collision-freedom condition fails.
Append an arbitrary fair tail.
 
Finally, if no output outside $(0,1]$ ever occurs, the default
alternating execution is fair and each
$f_r(t)=\|r(t)-r(0)\|$ is non-decreasing throughout.
The zig-zag condition therefore fails.
 
All infinite executions can be scheduled to be time-divergent,
and every exceptional repetition above is finite.
Applying this continuation property to the initial configuration
proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:zcc_not_fs_am}
$\mathrm{ZCC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We prove a continuation statement with the original initial
positions $a_0,b_0$ kept fixed. Suppose that no operation is
pending and that either the robots coincide, or their current
normalized color orbits have the same eventual cycle.
There is an admissible fair, time-divergent continuation
violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$.
 
If a safety violation has already occurred, append any fair
tail. If the robots coincide, use the coincidence continuation
from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}. Hence assume that
they are distinct and that safety has not yet failed.
 
If a state with solo ratio $c_1=0$ is reachable along the
normalized orbit of either robot, activate that robot alone
until it first lands on its stationary peer. All preceding
${\mathit{Look}}$s see distinct positions. At the resulting coincidence
neither robot has a pending operation, so the same coincidence
continuation applies.
 
We may therefore assume that all future solo ratios are
positive. Let $\Gamma>0$ be their product over the common
eventual color cycle. Consider the fair execution $E$ of
alternating singleton activations under normalized frames.
 
If $\Gamma\ge1$, then, after both color sequences have entered
their periodic parts, every block of one full period of each
robot multiplies the distance by $\Gamma^2\ge1$.
The distance thus has a positive subsequence bounded away
from zero, and convergence fails.
 
Assume $0<\Gamma<1$. If $E$ already violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, use $E$. Otherwise $E$ satisfies
both safety and convergence.
Put
\[
  e=\frac{b_0-a_0}{\|b_0-a_0\|},
  \qquad x_r(t)=\langle r(t),e\rangle .
\]
Adding the squared safety inequalities gives
\[
  2\langle a(t)-b(t),b_0-a_0\rangle\le0,
\]
hence $x_a(t)\le x_b(t)$ at every time.
 
The execution $E$ must contain a ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ with positive
displacement along $e$, or a ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ with negative
displacement along $e$. Indeed, otherwise $x_a$ would be
non-increasing and $x_b$ non-decreasing. Convergence would
then require both projections to be equal and constant.
Equality of the projections, together with safety, forces
both squared safety inequalities to be equalities.
During a singleton ${\mathit{Move}}$, the moving robot would consequently
have to remain on the intersection of two fixed circles
centered at $a_0$ and $b_0$. This finite set admits no
nonconstant continuous movement. Thus the distinct robots
could not converge, a contradiction.
Fix the first such ${\mathit{Move}}$ in $E$.
 
Suppose first that the selected ${\mathit{Move}}$ is a ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$
with displacement $v$ satisfying $\langle v,e\rangle<0$.
Follow $E$ through its ${\mathit{Look}}$ and ${\mathit{Comp}}$, but delay the start
of its ${\mathit{Move}}$. While $b$ stays fixed, activate $a$ through any
remaining transient part of its color orbit and then for
sufficiently many complete periods. Since $\Gamma<1$, the vector
$w$ from $b$ to $a$ can be made to satisfy
\[
  \|w\|<-\langle v,e\rangle/2.
\]
If safety fails during this finite interval, we are done.
Otherwise keep $a$ stationary and release the pending ${\mathit{Move}}$
of $b$. At its completion,
\[
  x_a-x_b=\langle w-v,e\rangle>0,
\]
contradicting the necessary projection order.
 
If the selected ${\mathit{Move}}$ is a ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ with
$\langle v,e\rangle>0$, delay that ${\mathit{Move}}$ and instead activate $b$
through any remaining transient part of its color orbit and then
for sufficiently many complete periods, bringing it arbitrarily
close to the fixed position of $a$. Choose the resulting
vector $w$ from $a$ to $b$ with
$\|w\|<\langle v,e\rangle/2$. Releasing the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ gives
\[
  x_a-x_b=\langle v-w,e\rangle>0,
\]
again violating safety.
 
All delays are finite and occur before the delayed ${\mathit{Move}}$
starts, as permitted by $A_M$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}.
No moving robot is stopped inside its ${\mathit{Move}}$.
After a finite violation, complete any pending operation
and append an arbitrary fair, time-divergent tail.
The initial configuration satisfies the continuation
hypotheses, which proves the stated impossibility.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:zcc_in_fs_s}
$\mathrm{ZCC}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{S})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:ZCC_FS_S}.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The algorithm of~\cite[Lemma~27]{NNW-SSS2025}, which approaches by
$D/2$ and retreats by $D/4$, makes the two robots coincide at the
midpoint when they are activated simultaneously, after which every ${\mathit{Move}}$
is zero and the zig-zag condition fails. We therefore approach by $D/4$
and retreat by $D/8$. Every movement takes place on the line through
$a(0)$ and $b(0)$, so we put a coordinate $x$ on that line with
$x_a(0)=0$ and $x_b(0)=1$, and write $D:=x_b-x_a$.

\emph{(i) The order is preserved.} Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ each round is atomic,
so the destinations of a round are computed from the configuration at
its beginning. The factor by which $D$ changes in one round is $1/2$
when both approach, $3/4$ when only one approaches, $7/8$ when one
approaches and the other retreats, $9/8$ when only one retreats, and
$5/4$ when both retreat; all of these are positive. Moreover the two
movement segments of a round are disjoint, since $a$ never goes beyond
$x_a+D/4$ while $b$ never goes below $x_b-D/4=x_a+3D/4$. Hence
$x_a(t)<x_b(t)$ at every time, movements included.

\emph{(ii) No robot leaves the outer side of its own initial position.}
Let $D_1$ be the distance at the ${\mathit{Look}}$ of some approach of $a$ and
$D_2$ the distance at the ${\mathit{Look}}$ of its next retreat. After the approach
round the distance is at most $7D_1/8$, and while $a$ is not activated
the robot $b$ alternates approach and retreat, so the distance
increases by a factor of at most $9/8$. Hence
$D_2\le\tfrac{63}{64}D_1$, and the retreat amount $D_2/8$ is smaller
than the preceding approach amount $D_1/4$. Therefore the position of
$a$ after each retreat is larger than its position before the preceding
approach, and inductively $x_a(t)\ge0$. Symmetrically $x_b(t)\le1$.

\emph{(iii) The collision-freedom condition.} By~(i) and~(ii) we have
$0\le x_a(t)<x_b(t)\le1$, so
$f_a(t)=x_a(t)<x_b(t)=\|b(t)-a(0)\|$, and symmetrically for $b$.

\emph{(iv) The convergence condition.} Give weight $1$ to the state
$\mathrm{A}$ and weight $6/5$ to the state $\mathrm{B}$, and put
$H:=D\cdot w_a\cdot w_b$. The factor by which $H$ changes in one round
is $\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac65=\tfrac9{10}$ when only one approaches,
$\tfrac98\cdot\tfrac56=\tfrac{15}{16}$ when only one retreats,
$\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{36}{25}=\tfrac{18}{25}$ when both approach,
$\tfrac54\cdot\tfrac{25}{36}=\tfrac{125}{144}$ when both retreat, and
$\tfrac78$ when one approaches and the other retreats; all of these are
at most $\tfrac{15}{16}$. At least one robot is activated in every
round, and $w_a,w_b\in[1,6/5]$, so $D\to0$ geometrically. Each
displacement is at most $D/4$, so the total length travelled by each
robot is finite and both converge to one and the same point $l$.

\emph{(v) The zig-zag condition.} By~(i) we have $D>0$, so every
activation produces a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, and by fairness each robot performs
infinitely many approaches and retreats alternately. By~(ii) we have
$x_a\ge0$, so an approach of $a$ increases $f_a$ and a retreat
decreases it. Let $t_{k-1}$ be the landing time of the $k$-th ${\mathit{Move}}$ of
$a$, with $t_{-1}:=0$. Then $[t_{2i-1},t_{2i}]$ is an approach and
$[t_{2i},t_{2i+1}]$ a retreat, and each ${\mathit{Move}}$ progresses monotonically
towards its destination, so $f_a$ takes the maxima $f_a(t_{2i})$ and
the minima $f_a(t_{2i+1})$ alternately. By~(ii) the position after each
retreat is larger than the position after the previous retreat, so
$f_a(t_{2i+1})>f_a(t_{2i-1})$. The same holds for $b$.

Finally the displacement is a fixed ratio of the observed distance, so
it requires no unit of length, and the state is private, so the
algorithm is admissible in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:vec}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions. The sequence of
configurations $C_i=(a_i,b_i)$, the vectors $d_i:=b_i-a_i$, the squares
$Q_i$ with $Q_{-1}:=\mathbb R^2$, and the rotations $R_\phi$ are
defined as in Definition~\ref{def:sro}. A vector $u$ is \emph{orthogonal
to $d_0$}, written $u\perp d_0$, if $u\neq0$ and $\langle u,d_0\rangle=0$.
The first condition (attainment) requires $d_i\perp d_0$ for some $i$.
The second condition (transition) requires that for every $i$ the
vector $d_{i+1}$ be equal to $d_i$, or its clockwise $90^\circ$
rotation, or its clockwise $45^\circ$ rotation scaled by $2^{\mp1/2}$,
and that $a_{i+1},b_{i+1}\in Q_{i-1}$. The third condition (stopping)
requires that if at a time at which both robots are at rest the segment
is orthogonal to $d_0$, then neither robot ever moves again.
\begin{align*}
\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}\equiv\big[\
 &\{\,\exists i\ge0:\ d_i\perp d_0\,\}\\
 &\text{and}\ \Bigl\{\,\forall i\ge0:\
   d_{i+1}\in\{d_i,\ R_{-90^\circ}d_i,\
     2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i,\ 2^{1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i\}\\
 &\qquad\wedge\bigl(a_{i+1},b_{i+1}\in Q_{i-1}\bigr)\,\Bigr\}\\
 &\text{and}\ \{\,\forall t\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}:\
   b(t)-a(t)\perp d_0\Rightarrow
   \forall t'\ge t:\ a(t')=a(t)\ \wedge\ b(t')=b(t)\,\}\ \big]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:vec_not_ob_f}
$\mathrm{VEC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Once an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F$ robot moves it keeps moving in every round and cannot
stop when the orthogonal configuration is reached. Consider the fully
synchronous execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}. If $\lambda=0$ the
robots do not move, the sequence reduces to $C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp
d_0$, so the attainment condition fails. If $c_2=0$ the two robots
coincide in round~$1$ and $d_1=0$, while all the transitions permitted
by the second condition are nonzero, so that condition fails. If
$c_2>0$ both robots perform a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in every round, so even if
$d_k\perp d_0$ holds at the end of some round they move again in the
next one and the stopping condition fails; and if no such round exists
the attainment condition fails.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:vec_not_fc_s}
$\mathrm{VEC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry the same color. If
$\lambda_\gamma=0$ for every color $\gamma$ occurring in that sequence,
this fair execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, the sequence reduces to
$C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition fails.
Otherwise let $\gamma$ be the first color with $\lambda_\gamma>0$ and
truncate the prefix at the round in which both robots carry $\gamma$;
the configuration is still the initial one.

Now activate $a$ alone repeatedly (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}; under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
the robot that is not activated has no pending operation). The color of
$b$ stays $\gamma$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the robot $a$
applies the same pair $(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$ at every
activation. With the peer at rest, a single nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ can satisfy
the transition condition only by making $d_{i+1}$ equal to
$R_{-90^\circ}d_i$ or to $2^{\mp1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i$, and each of
these applies the same rotation to $d$ at every activation. Hence $a$
reaches a configuration with $d_i\perp d_0$ in at most two moves, and
since $\lambda_\gamma>0$ it moves again at the very next activation, so
the stopping condition fails.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:vec_not_fs_a}
$\mathrm{VEC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A)$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:atomicity-equivalences} we have
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_{LC}}$, so it suffices to exhibit an admissible
$A_{LC}$ execution. Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible
under $A_{LC}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry
the same state. If $\lambda_s=0$ for every state $s$ occurring in that
common sequence, this fair execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, the
sequence reduces to $C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment
condition fails. Otherwise let $s$ be the first state with
$\lambda_s>0$ and truncate the prefix at the round in which both robots
carry $s$; no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ has occurred, so the configuration is still
the initial one.

Activate $a$ alone. It performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ from $p_B:=a_0$ to some
$p_E\neq p_B$. The robot $b$ has finished its cycle and has no pending
operation, so the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:mid} are met and, for
each $\mu\in(0,1)$, there is an execution in which $b$ observes $a$ at
$p_\mu=(1-\mu)p_B+\mu p_E$. Let the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ begin before the ${\mathit{Move}}$
of $a$ ends; then the two ${\mathit{Move}}$ intervals overlap, so no time of $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$
occurs between the two landings and the configuration after both
landings is $C_1$. In state $s$ the robot $b$ lands, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1), at $b_0+\lambda_sR_{\theta_s}(p_\mu-b_0)$, so
\[
  d_1(\mu)=b_0+\lambda_sR_{\theta_s}(p_\mu-b_0)-p_E
\]
is an affine function of $\mu$ whose slope
$\lambda_sR_{\theta_s}(p_E-p_B)$ is nonzero because $\lambda_s>0$.
Hence a suitable coordinate $h(\mu)$ of $d_1$ is continuous and
non-constant on $(0,1)$. For $i=0$ we have $Q_{-1}=\mathbb R^2$, so the
transition condition only requires
$d_1\in\{d_0,R_{-90^\circ}d_0,2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_0,
2^{1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_0\}$, and the corresponding values of $h$ are
only four. By Corollary~\ref{cor:continuum} there is a $\mu$ avoiding
those four values, and for it the transition condition fails.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:vec_in_fs_am}
$\mathrm{VEC}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:VEC_FS_AM}.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Since $A_M$ forbids a ${\mathit{Look}}$ of one robot during a ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the other,
every configuration observed at a ${\mathit{Look}}$ is one of the terms of the
sequence $(C_i)$.

Suppose first that the ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $b$ precedes the landing of $a$. Then
both robots take as destinations the two remaining vertices of the
square $Q_0$. If there is a time at which both robots are at rest
between the two landings, the intermediate configuration has
$d_1=2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_0$, and the next one has
$d_2=R_{-90^\circ}d_0=2^{1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_1$; if there is no such
time, the two landings produce a single term with
$d_1=R_{-90^\circ}d_0$.

Suppose instead that the ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $b$ follows the landing of $a$. Then
$d_1=2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_0$, and $b$ moves to a vertex of $Q_1$,
giving $d_2=2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_1$.

In every case, each transition has one of the permitted forms.
In the first case, the final positions are the two remaining
vertices of $Q_0$; in the second case, they are a vertex
and the centre of $Q_0$.
Thus, when an intermediate configuration exists, both positions
of $C_2$ belong to $Q_0$, as required.
The containment condition for the first transition is vacuous
since $Q_{-1}=\mathbb{R}^2$.
                                                                  
                                                                      
                                                                     
                                                          
The final
segment is orthogonal to $d_0$, which is the attainment condition, and
both robots are then in state $2$ and never move again; no earlier
segment is orthogonal to $d_0$, since the only intermediate one is at
$45^\circ$. Hence the stopping condition holds as well.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:six-dmsd}
Let $D_0=\|a(0)-b(0)\|>0$, and let
\(
  \mathbb Z[1/2]
  =\{m/2^k\mid m\in\mathbb Z,\ k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\}
\)
be the set of dyadic rationals. Using the moving predicate of
Section~\ref{subsec:problems-relationships}, define the set of \emph{joint stops}
\(
  \Sigma_{ab}
  =\{t\ge0\mid
       \lnot\operatorname{Move}_a(t)\land\lnot\operatorname{Move}_b(t)\},
\)
the set of times at which neither robot is inside a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
operation. Every execution must satisfy
\begin{align}
  &\forall t\in\Sigma_{ab}:\quad
      \frac{\|a(t)-b(t)\|}{D_0}\in\mathbb Z[1/2],
      \tag{D1}\label{eq:dmsd-dyadic}\\
  &\exists t\in\Sigma_{ab}:\quad
      \|a(t)-b(t)\|<D_0.
      \tag{D2}\label{eq:dmsd-progress}
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:dmsd_not_fs_a}
$\mathrm{DMSD}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
The argument extends~\cite[Lemma~6]{KSW-2-robot} to a general
displacement $(\lambda,\theta)$ including a rotation, and to the
internal states of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:atomicity-equivalences} we have
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A}\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_{LC}}$, so it suffices to exhibit, for an
arbitrary $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, an admissible $A_{LC}$
execution that violates $\mathrm{DMSD}$.

In the normalized frame of Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1), a robot in state
$s$ has displacement $\lambda_s R_{\theta_s}(w)$, where $w$ is the
vector to its peer, and its next state is determined by $s$ alone. The
local coordinate system may be chosen anew at each activation, and we
supply this frame independently at every activation below. Normalize
$a(0)=0$, $b(0)=e_1$ and $D_0=1$.

\emph{First stage.} Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible
under $A_{LC}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry
the same state; let $s_0,s_1,\dots$ be that common state sequence. If
$\lambda_s=0$ for every state $s$ occurring in the sequence, this fair
execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so $a$ and $b$ stay at their
initial positions and $\|a(t)-b(t)\|=D_0$ for every $t\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$, which
violates (D2). Otherwise let $s$ be the first state with
$\lambda_s>0$ and truncate the prefix at the round in which both robots
carry $s$; write $\lambda:=\lambda_s>0$ and $R:=R_{\theta_s}$. No
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ has occurred, so the robots are at their initial positions
and the ratio at every earlier joint stop is $1\in\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$.

\emph{Second stage.} Activate $b$ alone. It performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ to
\[
  p_E=e_1-\lambda Re_1\neq b(0),
\]
and for $\mu\in(0,1)$ we put
$p_\mu:=(1-\mu)b(0)+\mu p_E=e_1-\mu\lambda Re_1$. The robot $a$ has
finished its cycle and has no pending operation, so the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:mid} are met and there is an execution in which $a$
performs a ${\mathit{Look}}$ at a time when $b$ is at $p_\mu$. In state $s$ the
robot $a$ then lands at
\[
  \lambda Rp_\mu=\lambda Re_1-\mu\lambda^2R^2e_1 .
\]
Let both ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations complete, delay the next ${\mathit{Look}}$ of each robot
by a finite amount, and append a fair tail. Throughout that delay
neither robot is inside a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so the whole interval is
contained in $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$, and $m_b\ge1$ there.

\emph{Third stage.} On that interval the distance equals
\[
  h(\mu)=\|c+\mu w\|,\qquad
  c:=e_1-2\lambda Re_1,\qquad
  w:=\lambda^2R^2e_1\neq0 .
\]
Indeed $\|c+\mu w\|^2$ is a quadratic polynomial in $\mu$ with leading
coefficient $\|w\|^2>0$, so $h$ is continuous and non-constant on
$(0,1)$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:continuum} there is a $\mu$ with
$h(\mu)/D_0\notin\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$, and the corresponding execution violates (D1).
Since (D1) is of the form $\forall t\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$, a single violating time
suffices, and the joint stops produced in the first two stages need not
be inspected.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:dmsd_not_ob_a}
$\mathrm{DMSD}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
In $\mathcal Q$ the class $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A}$ lies below $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A}$, so this
follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:dmsd_not_fs_a} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-is-upset}.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:dmsd_in_ob_am}
$\mathrm{DMSD}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M})$, as witnessed by the Go-to-midpoint
algorithm.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Each robot moves to the midpoint of its own position and the observed
position of its peer. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:atomicity-equivalences} we have
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_{CM}}\equiv\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}$, so it is enough to argue under $A_M$.

\emph{Observed positions.} Under $A_M$ a ${\mathit{Look}}$ of one robot never falls
inside the closed interval $[t_B,t_E]$ of a ${\mathit{Move}}$ operation of the
other, so every observed position is an initial position or the landing
point of a completed nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. Moreover a robot is itself at rest
at its own ${\mathit{Look}}$, since $t_E(r,k-1)<t_L(r,k)<t_B(r,k)$. Consequently
every ${\mathit{Look}}$ time belongs to $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$.

\emph{Condition (D1).} We claim that at every time the position of each
robot is of the form $(1-\alpha)a(0)+\alpha b(0)$ with
$\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$, whenever that robot is not inside a ${\mathit{Move}}$ operation.
This holds initially with $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha=1$. A robot lands at
the midpoint of its own position and an observed position, and by the
previous paragraph both are of the stated form; the midpoint of
$(1-\alpha)a(0)+\alpha b(0)$ and $(1-\beta)a(0)+\beta b(0)$ is the
point with parameter $(\alpha+\beta)/2\in\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$. Since the destination
is computed from the snapshot taken at the ${\mathit{Look}}$, a delayed ${\mathit{Move}}$ does
not change the landing point (Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}), so the claim
is preserved even when a snapshot is stale. Hence for $t\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ we get
$\|a(t)-b(t)\|=|\beta-\alpha|\,D_0$ with $\beta-\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$, which
is (D1).

\emph{Condition (D2).} Every landing point is a midpoint of two points
of the segment $[a(0),b(0)]$, so by induction both robots always lie in
that segment. By fairness some robot, say $a$, is activated first; at
its ${\mathit{Look}}$ the two robots are still at their initial positions, so the
