observed distance is $D_0>0$ and $a$ performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, landing
at the midpoint $m$ of $a(0)$ and $b(0)$. Let $t:=t_L(a,2)$ be the next
${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$, which exists by fairness and satisfies
$t_E(a,1)<t<t_B(a,2)$, so $a(t)=m$; by the first paragraph
$t\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$. Since $b(t)$ lies in $[a(0),b(0)]$ and $m$ is the midpoint
of that segment,
\[
  \|a(t)-b(t)\|\le \tfrac{D_0}{2}<D_0 ,
\]
which is (D2).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:cv}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions and converge to a point
$l$.
\[
  \Phi_{\mathrm{Cv}}
  \equiv
  \{\,\exists l\in\mathbb R^2:\
    \lim_{t\to\infty}a(t)=\lim_{t\to\infty}b(t)=l\,\}
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:cv_in_ob_a}
$\mathrm{Cv}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:Cv_OB_A}.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Algorithm~\ref{alg:Cv_OB_A} is the two-robot case of the gravitational
algorithm of~\cite{CP}: each robot moves to the center of
gravity of the configuration it has observed, which for two robots is
the midpoint of the two observed positions. The destination is
determined by the midpoint alone, so it requires neither a unit of
length nor chirality, and it is computed from the current snapshot
alone, so the algorithm is admissible in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$.

All the motion takes place on the line through $a(0)$ and $b(0)$, since
the midpoint of two points of that line lies on it. Let $H(t)$ be the
convex hull, an interval of that line, of the current positions of the
two robots together with 
the destinations determined by all Looks whose cycles
have not yet completed at time $t$, including cycles
awaiting Compute
                                             
                                                      
We claim that
$H$ is non-increasing. Indeed, the destination determined by a \ensuremath{\mathit{Look}}\xspace is the
midpoint of two positions occupied at that time, both of which belong
to $H$ at that time, so the destination belongs to $H$ as well; and
every movement is a rigid motion along a segment whose two endpoints
belong to $H$, so it never leaves $H$. In particular
$H(t)\subseteq H(0)=[a(0),b(0)]$ for every $t$, which is the
containment hypothesis of~\cite{CP}.

Executions are fair, so each robot performs infinitely many $\ensuremath{\mathit{LCM}}\xspace$
cycles, and the adversary's freedom in $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ is exactly the one
allowed there: the destination carried into a ${\mathit{Move}}$ may have been
computed from a stale snapshot, and the two robots may be in flight
simultaneously. Under these hypotheses the gravitational algorithm
converges~\cite{CP}, so there is a point $l$ with
$a(t),b(t)\to l$, which is $\Phi_{\mathrm{Cv}}$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:epg-forces-simultaneity}
Suppose $\tfrac12(a_{i+1}+b_{i+1})=c_0=\tfrac12(a_i+b_i)$. Then
$a_{i+1}+b_{i+1}=a_i+b_i$, so $b_{i+1}=b_i$ would force $a_{i+1}=a_i$ and hence
$C_{i+1}=C_i$. Consecutive terms of the sequence being distinct, every step of
the sequence therefore moves \emph{both} robots. Equivalently, a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
performed by one robot while the other is stationary across the surrounding
joint stops displaces the center of gravity by half that displacement.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:epg}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions. The first condition (one
expansion) requires the joint-stop sequence to consist of exactly the two terms
$C_0$ and $C_1$. The second condition (expansion preserving gravity) requires
the step from $C_0$ to $C_1$ to keep the center of gravity at $c_0$ and to
double the segment. The third condition (stopping) requires both robots to
remain stationary from some time on.
\begin{align*}
  \Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}}\equiv\bigl[\ 
    &\{\,(C_i)_{i\ge0}\ \text{has exactly the two terms}\ C_0,C_1\,\}\\
    &\text{and}\ \bigl\{\,\tfrac12(a_1+b_1)=c_0\ \text{and}\ d_1=2d_0\,\bigr\}\\
    &\text{and}\ \{\,\forall r\in\{a,b\}:\mathrm{Stopped}(r)\,\}\ \bigr]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:epg-bounds}
Under the assumptions of this paper,
\[
  \mathrm{EPG}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F),
  \qquad
  \mathrm{EPG}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)\cup\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^R).
\]
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
The positive statement is Lemma~\ref{lem:epg_in_lu_f}, and the two
negative ones are Lemmas~\ref{lem:epg_not_ob_f}
and~\ref{lem:epg_not_lu_r} below.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:epg_in_lu_f}
$\mathrm{EPG}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{F})$, as witnessed by Algorithm~\ref{alg:epg} in
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{F}$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Both robots start with color $0$, so in round~$1$ both execute the first
branch. A robot at $p$ observing its peer at the local coordinate $v$ lands at
$p+L^{-1}(-v/2)=p-\tfrac12(p_{\bar r}-p_{r})$, that is, it moves away from the
peer by half the observed distance; the displacement is determined by the
snapshot alone and needs neither a unit of length nor chirality, so
Algorithm~\ref{alg:epg} is admissible in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$. The two displacements are
$\tfrac12(a_0-b_0)$ and $\tfrac12(b_0-a_0)$, opposite and of equal norm, so
after round~$1$
\[
  \tfrac12(a_1+b_1)=\tfrac12(a_0+b_0)=c_0,
  \qquad
  d_1=2d_0 ,
\]
which is the second condition. Both displacements are nonzero because
$d_0\neq0$, and under \textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace{} the two ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations occupy the same round, so
no time of $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ lies strictly between the two boundaries of round~$1$ and
$C_1=(a_1,b_1)$ is the term of the sequence following $C_0$.

Both robots end round~$1$ with color $1$ and thereafter execute the second
branch, so every later ${\mathit{Move}}$ is zero. The configuration never changes again, the
joint-stop sequence consists of exactly $C_0$ and $C_1$, and both robots are
permanently stationary. Hence $\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}}$ holds, and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^F$ is the class $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:equ-FCOMF-by-FSTAF}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:epg_not_ob_f}
$\mathrm{EPG}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under \textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace. An $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$
robot has no color and no memory, so its output at an activation is a function
of the observed local position $v$ of the peer alone; write it $f(v)$. The
adversary may give a robot a frame in which the peer appears at any prescribed
nonzero local position (Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1)). Fix frames for round~$1$ and
let $v_a,v_b$ be the resulting local inputs.

If $C_1$, the configuration at the end of round~$1$, violates
$\tfrac12(a_1+b_1)=c_0$ or $d_1=2d_0$, the second condition fails, provided
$C_1\neq C_0$. If $C_1=C_0$, both $f(v_a)$ and $f(v_b)$ are zero; repeating the
same frames in every round leaves the configuration unchanged forever, the
joint-stop sequence has the single term $C_0$, and the first condition fails.

So assume $C_1\neq C_0$ and the second condition holds at $i=0$. Then
$d_1=2d_0\neq0$, so in round~$2$ the adversary may choose a frame for $a$ with
$L'_a(b_1-a_1)=v_a$ and one for $b$ with $L'_b(a_1-b_1)=v_b$. Both robots
receive the local input they received in round~$1$, and by determinism they
output $f(v_a)$ and $f(v_b)$ again. At least one of these is nonzero, since
$C_1\neq C_0$, so the configuration at the end of round~$2$ differs from $C_1$
and contributes a third term to the joint-stop sequence. The first condition
fails.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:epg_not_lu_r}
$\mathrm{EPG}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2) with $K=R$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:epg_profile}
$\mathsf{Prof}(\mathrm{EPG})=\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{F}$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Table~\ref{tab:PP13} gives
$\operatorname{Max}(\mathcal Q\setminus\mathord{\uparrow}\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{F})=\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F},\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{R}\}$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-certificate} with
Lemma~\ref{lem:epg_in_lu_f} on the positive side and
Lemmas~\ref{lem:epg_not_ob_f} and~\ref{lem:epg_not_lu_r} on the negative side.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:epgs}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions, and $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$, the sequence
$(C_i)_{i\ge0}$, $c_0$ and $d_i$ are as in Appendix~\ref{app:epg}. The first
condition (perpetuity) requires the sequence to be infinite. The second
condition (expansion preserving gravity) requires every step of the sequence to
keep the center of gravity at $c_0$ and to double the segment.
\begin{align*}
  \Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}\equiv\bigl[\ 
    &\{\,(C_i)_{i\ge0}\ \text{is infinite}\,\}\\
    &\text{and}\ \Bigl\{\,\forall i\ge0:\ 
       \tfrac12(a_{i+1}+b_{i+1})=c_0\ \text{and}\ d_{i+1}=2d_i\,\Bigr\}\ \bigr]
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:epg-vs-cge}
Center of Gravity Expansion and its perpetual variant
\cite{BuFKPSW22,FSW19} prescribe each landing point by a coordinatewise floor,
which makes the expansion irregular and moves the center of gravity. That
formulation cannot be carried over to the present model. Evaluated on a lattice
common to the two robots, as in the global formula of \cite{BuFKPSW22}, the
destination is not computable under variable disorientation, so the profile
would be empty; evaluated on each robot's own lattice, the predicate refers to
the local frames chosen by the adversary and is therefore no longer a predicate
on the trajectory, contrary to
Section~\ref{subsec:problems-relationships}. We keep the exact doubling, drop
the floor, and recover the same boundary by requiring the center of gravity to
be preserved at every joint stop. By
Remark~\ref{rem:epg-forces-simultaneity} that requirement rules out a solo
expansion, which is the role the floor played in \cite{FSW19}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:epgs_in_ob_f}
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$, as witnessed by Algorithm~\ref{alg:epgs}.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
The destination is computed from the current snapshot alone and requires
neither a unit of length nor chirality, so the algorithm is admissible in
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$. We show by induction on $k\ge0$ that at the start of round $k+1$ the two
robots are stationary with no pending operation in the configuration
\[
  \Gamma_k:=\bigl(c_0+2^{k}(a_0-c_0),\ c_0+2^{k}(b_0-c_0)\bigr).
\]
This holds for $k=0$. Assume it for $k$ and let $\delta:=2^{k}d_0\neq0$ be the
distance. Under \textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace{} both robots are activated in round $k+1$ and compute
from the same configuration; each moves away from the peer by $\delta/2$, so
the two displacements are opposite and of equal norm. The midpoint is therefore
unchanged and the difference vector is doubled, which is $\Gamma_{k+1}$, and
both ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations are nonzero since $\delta\neq0$.

The two ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations of a round occupy the same interval, so no time of
$\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ lies strictly between consecutive round boundaries at which a Move
occurs, and the joint-stop sequence is exactly $(\Gamma_k)_{k\ge0}$. It is
infinite, consecutive terms are distinct because $\delta\neq0$, and every step
satisfies $\tfrac12(a_{k+1}+b_{k+1})=c_0$ and $d_{k+1}=2d_k$. Hence
$\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}$ holds.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:epgs_not_lu_r}
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2) with $K=R$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:osp}
Two robots $a,b$ start from distinct positions, and $d(t)$ is their
distance as in Definition~\ref{def:mcv}.
For $r\in\{a,b\}$, let $m_r(t)$ denote the number of nonzero
Move operations completed by $r$ by time $t$.

The task $\mathrm{OSPO}$ requires the robots to remain at distinct
positions throughout the execution and to alternate approach and
retreat forever, starting with approach at time $0$.
Each phase is delimited by joint stops, and each robot completes
exactly one nonzero Move during that phase.
More precisely, there is a strictly increasing sequence
$(t_j)_{j\ge0}$ of joint stops, with $t_0=0$ and $t_j\to\infty$,
such that on each interval $[t_{2i},t_{2i+1}]$ the distance is
monotonically non-increasing and decreases overall, and on each
interval $[t_{2i+1},t_{2i+2}]$ it is monotonically non-decreasing
and increases overall.
The move-count condition is
$m_r(t_{j+1})-m_r(t_j)=1$ for every $j\ge0$ and $r\in\{a,b\}$.

\begin{align*}
\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}\equiv{}
  &\{\,\forall t\ge0:\ d(t)>0\,\}\\
  &{}\land\exists\,(t_j)_{j\ge0}\subseteq\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}:\ \Bigl[
    t_0=0,\quad t_j\to\infty,\\
  &\qquad \forall j\ge0:\ t_j<t_{j+1},\\
  &\qquad \forall j\ge0\ \forall r\in\{a,b\}:
       m_r(t_{j+1})-m_r(t_j)=1,\\
  &\qquad \forall i\ge0:\ \Bigl(
       d(t_{2i+1})<d(t_{2i})\\
  &\qquad\qquad {}\land
       \forall h,h'\in[t_{2i},t_{2i+1}]:
       \bigl(h<h'\Rightarrow d(h')\le d(h)\bigr)\\
  &\qquad\qquad {}\land d(t_{2i+2})>d(t_{2i+1})\\
  &\qquad\qquad {}\land
       \forall h,h'\in[t_{2i+1},t_{2i+2}]:
       \bigl(h<h'\Rightarrow d(h')\ge d(h)\bigr)
       \Bigr)\Bigr].
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:osp_not_ob_f}
$\mathrm{OSPO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F)$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Fix any deterministic $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ algorithm and take the fully synchronous
execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}, with normalized local frames at
every ${\mathit{Look}}$ while the robots are distinct and with time-divergent
round timings.

If the two robots ever occupy the same point, the collision-freedom
condition of $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails at a finite time. This covers
$c_2=0$, where they coincide at the end of round~$1$, and also the
case in which they meet while travelling inside a round.

Otherwise $d(t)>0$ throughout. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1} every joint
stop of the execution carries one of the round-boundary distances
$d(k)=c_2^{\,k}d(0)$, so the restriction of $d$ to $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ is monotone.
The turning times required by $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ are joint stops,
so by the criterion stated after Definition~\ref{def:osp} their
distances cannot alternate between strict decrease and strict increase.
This admissible fair execution violates $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:osp_not_fc_s}
$\mathrm{OSPO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Fix any deterministic $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ algorithm.
Use normalized local frames and activate both robots synchronously
as long as their computed displacements are zero.
Their colors remain equal during this prefix.

If no nonzero displacement ever occurs, continuing synchronously
gives an admissible fair execution with no movement, which violates
$\mathrm{OSPO}$.
Otherwise, let $\gamma$ be the common color immediately before
the first round that would produce nonzero displacements.
Instead of activating both robots in that round, activate $a$
alone for two complete consecutive cycles, keeping $b$ inactive.

If a collision occurs, $\mathrm{OSPO}$ already fails.
Otherwise, $b$ remains at its initial position with color $\gamma$.
At both Looks of $a$, normalization presents the same relative
position and the same peer color.
Since an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot cannot read its own color, it computes
the same nonzero normalized displacement in both cycles.
At the completion time $T$ of the second Move,
\[
  m_a(T)=2,\qquad m_b(T)=0.
\]

In any execution satisfying $\mathrm{OSPO}$, the first phase
starts at $t_0=0$ and ends at a joint stop $t_1$ with
$m_a(t_1)=m_b(t_1)=1$.
Since $b$ has not moved by time $T$, such a $t_1$ would have
to satisfy $t_1>T$; but then $m_a(t_1)\ge2$, a contradiction.
Thus the finite prefix already makes $\mathrm{OSPO}$ impossible.
Append any admissible fair, time-divergent $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ continuation.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lem:osp_not_fs_s}
$\mathrm{OSPO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S)$.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Fix any deterministic $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ algorithm and use normalized
local frames whenever the robots are distinct.
Under these observations, a robot's next private state and
normalized displacement depend only on its current private state.
Let
\[
  s_0,s_1,s_2,\ldots
\]
be the resulting state sequence from the designated initial state,
and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ be the displacement magnitude associated
with state $s_j$.

Suppose first that this sequence contains at least two nonzero
displacements. Activate $a$ alone until it completes its second
nonzero Move, while keeping $b$ inactive.
This takes finitely many cycles.
If a collision occurs, the collision-freedom condition fails.
Otherwise, at the completion time $T$,
\[
  m_a(T)=2,\qquad m_b(T)=0.
\]
No endpoint $t_1$ of the first phase can then satisfy
$m_a(t_1)=m_b(t_1)=1$: it cannot occur by time $T$ because
$b$ has not moved, and it cannot occur later because
$a$ has already moved twice.
The violation persists under any admissible fair,
time-divergent continuation.

Suppose instead that the state sequence contains at most one
nonzero displacement.
Choose an infinite fully synchronous execution with normalized
frames. If the robots collide, $\mathrm{OSPO}$ fails.
Otherwise, each robot follows the state sequence above and
completes at most one nonzero Move.
This is incompatible with infinitely many phases, each requiring
one nonzero Move from each robot.
Hence this fair, time-divergent execution also violates
$\mathrm{OSPO}$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{lem:osp_in_fs_r}
$\mathrm{OSPO}\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R)$.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
\emph{The algorithm.}
Each robot keeps two private states, \texttt{approach} and
\texttt{retreat}, initially \texttt{approach}. Upon an activation, let
$p$ be its own position and $q$ the observed position of its peer. In
state \texttt{approach} its destination is $p+\tfrac14(q-p)$, in state
\texttt{retreat} it is $p-\tfrac14(q-p)$; in both cases it then
switches to the other state. The destination is a fixed fraction of
the observed displacement, so it depends neither on the orientation
nor on the unit distance of the local frame and is admissible under
variable disorientation. The two robots are always at distinct
positions, as shown below, so $q\neq p$ and every ${\mathit{Move}}$ is nonzero;
hence every activation increases $m_r$ by exactly one.

\emph{One round.}
Let $D>0$ be the distance at the start of a round, and for each robot
$r$ let $u_r\in[0,1]$ be the fraction of its movement segment covered
so far, set to $0$ before its ${\mathit{Move}}$ begins and to $1$ after its
completion; each $u_r$ is continuous and non-decreasing, and
$u_a+u_b$ runs from $0$ to the number of robots activated in the
round. If both robots are activated
and share their state, the distance during the round is
\[
  D\Bigl(1-\frac{u_a+u_b}{4}\Bigr)\ \text{(approach)},
  \qquad
  D\Bigl(1+\frac{u_a+u_b}{4}\Bigr)\ \text{(retreat)} ,
\]
since both displacements are collinear with the segment. Here
$u_a+u_b\in[0,2]$, so the approach factor lies in $[\tfrac12,1]$: the
distance is monotone in the required direction, stays positive, and
ends at $D/2$ or $3D/2$. If a single robot is activated, the same
expressions hold with $u_a+u_b\in[0,1]$, the approach factor lies in
$[\tfrac34,1]$, and the final distance is $3D/4$ or $5D/4$.

\emph{Phases.}
If the execution is fully synchronous forever, both robots always
share their state and successive rounds alternate between approach and
retreat; take each round as one phase.

Otherwise let $\ell\ge0$ be the length of the fully synchronous prefix,
after which the activations are alternating singletons
(Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}). Both robots share their state throughout the
prefix, and round $k\le\ell$ is an approach round exactly when $k$ is
odd; at the end of the prefix their common state is \texttt{approach}
exactly when $\ell$ is even. Partition the singleton tail into
consecutive pairs of rounds. In a pair the two robots are activated
once each; the second one has not yet switched, so both use the state
held in common at the start of the pair, and at the end of the pair
both hold the switched state. Take each such pair as one phase.
Consequently the first tail phase is an approach phase exactly when
$\ell$ is even, which for $\ell\ge1$ is the type opposite to round
$\ell$; the tail phases alternate, so the phase types alternate across
the whole execution, beginning with approach.

\emph{Within a phase.}
A phase of the first kind is a single round, treated above. A phase of
the second kind is two singleton rounds of the same type. Each of them
is monotone in the same direction and they agree at the round
boundary, so the distance is monotone on the whole phase; starting
from $D$ it ends at $\tfrac{9}{16}D$ in an approach phase and at
$\tfrac{25}{16}D$ in a retreat phase, so it also changes strictly.
In every case the distance stays positive, so $d(t)>0$ for all $t\ge0$.

\emph{The times $t_j$.}
Take $t_0=0$ and let $t_{j+1}$ be the end of the $(j+1)$-st phase.
Each phase ends at a round boundary, where neither robot is inside a
Move, so $t_j\in\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ for every $j$; the same holds at $t_0=0$, where
no cycle is pending. Each phase contains exactly one nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of
each robot, so
\(
  m_r(t_{j+1})-m_r(t_j)=1
\)
for every $j\ge0$ and $r\in\{a,b\}$. The phases exhaust the rounds of
the execution and each contains at least one round, so $t_j\to\infty$
by time divergence. Together with the monotonicity, strictness and
positivity established above, and with the first phase being an
approach phase, all conditions of Definition~\ref{def:osp} hold.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:six-cfsm}
Two robots $a$ and $b$, initially at distinct positions, must each
perform exactly one nonzero Move and remain stationary before that
Move begins and after it ends. They must never collide, including
during their movements. With $\operatorname{moves}(r)$ denoting the
number of nonzero Moves of robot $r$, the specification is
\[
  \Phi_{\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace}
  \equiv
  \bigl(\operatorname{moves}(a)=1\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\operatorname{moves}(b)=1\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\forall t\ge0:\ a(t)\ne b(t)\bigr).
\]
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{lem:cfsm_not_ob_f}
$\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace \notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be any $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ algorithm and consider the fully
synchronous execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}. Since an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot
has no visible state and the normalized local input of each robot is
the same in every round, the two robots apply one and the same pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$ in every round, and the configuration is updated by
the simultaneous contraction ratio $c_2=c_2(\lambda,\theta)$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii).

If $\lambda=0$, no robot ever performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=\mathrm{moves}(b)=0$ and the single-move condition fails. If
$c_2=0$, that is $(\lambda,\theta)=(1/2,0)$, both robots land on the
common midpoint in round~$1$, so $a(t)=b(t)$ at that time and the
collision-free condition fails. If $c_2>0$, the distance stays
positive, hence $\lambda>0$ makes every round a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ for both
robots and $\mathrm{moves}(a)=\mathrm{moves}(b)=\infty$, so the single-move condition
fails again. The execution is fair in all three cases.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{lem:cfsm_not_fc_s}
$\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace \notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be any deterministic $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ algorithm.

\emph{First stage.} Run a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible
under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry
the same color, and we write $\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\dots$ for that common
color sequence. If $\lambda_\gamma=0$ for every color $\gamma$
occurring in the sequence, then this fair execution contains no nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ and $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$, so the single-move condition fails. Otherwise
let $\gamma$ be the first color of the sequence with
$\lambda_\gamma>0$ and truncate the prefix at the round in which both
robots carry $\gamma$. Nothing has moved so far, so the robots are
still at their initial positions and the distance is $d>0$.

\emph{Second stage.} From that configuration, activate $a$ alone
repeatedly (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}; under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ the robot that is not
activated has no pending operation, and the activations of $b$ are
placed far enough in the future to keep the execution fair). The robot
$b$ is never activated, so its color remains $\gamma$, and the visible
state of $a$, which is the color of its peer, is constant along the
interval. By Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the robot $a$ therefore
applies the same pair $(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$ at every
activation. Since $\lambda_\gamma>0$ and the distance is positive, the
first activation is a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. If it lands on $b(0)$, the two
robots occupy the same point and the collision-free condition fails.
Otherwise the distance remains positive, so the second activation is a
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ as well and $\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2$, which violates the
single-move condition.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lemma-40: body_md -->
\label{lem:cfsm_in_fs_a}
$\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace \in \mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:CFSM_FS_A}.
<!-- end lemma-40 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Put a coordinate on the line through $a(0)$ and $b(0)$ so that
$b(0)<a(0)$. We claim the invariants
\[
  a(t)\ge a(0)\quad\text{and}\quad b(t)\le b(0)\qquad(\forall t\ge0),
\]
which give $b(t)\le b(0)<a(0)\le a(t)$ and hence the collision-free
condition at every instant, during movements included.

Each robot moves at most once, namely at the activation at which its
status is still $0$; at that moment it stands at its initial position.
Let $p$ be the position of $b$ recorded by the ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$. If $b$ has
not yet moved then $p=b(0)$; if $b$ is moving or has already landed
then $p\le b(0)$ by the invariant for $b$. In both cases $p<a(0)$, so
$D=a(0)-p>0$ and $a$ moves to
\[
  a(0)+\tfrac12\bigl(a(0)-p\bigr)>a(0),
\]
and it stays there because all its later ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations are zero. The
argument for $b$ is symmetric. The two inductions use only the fact,
valid from time $0$ on, that neither trajectory has ever crossed the
initial position of the other, so they are not circular.

For the single-move condition, fairness guarantees that each robot is
activated at least once. At its first activation the observed distance
is positive, so its displacement $D/2$ is nonzero; every later
activation produces a zero ${\mathit{Move}}$. Hence $\mathrm{moves}(r)=1$ for both robots.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- lemma-41: body_md -->
\label{lem:p1_no_null}
In every execution, starting from the initial configuration, of a
deterministic algorithm that solves a task containing
$(\mathrm{P1})$, at least one robot performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$.
<!-- end lemma-41 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
If neither robot ever performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, then $m_a(T)=m_b(T)=0$
for every $T$. Each of the three clauses of $(\mathrm{P1}\text{-}c)$
requires $m_a(T_1)+m_b(T_1)\ge1$, so no valid $T_1$ exists, a
contradiction.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{lem:p1_first_move}
In every execution satisfying $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ or $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$, each nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ with earliest completion time lands at $B$ if performed
by $a$, and at $A$ if performed by $b$.
If the Look associated with that ${\mathit{Move}}$ observes the initial
geometric configuration, its normalized displacement is
$(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Such a ${\mathit{Move}}$ exists by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}.
Suppose that $a$ completes one at the earliest completion
time $t^\ast$, and let $p$ be its landing point.
Then $m_a(t^\ast)=1$; the peer may complete its first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ simultaneously.

Any valid exchange time $T_1$ satisfies $T_1\ge t^\ast$,
since both completed-move counts are zero before $t^\ast$.
As $m_a(T_1)\ge1$, the witness cannot be $C_2$.
The remaining possibilities, $C_1$ and $C_3$, both require
\[
  a(T_1)=B,\qquad m_a(T_1)=1.
\]

Suppose that $p\ne B$.
Then $T_1>t^\ast$, and reaching $B$ requires another
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$.
In $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$, every movement remains in $[A,B]$.
In $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$, every movement is a straight segment with both
endpoints in $P\subseteq[A,B]$.
In either case, the exterior endpoint $B$ cannot be reached
in the interior of a nonzero movement.
Thus reaching $B$ requires completing another nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$,
giving $m_a(T_1)\ge2$, a contradiction.
Therefore $p=B$.
The argument for a first completion by $b$ is symmetric
and gives the landing point $A$.

Now assume that the Look associated with this ${\mathit{Move}}$ observes
the initial geometric configuration.
For a Move of $a$, the observed positions are $a_0,b_0$, and
\[
  B-a_0=2(b_0-a_0).
\]
Hence the displacement is twice the observed distance
in the direction of the peer, so its normalized form is
$(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.
For a Move of $b$, the same conclusion follows from
$A-b_0=2(a_0-b_0)$.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{lem:p1_replay}
Let $M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace\}$ and consider an execution that starts from the
initial configuration, consists of alternating singleton activations
(Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}), and is given normalized frames
(Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1)) up to and including the round following the
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. If that first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ complies with
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, then the robot activated in the next
round receives an isomorphic local input, applies the same displacement,
and lands at $4d$ if it is $b$, and at $-d$ if it is $a$. In particular
the landing point lies outside $P$ and outside the segment $[A,B]$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
As long as no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ has occurred, the configuration is unchanged,
so under alternating singleton activation the two robots traverse the
same sequence of states. In $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ the internal state of the
peer is not part of the local input, which consists of the relative
position of the peer together with the robot's own color in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ and of
the relative position alone in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$.

Suppose the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ is performed by $a$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} it lands at $B=3d$, while $b$ is still at
$b_0=2d$, so the distance is again $d$. In the next round $b$ is
activated, and since the adversary may supply the normalized frame, the
local input of $b$ is isomorphic to the one that $a$ received. By
determinism $b$ applies the same displacement $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$
and lands at $2d+2d=4d$. We have $4d\notin P$ and $4d\notin[A,B]=[0,3d]$.
The case in which $b$ moves first is symmetric: $b$ lands at $A=0$, $a$
is still at $d$, and $a$ lands at $d-2d=-d\notin P\cup[A,B]$.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:s-rdv}
An execution solves \textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace if the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Throughout the execution, both robots remain in the segment
      $[A,B]$.
\item There exists a time $T_1>0$ at which one of $C_1,C_2,C_3$ is
      formed, with the corresponding cumulative nonzero-move counts
      $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, or $(1,1)$. Before $T_1$, every robot that is
      not moving is located at one of $A,a_0,b_0,B$.
\item There exists $T_2>T_1$ such that $a(t)=b(t)$ for every
      $t\ge T_2$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-44: body_md -->
\label{lem:srdv_not_fc_a}
$\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A)$.
<!-- end lemma-44 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Stable Rendezvous is impossible in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A$ under variable
disorientation, regardless of the number of colors and without
restricting the algorithm to the $\mathcal L$-class
~\cite{MSW-rendezvous}.

Suppose, for contradiction, that an algorithm $\mathcal A$ solves
$\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A$. Every initial configuration of
Rendezvous with distinct robot positions is an instance of
$\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}$, since the auxiliary points $A$ and $B$ are
determined solely from the initial positions and are not landmarks
available to the robots. Moreover, every execution satisfying
$\mathrm{S\text{-}RDV}$ eventually satisfies
\[
  a(t)=b(t)
  \qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }t,
\]
which is exactly the stable Rendezvous requirement.
Hence $\mathcal A$ would solve Rendezvous in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- lemma-45: body_md -->
\label{lem:srdv_not_fs_r}
$\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-45 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
Suppose an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{R}$ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ solves \textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace. The local
input of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot is the pair consisting of the relative position
of the peer and its own state; the state of the peer is not included.
The adversary chooses the alternating singleton activation
$\{a\},\{b\},\{a\},\dots$ with an empty fully synchronous prefix
(Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}).

\emph{First stage.} The configuration is unchanged until the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. The initial configuration is symmetric under the rotation
by $\pi$ about the midpoint combined with exchanging $a$ and $b$, and
this rotation preserves chirality, so in the normalized frame
(Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1)) both local inputs have the form
$(e,\text{own state})$ and are isomorphic. The two robots start from
the same initial state $s_0$, so $a$ in round $2k-1$ and $b$ in round
$2k$ both pass from $s_{k-1}$ to $s_k$. If no state occurring in
$s_0,s_1,\dots$ produces a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, the configuration never
changes, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}. Let $j$ be the least
index that produces a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$; then $a$ performs the first nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ of the whole execution in round $2j+1$, from state $s_j$.

\emph{Second and third stages.} Since $\mathcal{A}$ is assumed to solve
\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace, Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} forces that ${\mathit{Move}}$ to land at
$B=3d$. The execution is an alternating singleton activation from the
initial configuration under normalized frames whose first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
complies with Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, which is exactly the
hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}. Hence the robot $b$, activated
in the next round, receives an isomorphic local input, performs the
same displacement and lands at $4d$. Since $4d\notin[A,B]$,
condition~1 of Definition~\ref{def:s-rdv} is violated.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- lemma-46: body_md -->
\label{lem:srdv_not_ob_f}
$\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-46 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Suppose an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F}$ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ solves \textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace. The local
input of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot is its current snapshot alone. In round~$1$ the
local input of both robots is ``the peer at distance $d$''. A zero ${\mathit{Move}}$
would leave all later inputs unchanged and the configuration fixed
forever, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null} the ${\mathit{Move}}$ is nonzero, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} the robot $a$ lands at $B$ and $b$ lands
at $A$, forming $C_3$ at distance $3d$.

The local input in round~$2$, ``the peer at distance $3d$'', coincides
with the round-$1$ local input of the initial instance of initial
distance $3d$, namely $A'=0$, $a'(0)=3d$, $b'(0)=6d$, $B'=9d$, and an
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot cannot distinguish the two. In that instance the same
argument as above shows that the first ${\mathit{Move}}$ is nonzero, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} the output is twice the observed distance
in the direction of the peer. Applying the same local rule in round~$2$
of the actual execution, $a$ lands at $3d-6d=-3d$ and $b$ lands at
$0+6d=6d$. Both lie outside $[A,B]=[0,3d]$, which violates condition~1
of Definition~\ref{def:s-rdv}.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- lemma-47: body_md -->
\label{lem:srdv_in_fc_s}
$\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:S_RDV_FC_S}.
<!-- end lemma-47 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Each robot carries a light with color set $\{0,1,2,3\}$,
initially $0$. Apart from the coincidence test, every rule
depends on the color of the peer alone.

\emph{(i) Both robots always lie in $[A,B]$.}
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$, all active robots compute from the configuration
at the beginning of the round.
Rules $\mathrm{R}$ and $2$ do not move, while rules $1$ and $3$
choose the midpoint and the peer's position, respectively.
These destinations belong to $[A,B]$ whenever both current
positions do.

For rule $0$, the peer still has color $0$ and remains
at its initial position.
While that color remains $0$, successive applications of
rule $0$ alternate the observing robot between its initial
position and the opposite outer point.
The possible configurations and destinations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
  (a,b)&=(d,2d): &&a\to3d=B, &
  (a,b)&=(3d,2d): &&a\to d=a_0,\\
  (a,b)&=(d,2d): &&b\to0=A, &
  (a,b)&=(d,0): &&b\to2d=b_0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every destination lies in $[A,B]$.
Since each Move follows a straight segment, both robots
remain in $[A,B]$ throughout the execution.

\emph{(ii) The first phase.}
Let $T_1$ be the end of the first round.
If both robots are activated, $C_3$ is formed with cumulative
nonzero-move counts $(1,1)$.
If only $a$ is activated, $C_1$ is formed with counts $(1,0)$;
if only $b$ is activated, $C_2$ is formed with counts $(0,1)$.
Moreover, up to $T_1$, every stationary robot is at its initial
position or at its first destination, all of which belong to $P$.
Hence $T_1$ is a valid witness for the exchange phase.

\emph{(iii) The second phase.}
By fairness, both robots are activated within finite time.
At the end of the first round by which this has happened,
the color pair is $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, or $(2,1)$.
From $(1,1)$, simultaneous activation brings both robots
to their common midpoint; a singleton activation produces
$(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$.

Consider $(1,2)$, the other case being symmetric.
Until $a$ is activated, only $b$ moves, repeatedly halving
the distance while preserving the color pair.
By fairness, $a$ is eventually activated: it sees color $2$,
stays in place, and changes its color to $3$.
Whether or not $b$ is activated in that round, the resulting
color pair is $(3,2)$.
Until the next activation of $b$, robot $a$ remains stationary.
When $b$ is activated, it sees color $3$ and moves to $a$;
if $a$ is activated simultaneously, it sees color $2$ and stays.
Thus the robots occupy the same point at the end of this round.
Fairness ensures that this occurs at some finite time $T_2>T_1$.

\emph{(iv) Stability of the rendezvous.}
At the round boundary $T_2$, both robots have completed
their Moves and occupy the same point.
Every subsequent Look therefore observes coincidence,
so rule $\mathrm{R}$ applies and neither robot moves again.
Hence $a(t)=b(t)$ for every $t\ge T_2$.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:six-vss}
Let $a_0=a(0)$ and $b_0=b(0)$ be distinct, and define
\(
  A_0=2a_0-b_0,
  \;
  B_0=2b_0-a_0.
\)
The four points $A_0,a_0,b_0,B_0$ occur in this order at equal
spacing on the initial line. Write $\gamma(t)=(a(t),b(t))$ and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \gamma_0&=(a_0,b_0), & \gamma_1&=(B_0,b_0),\\
  \gamma_2&=(a_0,A_0), & \gamma_3&=(B_0,A_0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Every completed Move must end at one of the four designated points.
The execution must first reach one of $\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3$,
with cumulative nonzero move counts $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, or $(1,1)$,
respectively. After this exchange configuration has been formed,
the robots must eventually remain permanently stationary in a
configuration belonging to
$\{\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3\}$.
The restriction to designated points concerns Move endpoints;
straight-line travel between them, including passage through the
peer's position, is allowed.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- lemma-48: body_md -->
\label{lem:vss_not_fs_r}
$\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-48 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Use the alternating singleton execution of the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_fs_r}. Its first stage holds word for word,
since it uses only $(\mathrm{P1})$, so the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the
whole execution is performed by $a$ in round $2j+1$ under a normalized
frame. Since the algorithm is assumed to solve \textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace,
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} forces that ${\mathit{Move}}$ to land at $B=3d$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay} then applies: the robot $b$, activated in the
next round, receives an isomorphic local input, performs the same
displacement and lands at $4d\notin P$. This contradicts the
requirement of Definition~\ref{def:six-vss} that every completed ${\mathit{Move}}$
end at one of the four designated points.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-49: body_md -->
\label{lem:vss_not_ob_f}
$\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-49 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_ob_f}, in round~$1$ the
robot $a$ lands at $B$ and $b$ lands at $A$, forming $C_3$, and in
round~$2$ the robots cannot distinguish their input from the round-$1$
input of the initial instance of initial distance $3d$, so $a$ lands at
$-3d$ and $b$ lands at $6d$. Neither point belongs to $P$, so the
endpoint requirement of Definition~\ref{def:six-vss} is violated.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- lemma-50: body_md -->
\label{lem:vss_in_fc_a}
$\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace\in\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$, as witnessed by
Algorithm~\ref{alg:VSS_FC_A}.
<!-- end lemma-50 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Here $D$ is the distance recorded at the robot's own ${\mathit{Look}}$.

\emph{(i) A robot of color $0$ is at its initial position and is not
moving.} The color of a robot is $0$ until its first ${\mathit{Comp}}$, and since
$t_L<t_C<t_B<t_E$, its first ${\mathit{Move}}$ starts after that ${\mathit{Comp}}$. Hence an
observation of a peer of color $0$ is an observation of a robot that
has not begun any ${\mathit{Move}}$. In particular the observations during a peer's
movement that $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ permits cannot affect the decision of rule $0$,
and no atomicity assumption is used below.

\emph{(ii) When rule $0$ fires, $D=d$ and the destination belongs to
$P$.} By~(i) the peer is at its initial position, and the observing
robot is itself not moving at its own ${\mathit{Look}}$, so by induction it stands
at a landing point of $P$. The possible cases and landing points are
the four listed in part~(i) of the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_in_fc_s}, all of which belong to $P$. In
particular each firing of rule $0$ toggles the robot between its own
initial position and $B$, respectively between its own initial position
and $A$. The destination is computed from the snapshot taken at the
${\mathit{Look}}$, so delaying the ${\mathit{Move}}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}) does not change
the landing point.

\emph{(iii) The first phase.} Let $t$ be the earliest completion of a nonzero Move,
say by $a$. By (ii), $a(t)=B$.
If $b$ has not begun a nonzero Move, then $C_1$ holds at $t$.
Otherwise, $b$ is executing its first nonzero Move towards $A$
(or completes it at $t$), and its color is already $1$.
Hence $a$ remains at $B$ until $b$ completes this Move,
when $C_3$ holds with cumulative counts $(1,1)$.
The case in which $b$ completes first is symmetric.

                                                                      
                                                                       
                                            
                                                                    
                     

\emph{(iv) Permanent stopping.} A robot applies rule $0$ only if its
${\mathit{Look}}$ took place before the first ${\mathit{Comp}}$ of its peer. That ${\mathit{Comp}}$ occurs
at some finite time $T$, and each cycle is finite, so each robot
performs only finitely many ${\mathit{Look}}$ operations before $T$ and therefore
fires rule $0$ finitely often. Under either rule the activated robot
sets its color to $1$, and after the last of these finitely many
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations has been completed, only rule $1$ fires and
neither robot moves again. Hence $\mathrm{Stopped}(a)$ and $\mathrm{Stopped}(b)$ hold.

\emph{(v) The terminal configuration.} By~(ii), a robot that fired rule
$0$ an even number of times is back at its initial position, and one
that fired it an odd number of times stands at $B$, respectively at
$A$. The four combinations are exactly $C_0,C_1,C_2,C_3$, and
Definition~\ref{def:six-vss} admits each of them as a terminal
configuration.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-51: body_md -->
\label{lem:norm}
Fix a reference vector $e\neq0$ of the plane. For every algorithm
$\mathcal A$ there are constants $\lambda_\gamma\ge0$ and
$\theta_\gamma$, determined by $\mathcal A$ alone, and a map $g$ on
visible states, such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] Suppose that at an activation of a robot $r$ the peer is at
  global vector $w\neq0$ and the visible state of $r$ is $\gamma$.
  Then the adversary may choose the local coordinate system of $r$ so
  that the global displacement of $r$ is
  \[
    v=\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}(w),
  \]
  where $R_\theta$ denotes the rotation by angle $\theta$, and the
  color set by $r$ is $g(\gamma)$.
\item[(2)] If $w=0$, the local output is determined by $\gamma$ alone,
  but the adversary may choose the direction and the magnitude of the
  resulting global displacement. In particular, two robots with equal
  visible states can be given equal global displacements.
\end{enumerate}
Unless stated otherwise, we use this coordinate system, called the
\emph{normalized frame}.
<!-- end lemma-51 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
(1) Place $r$ at the origin. By chirality there is a unique
orientation-preserving similarity $\psi$ of the plane that maps $w$ to
$e$, and variable disorientation admits $\psi$ as a local coordinate
system. The local input is then $(e,\gamma)$, so by determinism the
output is a fixed pair $(q_\gamma,g(\gamma))$. Writing
$q_\gamma=\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}(e)$ and observing that
$\psi^{-1}$ is a composition of a rotation and a positive scaling,
hence commutes with rotations, the global displacement is
\[
  \psi^{-1}(q_\gamma)
  =\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}\bigl(\psi^{-1}(e)\bigr)
  =\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}(w).
\]
(2) If $w=0$, the geometric part of the input is the origin in every
local coordinate system, so the output $q$ depends only on $\gamma$.
The global displacement $\psi^{-1}(q)$ changes direction and magnitude
with the choice of $\psi$, and choosing the same $\psi$ for two robots
with equal visible states makes the two displacements equal.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- lemma-52: body_md -->
\label{lem:ratios}
Put
\[
  c_1(\gamma):=\sqrt{1-2\lambda_\gamma\cos\theta_\gamma+\lambda_\gamma^{2}},
  \qquad
  c_2(\gamma):=\sqrt{1-4\lambda_\gamma\cos\theta_\gamma+4\lambda_\gamma^{2}}.
\]
Under normalized frames the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If exactly one robot with visible state $\gamma$ completes a
  cycle while its peer is stationary, then $d\mapsto c_1(\gamma)\,d$.
\item[(ii)] If two robots, both with visible state $\gamma$, complete
  cycles simultaneously from the same snapshot, then
  $d\mapsto c_2(\gamma)\,d$ and the midpoint is invariant.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover
\[
  c_1(\gamma)=0\iff(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)=(1,0),
  \qquad
  c_2(\gamma)=0\iff(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)=(1/2,0).
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(iii)] Identify the plane with the complex plane and $R_\theta$
  with multiplication by $e^{\mathrm i\theta}$. The transformations of
  the difference vector in (i) and (ii) are multiplication by
  \[
    \sigma_1(\gamma):=1-\lambda_\gamma e^{\mathrm i\theta_\gamma},
    \qquad
    \sigma_2(\gamma):=1-2\lambda_\gamma e^{\mathrm i\theta_\gamma},
  \]
  and $c_j(\gamma)=|\sigma_j(\gamma)|$. When $c_j(\gamma)\neq0$, put
  $\psi(\gamma):=\arg\sigma_1(\gamma)$ and
  $\varphi(\gamma):=\arg\sigma_2(\gamma)$. If
  $\psi\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, then there is $k\ge1$ with
  $\cos(k\psi)\le-\tfrac12$, and for every $\theta_0$ there is $k\ge1$
  with $\cos(\theta_0+k\psi)\le0$. The same statements hold for
  $\varphi$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-52 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
Let $w:=b-a$ and $\hat u:=w/d$.

(i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) the new difference vector is
$d(\hat u-\lambda R_\theta\hat u)$, whose squared norm is
$d^{2}(1-2\lambda\cos\theta+\lambda^{2})$.

(ii) The displacement of $b$ is the negative of that of $a$, so the new
difference vector is $d(\hat u-2\lambda R_\theta\hat u)$ and $a+b$ is
unchanged. The conditions for vanishing follow immediately.

(iii) The first assertion is the computation in (i) and (ii) read as
multiplication of complex numbers, together with
$|1-\lambda e^{\mathrm i\theta}|^{2}=1-2\lambda\cos\theta+\lambda^{2}$
and
$|1-2\lambda e^{\mathrm i\theta}|^{2}=1-4\lambda\cos\theta+4\lambda^{2}$.

For the second assertion, suppose first that $\psi/2\pi$ is irrational.
Then $\{k\psi\bmod2\pi\}_{k\ge1}$ is dense in $[0,2\pi)$: by the
pigeonhole principle some integer multiple of $\psi$ is arbitrarily
close to $0$, and its own multiples then fill the circle. Both
assertions follow. Suppose next that $\psi/2\pi=p/q$ in lowest terms
with $q\ge2$. Then
$\{k\psi\bmod2\pi\}_{k\ge1}=\{2\pi j/q:0\le j<q\}$. If $q$ is even,
the value $j=q/2$ belongs to this set and $\cos\pi=-1$. If $q$ is odd,
and therefore $q\ge3$, the points are spaced by $2\pi/q$, so one of
them lies within $\pi/q$ of $\pi$, where
$\cos\le-\cos(\pi/q)\le-\cos(\pi/3)=-\tfrac12$. For the version with an
offset, the set $\{\theta_0+k\psi\bmod2\pi\}_{k\ge1}$ consists of $q$
equally spaced points with gap $2\pi/q\le\pi$, so the closed arc
$[\pi/2,3\pi/2]$, which has length $\pi$, contains at least one of
them, and there $\cos\le0$. The argument for $\varphi$ is identical.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:epgs-normalized-rule}
Write $(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star}):=(\tfrac12,\pi)$, the
displacement that moves a robot away from its observed peer by half the
observed distance; this is the rule of Algorithm~\ref{alg:epgs}. In a
round in which both robots are activated from the same configuration
and apply the same rule $(\lambda,\theta)$, the midpoint is preserved
and the difference vector is multiplied by
$\sigma_2=1-2\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii),(iii)). The expansion condition
$d_{i+1}=2d_i$ of Definition~\ref{def:epgs} therefore holds at such a
step if and only if $\sigma_2=2$, that is if and only if
$(\lambda,\theta)=(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star})$. In that case
$\sigma_1=1-\lambda^{\star}e^{\mathrm{i}\theta^{\star}}=\tfrac32$, so a
solo activation multiplies the distance by $c_1^{\star}=\tfrac32$ and
$\psi^{\star}\equiv0$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-53: body_md -->
\label{lem:solo}
Let $K\in\{S,A_{LC},A_M,A\}$, and suppose that at the end of a finite
admissible prefix the robot $b$ has no pending operation. For every
$k\ge1$ there is an execution that extends this prefix by an interval
in which $a$ completes $k$ consecutive $\ensuremath{\mathit{LCM}}\xspace$ cycles while $b$ is never
activated, followed by a fair tail. Throughout this interval the
position and the color of $b$ are unchanged, and $\texttt{Stop}_b(t)$ holds at
every time $t$ of the interval.
<!-- end lemma-53 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ it suffices to take $\{a\}$ as the activation set of $k$
consecutive rounds. Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ and its subclasses, delay the next
${\mathit{Look}}$ of $b$ and place the $k$ cycles of $a$ one after another inside
that delay. The atomicity constraints only forbid a ${\mathit{Look}}$ of one robot
during prescribed phases of the other robot's cycle, and $b$ executes
no cycle during the interval, so no constraint is violated. Appending a
tail that activates both robots infinitely often makes the execution
fair.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-54: body_md -->
\label{lem:suspend}
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ and its subclasses, the adversary may insert a finite
delay before any of the first three phase times of a cycle of a robot
$r$, that is, before $t_L(r,i)$, inside $(t_L(r,i),t_C(r,i))$, or
inside $(t_C(r,i),t_B(r,i))$, and place events of the other robot
inside that delay, within the limits imposed by the atomicity
constraints. No delay is inserted inside a ${\mathit{Move}}$ operation: once the
${\mathit{Move}}$ of $r$ begins at $t_B(r,i)$, the robot proceeds to the destination
computed at $t_C(r,i)$ and the ${\mathit{Move}}$ ends at $t_E(r,i)$ without
interruption. The values used by $r$ in the later phase are those
obtained in the earlier one.
<!-- end lemma-54 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
The times $t_L,t_C,t_B,t_E$ are chosen by the adversary subject only
to the ordering constraint and to finiteness of each phase
(Section~\ref{subsec:schedulers-events}); in particular the adversary
controls the duration $t_E(r,i)-t_B(r,i)$ of a ${\mathit{Move}}$ operation, but not
an interruption of it, which is why every delay used here is placed
before $t_B(r,i)$. The second assertion is the determinism of the
algorithm: the destination and the new color computed at $t_C(r,i)$ do
not depend on anything occurring afterwards.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:stale}
Let $K\in\{A_{LC},A_M,A\}$. The adversary can construct a fair
execution in which $a$ computes its destination at $t_C(a,i)$, is then
delayed, the robot $b$ completes at least one nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ during the
delay, and only afterwards does $a$ move to the destination it had
already computed. The delay is placed before the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ begins,
and the ${\mathit{Move}}$ itself, once begun, is carried out in full. Writing
$w_{\mathrm{old}}$ and $w_{\mathrm{new}}$ for the vector from $a$ to
$b$ at $t_C(a,i)$ and at $t_B(a,i)$ respectively, the difference vector
after the move of $a$ is
\[
  w_{\mathrm{new}}-\lambda_\gamma R_{\theta_\gamma}(w_{\mathrm{old}}).
\]
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:suspend} with the delay placed between
$t_C(a,i)$ and $t_B(a,i)$, and place the whole cycle of $b$ inside it.
What $A_{LC}$ forbids is a ${\mathit{Look}}$ in $(t_L(a,i),t_C(a,i)]$, and what
$A_M$ forbids is a ${\mathit{Look}}$ in $[t_B(a,i),t_E(a,i)]$; the delay
interval $(t_C(a,i),t_B(a,i))$ meets neither, so the segment is
admissible under $A_{LC}$, $A_M$ and $A$ alike. The displacement
formula is Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) applied to the snapshot that $a$
obtained at its ${\mathit{Look}}$, which is released unchanged when the ${\mathit{Move}}$
begins.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- lemma-55: body_md -->
\label{lem:mid}
Let $K\in\{A_{LC},A\}$, and suppose that $b$ performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
from $p_B$ to $p_E\neq p_B$ while $a$ has no pending operation. For
every $\mu\in(0,1)$ there is a fair execution in which $a$ performs a
${\mathit{Look}}$ at a time when $b$ is at
\[
  p_\mu=(1-\mu)p_B+\mu p_E .
\]
<!-- end lemma-55 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
The movement of $b$ is an uninterrupted continuous motion along the
segment $[p_B,p_E]$, whose duration the adversary may choose, so by the
intermediate value theorem there is
$\tau_\mu\in(t_B(b,i),t_E(b,i))$ with $b(\tau_\mu)=p_\mu$. Setting
$t_L(a,j)=\tau_\mu$ is unconstrained under $A$, and it is admissible
under $A_{LC}$ as well, because $\tau_\mu>t_C(b,i)$.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- lemma-56: body_md -->
\label{lem:altA}
Let $K=R$. For every $p\ge0$ there is a fair execution whose first $p$
rounds are fully synchronous and whose tail activates
$\{a\},\{b\},\{a\},\ldots$ or $\{b\},\{a\},\ldots$. In this tail,
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the distance $d$ is updated by the factor $c_1$ at every
  round;
\item[(ii)] the robot that is not activated remains stationary during
  that round;
\item[(iii)] if the displacement of the moving robot is $v$, then
  $a+b$ is translated by $v$;
\item[(iv)] the two colors may evolve independently.
\end{enumerate}
Once the alternating tail has begun, no fully synchronous round is
admissible.
<!-- end lemma-56 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
This is the definition of $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ in
Section~\ref{subsec:schedulers-events}, and (i)--(iv) follow from the
fact that exactly one displacement is applied in each round of the
tail; for (i) this is Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i).
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:silent}
A finite execution segment $\sigma$ is \emph{$r$-invisible} if the
normalized local input that $r$ receives at its next activation is the
same before and after $\sigma$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- lemma-57: body_md -->
\label{lem:silent}
Let $M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace\}$. If $r$ is not activated during $\sigma$ and the
peer $\overline r$ occupies a position distinct from that of $r$ both
before and after $\sigma$, then $\sigma$ is $r$-invisible. Consequently,
however the internal state of $\overline r$ changes during $\sigma$,
the robot $r$ computes the same output at its next activation.
<!-- end lemma-57 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
Neither $\operatorname{Obs}_{\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace}(r)=(p_r,c_r)$ nor
$\operatorname{Obs}_{\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace}(r)=p_r$ contains the color of the peer, so
only two components have to be preserved. The own color $c_r$ is
unchanged because $r$ is not activated. The relative position of the
peer may change by a similarity during $\sigma$, but as long as it is
nonzero it is mapped to $e$ in the normalized frame by
Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1). The last assertion is then the determinism of
the algorithm.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- lemma-58: body_md -->
\label{lem:pumpB2}
Let $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ and $K\in\{S,A_{LC},A_M,A\}$. Consider a solo activation
interval of $a$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}) in which every ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$
observes its peer at a position different from its own. Along such an
interval, the color of $a$ evolves as
\[
  c_0,\;g(c_0),\;g^{2}(c_0),\;\ldots,
\]
which is eventually periodic, say with preperiod $p$ and period $q$.
For every $n\ge1$ such that the first $p+nq$ activations of $a$
satisfy this condition, there is a fair execution in which $a$ is
activated alone $p+nq$ times; at the end of that interval the color
of $a$ is $\gamma_p:=g^{p}(c_0)$, and $b$, never being activated,
stays at its position throughout the interval. If moreover $a$ never
reaches the position of $b$ during the interval, then the inserted
interval is $b$-invisible.
<!-- end lemma-58 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
The visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot is its own color. Every ${\mathit{Look}}$ of
$a$ in the interval observes a nonzero relative position of its peer,
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) each activation updates the color by $g$.
The color sequence is therefore the orbit of $g$ and is eventually
periodic. After $p+nq$ steps the orbit is back at $\gamma_p$. The robot
$b$ is not activated, so its own color is unchanged, and the color of
$a$ is not part of the input of $b$. The relative position of $a$
changes by a similarity, but as long as it is nonzero the adversary can
present the same normalized input to the next activation of $b$; hence
the interval is $b$-invisible by Lemma~\ref{lem:silent}.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- lemma-59: body_md -->
\label{lem:keep-coincident}
Suppose that $a(t_0)=b(t_0)$, that neither robot has a pending operation
at $t_0$, and that the scheduler class permits activating both robots
in every round from $t_0$ on. The last condition always holds under
$\textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace$; under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ and the subclasses of $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ it holds for the full
activation set with aligned phase times; under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ it holds only
while the execution is still in its fully synchronous prefix. Suppose
moreover that in each such round the two local outputs are either both
zero or both nonzero; this is in particular the case when the two
visible states are equal. Then the adversary can construct a fair
execution with $a(t)=b(t)$ for every $t\ge t_0$.
<!-- end lemma-59 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
At a coincidence the geometric part of both local inputs is the origin
(Section~\ref{subsec:robots-capabilities}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(2)
the direction and the magnitude of the global displacement obtained
from a nonzero local output are chosen by the adversary, so two nonzero
outputs can be mapped to the same global displacement, while two zero
outputs produce no movement. Activating both robots in every round
therefore preserves the coincidence. If one output is zero and the
other is not, the coincidence is destroyed, so the condition on the
outputs cannot be omitted. In $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ the output at a coincidence is
unique, hence that condition always holds.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- lemma-60: body_md -->
\label{lem:rigidA1}
Let $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ and $K=F$, so that the displacement rule is a single pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a), and put
$c_2:=c_2(\lambda,\theta)$. The adversary can construct a fair
execution in which, in every round $k$ with $d(k)>0$, the midpoint is
fixed at $m$ and $d(k)=c_2^{\,k}d(0)$, and in which exactly one of the
following occurs.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\lambda=0$: neither robot moves, and
  $\mathrm{moves}(a)=\mathrm{moves}(b)=0$.
\item[(b)] $c_2=0$: in round $1$ the two robots coincide at $m$, and
  the coincidence is maintained by Lemma~\ref{lem:keep-coincident}.
\item[(c)] $0<c_2<1$: the sequence $d(k)$ decreases strictly to $0$ but
  remains positive, and $\mathrm{moves}(a)=\mathrm{moves}(b)=\infty$.
\item[(d)] $c_2\ge1$: $d(k)\ge d(0)$ for every $k$, and
  $\mathrm{moves}(a)=\mathrm{moves}(b)=\infty$.
\end{enumerate}

Moreover the adversary lets the two robots start and complete their
Moves simultaneously, with the same fractional progress along their
segments. The two robots are then simultaneously stationary only
before and after the common Move interval of a round, so every joint
stop of the execution carries one of the round-boundary distances
$d(k)$. In particular the restriction of $d$ to $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ is monotone.
<!-- end lemma-60 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Give the normalized frame in every round, so that
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii) applies to each round. In case~(b) the
execution is fully synchronous and the model is $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$, so the output
condition of Lemma~\ref{lem:keep-coincident} is satisfied. In
cases~(c) and~(d) a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs in every round, and since
$t_E(r,i)<t_L(r,i+1)$ these are counted as distinct moves.

Activating both robots in the same round with a common speed profile
is admissible under $\textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace$. In a round containing a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ the
two Move intervals then coincide, so the instants at which both robots
are stationary are those preceding the common Move, where the distance
is $d(k)$, and those following it, where it is $d(k+1)$. In a round
containing no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ the distance is constant and equal to both.
Hence $d$ takes only the values $d(k)=c_2^{\,k}d(0)$ on $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$, and
that sequence is monotone in each of the four cases: constant in~(a),
constant at $0$ from round~$1$ on in~(b), strictly decreasing in~(c),
and non-decreasing in~(d).
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- lemma-61: body_md -->
\label{lem:rigidA2}
Let $M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace,\allowbreak\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace,\allowbreak\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace\}$ and let $K$ be any
scheduler class that permits activating both robots in every round;
under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ this means during the fully synchronous prefix. The
adversary can construct a fair execution in which, in every round $k$,
the two robots carry the same color $\gamma_k$, where $\gamma_0=c_0$,
and the distance satisfies $d(k+1)=c_2(\gamma_k)\,d(k)$; moreover, in
every round $k$ with $d(k)>0$ the midpoint is fixed at $m$.
While the robots occupy distinct positions, their common color
satisfies $\gamma_{k+1}=g(\gamma_k)$.
After a coincidence, the common color instead follows the transition
map for the zero geometric observation.
In either case the two colors remain equal.
Since coincidence is thereafter maintained, the common color sequence
$(\gamma_k)$ is eventually periodic.
<!-- end lemma-61 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Activate both robots in every round and give them the normalized
frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ at which they are distinct. The designated
initial colors are equal, and equal colors give the two robots equal
visible states, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm} their next colors are equal
as well; while the robots are distinct, this common next color is
$g(\gamma_k)$. While the robots are distinct, the distance update and
the invariance of the midpoint are Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii). If
$c_2(\gamma_k)=0$, the robots coincide at $m$ at the end of round $k$;
from then on their visible states are still equal, so the coincidence
is preserved by Lemma~\ref{lem:keep-coincident} and $d(k+1)=0
=c_2(\gamma_k)\,d(k)$ holds trivially, whereas the common position may
move, since by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(2) the adversary chooses the
displacement at a coincidence. At every such round both robots observe
the zero geometric configuration with equal visible states, so they
apply the same transition map for that observation and their colors
remain equal. Before a coincidence the common color sequence is an
orbit of $g$; after it, the sequence is an orbit of the transition map
for the zero observation. Either is the orbit of a map on a finite set,
so $(\gamma_k)$ is eventually periodic.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- lemma-62: body_md -->
\label{lem:pumpB1}
Let $M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace,\allowbreak\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace\}$ and $K\in\{S,A_{LC},A_M,A\}$. Let $\gamma_\star$
be the visible state of $a$ at the beginning of a solo activation
interval of Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}, and put
$\lambda:=\lambda_{\gamma_\star}$, $\theta:=\theta_{\gamma_\star}$ and
$c:=c_1(\gamma_\star)$. Assume that the robots occupy distinct
positions at the beginning of the interval. Throughout the interval
$\texttt{Stop}_b(t)$ holds, so
the peer remains stationary. At every cycle whose ${\mathit{Look}}$ observes
distinct positions, the vector from $a$ to $b$ is transformed by
$I-\lambda R_\theta$. Hence $d(j)=c^{\,j}d(0)$ up to and including the
first landing at the peer, if such a landing occurs. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] if $\lambda=0$, then $a$ does not move during the interval;
  in particular, if $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ then $b$ obeys the same rule, so the
  configuration stays at $\iota$ along every fair infinite execution;
\item[(b)] if $c=0$, the first activation makes $a$ reach its peer.
  The normalized rule does not determine subsequent outputs at
  coincidence; those must be treated separately;
\item[(c)] if $\lambda>0$ and $c>0$, every activation in the solo
  interval is a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, and any prescribed finite number of such
  ${\mathit{Move}}$s can be scheduled.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-62 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
While $b$ is not activated, the visible state of $a$ is constant: the
model $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has no visible state, and in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ it is the color of $b$,
which does not change, since $a$ cannot observe its own color. Hence,
at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ that observes distinct positions, the same pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$ is applied, and the transformation of the vector
from $a$ to $b$ and the distance formula follow from
Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i). In case~(c) the
distance stays positive, so every ${\mathit{Look}}$ observes distinct positions and
every displacement has length $\lambda d(j)>0$. Concerning~(a), when
$M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ the color of $a$ may change during the interval, so the
subsequent behavior of $b$ is not determined by $\lambda$ alone; this
is why immobility of the whole configuration is asserted only for
$M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- lemma-63: body_md -->
\label{lem:single-rule}
In each of the following two cases, the displacement rule of the
activated robot is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] any algorithm with $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$;
\item[(b)] an algorithm with $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$, together with an interval during
  which the peer is not activated.
\end{enumerate}
When these activations are performed one at a time, with
each cycle completed before the next begins, and every
${\mathit{Look}}$ observes distinct positions, successive landing
distances are multiplied by the same factor
$c_1(\lambda,\theta)$, so that $d(k)=c_1^{\,k}d(0)$ after $k$
activations. Their sequence is therefore monotone and cannot alternate
between strict decreases and strict increases. A landing at the peer
ends this normalized argument and must be handled separately. If
$\lambda=0$, the robot does not move at all.
<!-- end lemma-63 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:norm} the displacement is determined by the pair
$(\lambda_\gamma,\theta_\gamma)$ attached to the visible state $\gamma$.
In case~(a) the model $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has a unique visible state, so the family of
constants degenerates to a single pair. In case~(b) the visible state of
an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot is the color of its peer alone, since it cannot observe
its own color; as long as the peer is not activated that color is
unchanged, hence the visible state is constant
(Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB1}). For such singleton cycles, the landing
distance is multiplied by $c_1(\lambda,\theta)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i), so the landing distances form a geometric
sequence and are monotone. If $\lambda=0$ the displacement is
identically zero.
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:first-nonzero}
Let $M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace,\allowbreak\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace,\allowbreak\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace\}$ with the designated common initial color
$c_0$, and let the execution begin with rounds activating both robots,
as in Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}, so that the common color evolves by
$\gamma_0=c_0$, $\gamma_{k+1}=g(\gamma_k)$ and is eventually periodic.
Exactly one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\lambda_{\gamma_k}=0$ for every $k$. Then this fair
  execution contains no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ at all, the configuration remains
  $\iota$ forever, and both robots are permanently stationary.
\item[(b)] There is a least $t$ with $\lambda_{\gamma_t}\neq0$. Then the
  configuration at the beginning of round $t$ is still $\iota$, both
  robots are stationary with no pending operation, and their common
  visible state is $\gamma_t$. Hence any segment of
  Appendix~\ref{app:admissible-segments} may be appended there. In
  particular, replacing round $t$ by a solo activation interval of $a$
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}) leaves the local input of $a$ unchanged, so
  the rule applied at its first activation is
  $(\lambda_{\gamma_t},\theta_{\gamma_t})$ with
  $\lambda_{\gamma_t}\neq0$; the visible state then stays equal to
  $\gamma_t$ throughout the interval when $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB1}), whereas for $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ it follows the orbit of
  $g$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB2}).
\end{enumerate}
In case~(a) the joint-stop sequence of Definition~\ref{def:epg} has the
single term $C_0$, so the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$
fails. In case~(b) the configuration is unchanged until round $t$, so
the first activation of $a$ in the solo activation interval is the
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and it is performed while $b$ is not
activated; Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) then makes the expansion
condition fail at $i=0$.
Since the color sequence is eventually periodic, the dichotomy is
decided by a finite check. For $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ the same statement holds with
the single rule $(\lambda,\theta)$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a), case~(a) being $\lambda=0$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots carry the same color
$\gamma_k$ in round $k$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) both apply
$(\lambda_{\gamma_k},\theta_{\gamma_k})$, and the displacement is
nonzero exactly when $\lambda_{\gamma_k}\neq0$. In case~(a) no
displacement is ever nonzero, so the configuration never changes. In
case~(b) every round before $t$ applies a zero displacement, hence the
configuration at the beginning of round $t$ is still $\iota$; the robot
$a$ then has the same peer position and the same visible state as it
would under simultaneous activation, so its rule there is
$(\lambda_{\gamma_t},\theta_{\gamma_t})$. The finite check is the
eventual periodicity of the orbit of $g$ on a finite color set.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- lemma-64: body_md -->
\label{lem:concat}
The violations exhibited by a common-failure construction split into
two kinds. A \emph{safety violation}, namely landing at a forbidden
point, a forbidden overtaking, a forbidden coincidence, a forbidden
transition, or an expansion that moves the center of gravity, occurs at
a finite time and cannot be repaired by any continuation. A \emph{liveness
violation}, namely the failure of infinitely many alternations, of
perpetuity, of reaching, of convergence, or of stable gathering or
stopping, is decided only on an infinite execution. The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A finite segment that forces a safety violation may be followed
  by any continuation permitted by the scheduler class, in particular
  by a fair tail, and the violation is preserved.
\item Segments are concatenated starting from the state actually
  reached by the preceding prefix. Positions, colors, internal states,
  and pending operations are carried over and are not reset. A segment
  may be appended only if its applicability conditions hold in that
  state and if the concatenation is an execution of the scheduler class
  under consideration. In particular, no fully synchronous round may be
  placed after an alternating singleton tail under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}); a solo activation interval
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}) requires the robot that is not activated to
  have no pending operation; and a delayed move
  (Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}) requires $K\in\{A_{LC},A_M,A\}$.
\item A liveness violation requires an explicit fair infinite
  continuation along which the violation persists; an arbitrary fair
  tail does not suffice. When a safety violation of one predicate is
  combined with a liveness violation of another, the segment forcing
  the safety violation is placed first, and the infinite continuation
  witnessing the liveness violation is built from the state that this
  segment leaves.
\end{enumerate}
Since the predicate of each task is evaluated relative to the fixed
initial instance $\iota$, the argument for a later segment remains
valid even when earlier segments have already changed the
configuration.
<!-- end lemma-64 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
A safety violation is witnessed by a finite prefix, and every extension
of that prefix contains it; this gives~(1).

Claim~(2) records that a concatenation is an execution of the algorithm
in the given scheduler class exactly when each stage is admissible from
the state already reached. The conditions listed are precisely those
required by the corresponding segment lemmas.

For~(3), a liveness property is not decided by any finite prefix, so
an infinite continuation violating it has to be exhibited. Finally,
the task predicates refer to $\iota$ and to the trajectory, not to the
configuration at which a segment happens to begin; hence a change of
configuration by an earlier segment does not invalidate the argument
for a later one.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
(1) Say $\bar r$ completes no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so $\bar r_{i+1}=\bar r_i$.
Consecutive terms of the sequence are distinct, hence $r_{i+1}\neq r_i$ and
\(
  a_{i+1}+b_{i+1}=(a_i+b_i)+(r_{i+1}-r_i)\neq a_i+b_i .
\)

(2) For $K=R$ take the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:altA} with an empty fully
synchronous prefix; every round activates exactly one robot. For
$K\in\{S,A_{LC},A_M,A\}$ the adversary places the whole cycle of one robot after
