the whole cycle of the other, alternately: while one robot runs its cycle the
other performs no operation, so no $\ensuremath{\mathit{Look}}\xspace$ falls inside a ${\mathit{Move}}$ interval of the
peer and every atomicity constraint of
Section~\ref{subsec:schedulers-events} is met; both robots are activated
infinitely often, so the execution is fair.

In such an execution the boundaries between consecutive cycles are times of
$\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$. If no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, the configuration never changes and
$(C_i)$ has the single term $C_0$; then the first condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}$ (exactly two terms) and the first condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ (an infinite sequence) both fail. Otherwise consider the
first cycle containing a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, performed by $r$. Every earlier cycle
left the configuration unchanged, so the joint stop preceding that cycle
realizes $C_0$ and the joint stop following it realizes $C_1\neq C_0$, while
$\bar r$ ran no cycle in between. By (1),
$\tfrac12(a_1+b_1)\neq c_0$, so the second condition of both tasks fails at
$i=0$. This is a safety violation and is preserved by any fair continuation.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- lemma-65: body_md -->
\label{lem:cf-sro-two-moves}
Consider a situation in which only one robot moves while its peer
remains stationary. The displacement that can satisfy $\mathbf{C1}$ is
unique, namely the one rotating the segment by $90^\circ$ clockwise
about the peer, and the displacement that can satisfy $\mathbf{C2}$ is
also unique, namely the one rotating the moving robot by $90^\circ$
clockwise about the midpoint. No other displacement satisfies
$\mathbf{C1}$ or $\mathbf{C2}$. If the same robot performs two
consecutive nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations while its peer stays still, the
rotation condition and $\mathbf{C3}$ cannot both be satisfied.
Consequently, two solo nonzero moves of one robot violate
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$, irrespective of the internal states. Zero ${\mathit{Move}}$
operations do not advance the sequence $(C_i)$.
<!-- end lemma-65 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
After each nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the moving robot, both robots are stationary
until the next ${\mathit{Look}}$, so the configurations reached after the two moves
are consecutive terms $C_{i+1},C_{i+2}$ of the sequence $(C_i)$.

Condition $\mathbf{C1}$ requires $\|d_{i+1}\|=\|d_i\|$ together with
$d_{i+1}=R_{-90^\circ}d_i$, so with the peer held fixed the new
position of the moving robot is uniquely determined. Condition
$\mathbf{C2}$ requires $d_{i+1}=2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i$ and
determines it uniquely in the same way. Both conditions are purely
geometric and do not depend on the internal states.

Exchanging the names of the robots replaces each $d_j$ by $-d_j$,
which leaves the conditions unchanged, and they are also invariant
under orientation-preserving similarities. We may therefore assume
that $a$ is the moving robot and that
\[
  b_i=(0,0),\qquad a_i=(-1,0),
\]
so that $d_i=(1,0)$ and
\[
  Q_i=\Bigl\{(x,y):\ \bigl|x+\tfrac12\bigr|+|y|\le\tfrac12\Bigr\}.
\]

If the first move satisfies $\mathbf{C1}$, then $a_{i+1}=(0,1)$, and
the second move gives $a_{i+2}=(1,0)$ under $\mathbf{C1}$ and
$a_{i+2}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ under $\mathbf{C2}$. If the first move
satisfies $\mathbf{C2}$, then $a_{i+1}=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, and the
second move gives $a_{i+2}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ under $\mathbf{C1}$ and
$a_{i+2}=(0,\tfrac12)$ under $\mathbf{C2}$. In each of the four cases
$a_{i+2}\notin Q_i$, so $\mathbf{C3}$ fails at $C_{i+2}$. This is the
computation of~\cite[Lemma~23, Fig.~5]{FSW19}.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- lemma-66: body_md -->
\label{lem:overtake}
Let $K\in\{A_{LC},A_M,A\}$. Suppose that $b$ computes at its ${\mathit{Comp}}$ a
destination from its saved ${\mathit{Look}}$ snapshot, with global displacement
$v\neq0$, that its ${\mathit{Move}}$ is then
delayed as in Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}, and that only $a$ is activated
during the delay. Let $w$ be the vector from $b$ to $a$ at the moment
at which the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ is released. Keep $a$ stationary while $b$
executes this pending ${\mathit{Move}}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\|w\|<\|v\|/2$, then the distance after the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ is
  larger than $\|w\|$. Hence the second condition of
  $\Phi_{\mathrm{MCv}}$, monotonicity, is violated.
\item If $b(0)$, the current position of $b$, and $a$ lie on a line in
  this order, if $v$ points towards $a$, and if $\|w\|<\|v\|$, then $b$
  lands beyond $a$, and at its landing time $t$ one has
  $\mathit{dis}(b(0),b(t))>\mathit{dis}(b(0),a(t))$. Hence the second condition of
  $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, collision freedom, is violated.
\end{enumerate}
The delay is placed between $t_C(b,i)$ and $t_B(b,i)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:suspend} and Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}, it is admissible
under $A_{LC}$, $A_M$ and $A$, and any prescribed finite number of
complete cycles of $a$ may be placed inside it. Throughout the delay
$b$ stays at its position, and its pending ${\mathit{Move}}$ uses the destination
computed at $t_C(b,i)$, independently of these cycles. When
$M\in\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace\}$ the visible state of $a$ is constant during the delay
(for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ it is the color that $b$ adopted at $t_C(b,i)$); when
$M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ the color of $a$ follows the orbit of $g$ as long as every
${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$ observes distinct positions. Hence the distance formulas
of Lemmas~\ref{lem:pumpB1} and~\ref{lem:pumpB2} apply to these cycles,
although $b$ has a pending operation.
<!-- end lemma-66 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
(1) After the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$, the vector from $b$ to $a$ is $w-v$, and
\[
  \|w-v\|\ \ge\ \|v\|-\|w\|\ >\ \|w\| .
\]
 
(2) On the line we have
\[
  \mathit{dis}(b(0),b+v)
  =\mathit{dis}(b(0),b)+\|v\|
  >\mathit{dis}(b(0),b)+\|w\|
  =\mathit{dis}(b(0),a),
\]
which is the stated inequality at the landing time.
 
The admissibility of the delay and of the cycles of $a$ placed inside
it is Lemma~\ref{lem:suspend} together with Corollary~\ref{cor:stale};
the last assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:suspend} shows that the pending
${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ is unaffected by them. The distance formulas follow from
Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i), exactly as in
the proofs of Lemmas~\ref{lem:pumpB1} and~\ref{lem:pumpB2}, since $b$
does not move during the delay.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:overtake-reachability}
Neither $\|w\|<\|v\|/2$ nor $\|w\|<\|v\|$ holds by construction: they
require the solo activations of $a$ during the delay to bring $a$
close enough to $b$. When the solo contraction ratio of $a$ satisfies
$c<1$, we have $d(j)=c^{\,j}d(0)\to0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB1}, and
the hypothesis can be met. For $M=\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ the relevant quantity is the
product $\Gamma=\prod_j c_1(\gamma_j)$ over one color period, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB2}, and the hypothesis can be met when
$\Gamma<1$. The reachability condition and, for part~(2), the required
collinearity and order must be verified in each application.
The continuation arguments for $\mathrm{MCv}$ and
$\mathrm{ZCC}$ are given directly in
Lemmas~\ref{lem:mcv_not_fs_am} and~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fs_am}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:continuum}
Let $K\in\{A_{LC},A\}$, suppose that $b$ performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, and
suppose that $a$ observes it with parameter $\mu\in(0,1)$ as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:mid}. Let $h:(0,1)\to\mathbb R$ assign to $\mu$ some
quantity of the resulting execution. If $h$ is continuous and
nonconstant, then for every countable set $G\subset\mathbb R$ the
adversary can choose $\mu$ with $h(\mu)\notin G$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
The image of a nonconstant continuous function on an interval contains
a nondegenerate interval, hence is uncountable, and therefore is not
contained in $G$.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- lemma-67: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-1-FC-S}
$\mathrm{EH}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-67 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
Normalize the edge length of the hexagon of $\iota$ to $1$, with
$a(0)=v_0$ and $b(0)=v_3$; the initial colors are common. The visible
state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ robot is the color of its peer, so while both robots
are activated in every round their colors stay equal and follow a
common sequence $c_0,g(c_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}), which is
eventually periodic since the palette is finite. During this prefix the
configuration stays at $\iota$.

If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, this fair execution contains no
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$ and the perpetuity condition of
$\mathrm{HET}$ fails, while the joint-stop sequence has the single term
$C_0$ and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails as well
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2)). Both are liveness violations of the
same fair infinite execution, so Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(3) is
satisfied.

Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$, replace
round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated $k\ge2$ times
in a row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and append a fair tail. Since $b$ is
not activated, the visible state of $a$ is constantly $c_t$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) its rule is the single pair
$(\lambda,\theta)=(\lambda_{c_t},\theta_{c_t})$, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB1} the distance satisfies $d(j)=c_1^{\,j}d(0)$.

All rounds before the interval left the configuration at $\iota$, so
the first activation of $a$ in the interval is the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
of the execution and it is performed while $b$ is not activated. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the center of gravity of the next term of
the joint-stop sequence is not $c_0$, so the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$; this is a safety violation and is
preserved by the tail.

For $\mathrm{HET}$, as $b$ stands still at $v_3$, the second condition
requires $a$ to be at $v_0,v_{-1},v_0$ after $0,1,2$ nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
operations, that is $d=2,\sqrt3,2$; this would force $c_1=\sqrt3/2$ and
$c_1=2/\sqrt3$ simultaneously, which is impossible. (If $c_1=0$ then
$a$ reaches $v_3\neq v_{-1}$ in one activation.) Hence the second
condition fails, and being a safety violation it is preserved by the
tail (Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)).

In both cases a single execution violates both predicates, so the
common-failure property holds at $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S}$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- lemma-68: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-1-FS-R}
$\mathrm{EH}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-68 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$.
Take the alternating singleton activation with an empty fully
synchronous prefix (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}) followed by an arbitrary fair
tail, with edge length $1$, $a(0)=v_0$, $b(0)=v_3$, common initial
colors, and normalized frames up to and including the round following
the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. Every round of this execution activates exactly
one robot, so Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2) applies to it. The initial
configuration is symmetric under the rotation by $\pi$ about the
midpoint combined with exchanging the robots, and in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ the state of
the peer does not appear in the local input
(Lemma~\ref{lem:silent}), so until the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ both robots
follow the same color sequence $\gamma_0,g(\gamma_0),\dots$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB2}).
 
If $\lambda_{g^j(\gamma_0)}=0$ for every $j$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs,
so $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0$ and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{HET}$ fails,
while the joint-stop sequence has the single term $C_0$ and the
perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails.
 
Otherwise let $j$ be least with $\lambda_{g^j(\gamma_0)}\neq0$. The first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ is the $(j+1)$-st activation of $a$, performed while $b$
is not activated, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion
condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$. Write $(\lambda,\theta)$
for the displacement of that activation, with $\lambda\neq0$, and
$a^{*}$ for its landing point. If $a^{*}=b(0)$, then
$a^{*}=v_3\neq v_{-1}$ violates the second condition of $\mathrm{HET}$.
If $a^{*}\neq b(0)$ and $a^{*}\neq v_{-1}$, the second condition fails
at once. If $a^{*}=v_{-1}$, the robot $b$ activated next has the same
visible state as $a$ had, so it applies the same $(\lambda,\theta)$;
since $\lambda R_\theta$ maps $v_3-v_0$, of length $2$, to
$v_{-1}-v_0$, of length $1$, we have $\lambda=1/2$, and the
displacement of $b$ has length $\tfrac12\|v_{-1}-v_3\|=\sqrt3/2$, which
differs from the $\|v_2-v_3\|=1$ required by the second condition
(Lemma~\ref{lem:het_not_fs_r}).
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- lemma-69: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-2-FC-S}
$\mathrm{EO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-69 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
Run fully synchronous rounds with normalized frames. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the colors follow a common sequence
$c_0,g(c_0),\dots$, and the configuration stays at $\iota$ while every
${\mathit{Move}}$ is zero.

If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, continue forever. Then $d$ is
constant, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ has no strictly decreasing phase.
The joint-stop sequence is $(C_0)$, so the perpetuity condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails. This fair execution witnesses both liveness
violations.

Otherwise let $t$ be least with $\lambda_{c_t}\neq0$. Replace round $t$
by two consecutive solo activations of $a$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and
append a fair tail. Since $b$ is inactive, the visible state of $a$
stays $c_t$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the robot $a$ applies
$(\lambda_{c_t},\theta_{c_t})$ with $\lambda_{c_t}\neq0$ both times.

The first of these activations is the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the
execution, and it is solo. Hence the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1)).

For OSPO: if $d$ vanishes during the interval, the collision-freedom
condition of $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails. Otherwise the second
activation is also a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. At its completion $m_a=2$ and
$m_b=0$, which no execution satisfying $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ admits
(as in Lemma~\ref{lem:osp_not_fc_s}).

In the latter case, all these violations are safety violations, preserved by the tail
(Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)). Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure}
gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- lemma-70: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-2-FS-S}
$\mathrm{EO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-70 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
Give normalized frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ at which the robots are distinct.
Then each robot advances along $c_0,g(c_0),\dots$, one step per
activation and independently of the schedule, and its displacement
depends only on its color. Let
$J:=\{i\ge0:\lambda_{g^i(c_0)}\neq0\}$.

A collision violates the collision-freedom condition of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ as a safety violation, so we assume none below.

Any witness $(t_i)$ of $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ has
$m_a(t_i)=m_b(t_i)=i$. Hence
\begin{equation}
  |m_a-m_b|\le1 \text{ at all times, and } m_a,m_b \text{ are unbounded.}
  \tag{$\ast$}
\end{equation}

\emph{Case $J=\emptyset$.} Run fully synchronously forever. No nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs. So $d$ is constant, and the joint-stop sequence is
$(C_0)$. Both $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ and the perpetuity condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fail, and this execution witnesses both liveness
violations.

\emph{Case $J\neq\emptyset$.} Let $j:=\min J$, and activate $a$ alone
$j+1$ times (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}). The last of these activations is
the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, and it is solo. So the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1)); this
is a safety violation.

If $|J|\ge2$, let $j'$ be the second element of $J$. Continue
activating $a$ alone up to its $(j'+1)$-st activation, then append a
fair tail. The robot $a$ performs a second nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ while $b$
performs none. This contradicts $(\ast)$, a safety violation.

If $|J|=1$, append a fully synchronous tail. Each robot performs at
most one nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in the whole execution, contradicting the
unboundedness in $(\ast)$. This tail witnesses the liveness violation,
and the safety violation of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ precedes it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied in every case, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- lemma-71: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-2-OB-R}
$\mathrm{EO}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-71 -->
<!-- proof-93: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$.
An $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot has a unique visible state, so in a normalized frame the
rule of $\mathcal A$ is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)).

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star})$.}
Since $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ contains the fully synchronous executions, take the
execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}, with both robots activated in
every round and a normalized frame at every ${\mathit{Look}}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:osp_not_ob_f} it violates $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$, the
degenerate cases $\lambda=0$ and $c_2=0$ being treated there as well.
For $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$: if $\lambda=0$ the configuration never changes,
the joint-stop sequence has the single term $C_0$ and the perpetuity
condition fails; if $\lambda\neq0$ then $C_1\neq C_0$ and, by
Remark~\ref{rem:epgs-normalized-rule}, $d_1=\sigma_2 d_0$ with
$\sigma_2\neq2$, so the expansion condition fails at $i=0$.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)=(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star})$.} Take
the alternating singleton activation with an empty fully synchronous
prefix (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}) and a normalized frame at every ${\mathit{Look}}$.
Since $\lambda^{\star}\neq0$, the first activation of $a$ is the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and is performed while $b$ is not
activated, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition
of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$. For $\mathrm{OSPO}$: each
activation moves the active robot directly away from its peer by half
the observed distance, so $d$ is non-decreasing throughout the
execution and in fact $d\mapsto\tfrac32 d$ at every activation, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i) with
$\sigma_1=1-\lambda^{\star}e^{\mathrm{i}\theta^{\star}}=\tfrac32$.
Hence no interval on which $d$ strictly decreases exists and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails.

In both cases a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-93 -->
<!-- lemma-72: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-3-FC-A}
$\mathrm{ES}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-72 -->
<!-- proof-94: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Fix distinct initial positions $a_0,b_0$, and put
$A=2a_0-b_0$, $B=2b_0-a_0$, and $P=\{A,a_0,b_0,B\}$.

Run fully synchronous cycles, choosing local frames that give
the two robots identical normalized observations.
Their colors remain equal.
If every computed Move is zero, this fair, time-divergent execution
keeps the robots at their distinct initial positions.
Thus $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails, and the joint-stop sequence consists
only of $C_0$, violating the perpetuity condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$.

Otherwise, consider the first round with a nonzero output.
Let both robots perform their Looks before either performs its
Compute, and then let both complete their Computes.
They obtain the same normalized displacement $(\lambda,\theta)$,
with $\lambda>0$, and the same new color $\gamma'$.
Delay the Move of $b$ until after $a$ completes its Move.
At the landing of $a$, both robots are stationary, although
$b$ still has a pending Move.
Writing $p\ne a_0$ for the landing point of $a$, this joint stop
has midpoint
\[
  \frac{p+b_0}{2}\ne\frac{a_0+b_0}{2}.
\]
Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) gives a finite violation
of $\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}$, which persists under every extension.

Suppose first that $(\lambda,\theta)\ne(2,0)$.
Since the Look of $a$ observed the initial configuration,
its landing point satisfies $p\ne B$.
No valid exchange time $T_1$ precedes this first completion,
because both cumulative nonzero-move counts were zero.
If $p\notin P$, the stationary-position requirement of
$\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ is already violated.
Otherwise $p\in\{A,b_0\}$.
The exchange configuration requiring zero Moves by $a$
is now impossible.
The other two require $a$ to reach $B$ with exactly one
completed nonzero Move.
However, any subsequent arrival at $B$ while respecting
the segment constraint requires a second completed nonzero Move:
the exterior endpoint $B$ cannot lie in the interior of
a straight movement contained in $[A,B]$.
Thus no continuation satisfies the exchange phase.
Complete the pending cycle of $b$ and append an arbitrary
admissible fair, time-divergent continuation.
Both predicates fail on the resulting execution.

It remains to consider $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.
Then $a$ lands at $B$.
Without reactivating $a$, let $b$ complete its already computed
Move, whose destination is $A$.
The robots are now at the distinct positions $(B,A)$,
both have color $\gamma'$, and neither has a pending cycle.

Let $\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$ have exactly the same transition
rule as $\mathcal A$, but designated initial color $\gamma'$.
Apply the general impossibility of stable $\mathrm{RDV}$
in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A}$ used in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_fc_a} to $\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$.
It supplies an admissible fair, time-divergent execution
from some distinct initial positions that fails stable rendezvous.
An orientation-preserving similarity maps those positions
to $(B,A)$.
Transforming the local frames accordingly preserves every
local observation and color transition, so variable
disorientation allows this counterexecution to be reproduced
from the reached configuration.

Append that execution to the finite prefix.
The resulting execution is admissible, fair, and time-divergent.
Its failure of stable rendezvous violates the terminal
condition of $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$, while the earlier violation of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}$ persists.
Thus a single execution violates both predicates, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-94 -->
<!-- lemma-73: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-4-FC-S}
$\mathrm{EZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-73 -->
<!-- proof-95: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
The initial colors being common, while both robots are activated
simultaneously their colors follow a common eventually periodic
sequence $c_0,g(c_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) and the
configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, the two robots never move and
remain at distinct positions, so the convergence condition of
$\mathrm{ZCC}$ fails, while the joint-stop sequence has the single term
$C_0$ and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails. This
fair execution witnesses both liveness violations.
 
Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$ and
replace round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated
repeatedly (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}); the interval may be made arbitrarily
long, the activations of $b$ being placed far enough in the future to
keep the execution fair. The configuration was unchanged before the
interval, so the first activation of $a$ in it is the first nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and it is solo; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety violation.
 
The visible state of $a$ is constantly $c_t$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) its rule is a single pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$ with $\lambda\neq0$, and $b$ is at rest throughout.
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ every activation of $a$ is a complete cycle, so no
operation is pending at the end of any of them. Put
$\sigma_1:=1-\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}$ and $c_1:=|\sigma_1|$, and
write $a_0:=a(0)$, $b_0:=b(0)$ and $d:=\|b_0-a_0\|$.
 
If $c_1=0$, the robot $a$ reaches the position of $b$ at the first
activation, and no operation is pending at that time. Use the
coincidence continuation described in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}, with $a_0,b_0$ kept fixed. It either
keeps both positions fixed forever, so that the zig-zag condition
fails, or produces a finite violation of the collision-freedom
condition; in either case $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$ fails.
 
Assume $c_1\neq0$, and put $\psi:=\arg\sigma_1$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(iii)). The vector $w_j:=b_0-a(j)$ satisfies
$w_j=\sigma_1^{\,j}w_0\neq0$, so every ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$ in the interval
observes distinct positions, and
\[
  f_a(j)=\|a(j)-a_0\|=\|w_0-\sigma_1^{\,j}w_0\|
        =d\,\bigl|1-c_1^{\,j}e^{\mathrm{i}j\psi}\bigr| .
\]
As $b$ stands still, $\|b(j)-a_0\|=d$, so the collision-freedom
condition requires $f_a(j)\le d$, that is $c_1^{\,j}\le2\cos(j\psi)$.
Note that $\sigma_1=1$ would force $\lambda=0$, so $c_1\neq1$ whenever
$\psi\equiv0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\psi\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(iii)
  provides $k\ge1$ with $\cos(k\psi)\le-\tfrac12<0$; making the
  interval long enough to reach the $k$-th activation, the
  collision-freedom condition fails there, a safety violation.
  Append an arbitrary fair, time-divergent continuation.
\item If $\psi\equiv0$ and $c_1>1$, that is $\theta=\pi$, then
  $f_a(j)=(c_1^{\,j}-1)d$ exceeds $d$ as soon as $c_1^{\,j}>2$, and the
  collision-freedom condition again fails after finitely many
  activations. Append an arbitrary fair, time-divergent continuation.
\item In the remaining contraction case $\psi\equiv0$ and $0<c_1<1$,
  that is $\sigma_1\in(0,1)$, end the solo interval after its first
  activation. Then $a(1)=b_0-\sigma_1(b_0-a_0)$ lies in the open
  segment $(a_0,b_0)$ and $b$ is still at $b_0$, so the robots still
  lie in the original initial segment in their original order, and
  neither has a pending operation. Apply the continuation property
  proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}, keeping the original initial
  positions fixed. It supplies a fair, time-divergent continuation
  violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$.
\end{itemize}
 
In every case the safety violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{EPG}^{*}}$ occurs
at the first activation of the solo interval, which belongs to the
prefix of each construction above, and every construction is a fair,
time-divergent continuation of that prefix. The violation therefore
persists (Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)), one fair infinite execution
violates both predicates, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-95 -->
<!-- lemma-74: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-4-FS-AM}
$\mathrm{EZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-74 -->
<!-- proof-96: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $A_M$,
which admits synchronous activations of one robot at a time
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}). Start with alternating singleton activations,
each cycle being completed before the next one begins, with normalized
frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ that observes distinct positions. This interval
activates one robot at a time, so Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift} applies
to it.
 
If no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, the two robots stay at $\iota$ at
distinct positions, so the convergence condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$
fails, and the joint-stop sequence has the single term $C_0$, so the
perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails. This fair execution
witnesses both liveness violations.
 
Assume therefore that a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs. The first one is performed
while the peer is not activated, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1)
the expansion condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety
violation. End the prefix at the completion of the cycle containing
this ${\mathit{Move}}$. This is a joint stop, with no pending operation.
 
Every ${\mathit{Look}}$ in the prefix observes distinct positions: before the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ the configuration is $\iota$, and that ${\mathit{Move}}$ is the last
operation of the prefix. Since the visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot is
its own color, Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1) shows that each robot that has
been activated $k$ times carries $g^{k}(c_0)$. Hence the two colors lie
on the same normalized color orbit, the orbit of $c_0$ under $g$.
 
If the robots coincide, use the coincidence continuation from
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}. Otherwise their colors lie on the same
normalized color orbit, so the continuation statement proved in
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fs_am} applies. In either case it supplies a
fair, time-divergent continuation violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, with
the original initial positions kept fixed. The safety violation
established in the prefix persists (Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)).
 
A single fair infinite execution therefore violates both predicates,
so Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-96 -->
<!-- lemma-75: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-4-OB-R}
$\mathrm{EZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-75 -->
<!-- proof-97: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$.
An $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot has a unique visible state, so in a normalized frame the
rule is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)).

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star})$.}
Since $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$ contains the fully synchronous executions, take the
execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1}, with both robots activated in
every round and a normalized frame at every ${\mathit{Look}}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_ob_f} that execution violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, the degenerate cases $\lambda=0$ and $c_2=0$
being treated there as well. For $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$: if $\lambda=0$ the
joint-stop sequence has the single term $C_0$ and the perpetuity
condition fails; if $\lambda\neq0$ then $C_1\neq C_0$ and, by
Remark~\ref{rem:epgs-normalized-rule}, $d_1=\sigma_2 d_0$ with
$\sigma_2\neq2$, so the expansion condition fails at $i=0$.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)=(\lambda^{\star},\theta^{\star})$.} Take
the alternating singleton activation with an empty fully synchronous
prefix (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}) and a normalized frame at every ${\mathit{Look}}$.
Since $\lambda^{\star}\neq0$, the first activation of $a$ is the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and is performed while $b$ is not
activated, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition
of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety violation. For ZCC: by Remark~\ref{rem:epgs-normalized-rule}, $c_1=\tfrac32$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i) each activation maps
$d\mapsto\tfrac32 d$; hence $d\to\infty$, the two robots do not
converge to a single point, and the convergence condition fails.

In both cases a single execution violates both predicates, the safety
violation being placed first and a fair infinite continuation of the
liveness violation being exhibited, so Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is
satisfied and Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-97 -->
<!-- lemma-76: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-6-FC-S}
$\mathrm{EX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-76 -->
<!-- proof-98: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
The initial colors being common, while both robots are activated
simultaneously their colors follow a common eventually periodic
sequence $\gamma_0,g(\gamma_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) and the
configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, the two robots never move, the
joint-stop sequence reduces to $C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the
attainment condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails, while the perpetuity
condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails as well
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2)).
 
Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$, replace
round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated $k\ge3$ times
in a row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and append a fair tail. The
configuration was unchanged before the interval, so the first
activation of $a$ in it is the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and
it is performed while $b$ is not activated; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety violation.
 
The visible state of $a$ is constantly $c_t$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) it applies the same displacement rule at
every activation. With the peer at rest, the only displacements that
satisfy the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ are those rotating
the segment clockwise by $45^\circ$ or by $90^\circ$; in particular if
$c_1=0$ then $d_i=0$, while all the permitted targets are nonzero, so
the transition condition fails. If $a$ departs from those two
displacements the transition condition fails at that point, and
otherwise $a$ reaches a configuration with $d_i\perp d_0$ in at most
two moves. At that moment both robots are at rest, but $a$ repeats the
same displacement at its next activation, so the stopping condition
fails (Lemma~\ref{lem:vec_not_fc_s},
\cite[Lemma~21]{NNW-SSS2025}). All of these are safety violations and
may be concatenated by Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2).
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-98 -->
<!-- lemma-77: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-6-FS-A}
$\mathrm{EX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-77 -->
<!-- proof-99: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Begin with a fully synchronous prefix, which is admissible under
$\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2} the two robots always carry the same
state $s_0,s_1,\dots$.

If $\lambda_{s_k}=0$ for every $k$, this fair execution contains no
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, the joint-stop sequence reduces to $C_0$, and
$d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails
and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails as well
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2)).

Otherwise take the least $k$ with $\lambda_{s_k}>0$. All earlier rounds
left the configuration at $\iota$. Activate $a$ alone in round $k$, so
that it performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution, and use the
freedom of $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ in the choice of ${\mathit{Look}}$ times: by
Lemma~\ref{lem:mid} the robot $b$ observes $a$ at a point $p_\mu$,
$\mu\in(0,1)$, of its movement segment. Let $b$ begin its ${\mathit{Move}}$ before
the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ ends, so that no time of $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ lies between the two
landings and the configuration after both landings is the term $C_1$ of
the joint-stop sequence following $C_0$.

An $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot cannot consult the internal state of its peer and
retains no previously observed angle or distance, so the displacement
of $b$ is determined by $p_\mu$ alone, and $C_1$ varies continuously
and non-constantly with $\mu$. The transition condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$ admits only finitely many successors of $C_0$, and the
expansion condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ admits exactly one, namely
the configuration with midpoint $c_0$ and difference vector $2d_0$.
Adding the countably many values of $\mu$ at which the two robots
coincide, Corollary~\ref{cor:continuum} provides a $\mu$ avoiding all
of them, and both the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:vec_not_fs_a}, \cite[Lemma~22]{NNW-SSS2025}) and the
expansion condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fail at $i=0$.

Both are safety violations witnessed at a finite time, hence preserved
by any fair tail (Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-99 -->
<!-- lemma-78: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-6-OB-R}
$\mathrm{EX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-78 -->
<!-- proof-100: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$.
Take the alternating singleton activation of $a$ and $b$ with an empty
fully synchronous prefix (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}) followed by an
arbitrary fair tail, and supply normalized frames. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a) the rule of $\mathcal A$ is a single
pair $(\lambda,\theta)$. Every round activates exactly one robot, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift} applies to this execution.

If $\lambda=0$, then since $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has no colors the two robots do not
move under any schedule, the joint-stop sequence reduces to $C_0$, and
$d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails
and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails.

Assume $\lambda\neq0$. The activation of $a$ in round~$1$ is then the
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and $b$ is not activated in that
round, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety violation.

For $\mathrm{VEC}$: if $c_1=0$, then $a$ lands on the position of $b$ in
round~$1$ and $d_1=0$, while all the targets permitted by the
transition condition are nonzero, so that condition fails. Otherwise
the only single displacements satisfying the transition condition are
those rotating the segment clockwise by $45^\circ$ or by $90^\circ$. If
$a$ departs from them the transition condition fails at that point;
otherwise $a$ reaches a configuration with $d_i\perp d_0$ in at most
two moves, and since the same displacement is applied at every
activation the robots move again immediately afterwards, so the
stopping condition fails. All of these are safety violations.

In every case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-100 -->
<!-- lemma-79: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-7-FC-S}
$\mathrm{EC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-79 -->
<!-- proof-101: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
The initial colors being common, while both robots are activated
simultaneously their colors follow a common eventually periodic
sequence $\gamma_0,g(\gamma_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) and the
configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, this fair execution contains no
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, so $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0\neq1$ and the single-move condition of
$\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace$ fails, while the joint-stop sequence reduces to $C_0$
and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(2)).
 
Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$, replace
round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated twice in a row
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and append a fair tail. The configuration was
unchanged before the interval, so the first activation of $a$ in it is
the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and it is performed while $b$
is not activated; by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion
condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$.
 
Since $b$ is not activated, the visible state of $a$ is constantly
$c_t$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) it applies the same pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$, with $\lambda\neq0$, at both activations. If
$c_1=0$ then $a$ lands on the position of $b$ at the first activation,
so $a(t)=b(t)$ at that time and the collision-freedom condition fails.
If $c_1\neq0$ the distance stays positive, so both activations are
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations and $\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2\neq1$, which violates the
single-move condition. All of these are safety violations
witnessed at a finite time, hence preserved by the fair tail
(Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2)).
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-101 -->
<!-- lemma-80: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-7-OB-R}
$\mathrm{EC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{R})$.
<!-- end lemma-80 -->
<!-- proof-102: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Rsynch}}\xspace$.
Take the alternating singleton activation of $a$ and $b$ with an empty
fully synchronous prefix (Lemma~\ref{lem:altA}) followed by an
arbitrary fair tail, and supply normalized frames. The visible state of
an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot is unique, so the rule is a single pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)). Every round
activates exactly one robot, so Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift} applies.

If $\lambda=0$, then since $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has no colors the two robots do not
move under any schedule, so $\mathrm{moves}(a)=0\neq1$ and the single-move
condition of $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace$ fails, while the joint-stop sequence
reduces to $C_0$ and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$
fails.

Assume $\lambda\neq0$. The activation of $a$ in round~$1$ is the first
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution and $b$ is not activated in that round,
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:solo-drift}(1) the expansion condition of
$\mathrm{EPG}^{*}$ fails at $i=0$, a safety violation.

For $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace$: if $c_1=0$, then $a$ lands on the position of $b$
in round~$1$, so $a(t)=b(t)$ at that time and the collision-freedom
condition fails. Otherwise each activation maps $d\mapsto c_1d$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i)) and $d$ stays positive, so the activations
of $a$ in rounds~$1$ and~$3$ are both nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations and
$\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2\neq1$, which violates the single-move condition.

In every case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-102 -->
<!-- proof-103: body_md -->
Fix an algorithm and initial positions $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, with outer
points $0$ and $3d$. Under normalized observations, write the state
transition as $s\mapsto g(s)$ and the global displacement as
$\Lambda_s w$, where $w$ points to the peer and
$\Lambda_s=\lambda_sR_{\theta_s}$.

If the state orbit from the designated initial state contains no
nonzero output, fair alternating activations leave both robots
stationary. Neither the exchange phase nor the perpetual-motion
requirement of $\mathrm{SRO}$ is satisfied. Otherwise, let $s$ be the
first state in that orbit with a nonzero output. Activate only $a$
until it completes that first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$; all preceding ${\mathit{Move}}$
operations are zero. We distinguish two cases.

\emph{Case 1: $\Lambda_s=2I$.}
Robot $a$ moves to $3d$. The relative segment reverses direction
without shrinking, violating both permitted rotation types of
$\mathrm{SRO}$. Keep $a$ inactive and activate $b$ until it reaches
state $s$; its preceding normalized outputs are zero, so the
configuration is unchanged and $b$ sees a peer at distance $d$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay} the robot $b$ then lands at $4d$,
outside the interval allowed by $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ and outside the endpoint set
allowed by $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$. All three violations are irreversible, so append a
fair suffix.

\emph{Case 2: $\Lambda_s\neq2I$.}
The first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ makes the common exchange phase unattainable, so
both exchange tasks have already failed. If it also violates
$\mathrm{SRO}$, append a fair suffix. Otherwise the robots remain
distinct. If the normalized state orbit of $a$ after this ${\mathit{Move}}$ contains
another nonzero output, keep $b$ inactive until that output is
executed; Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} then violates $\mathrm{SRO}$,
and a fair suffix again completes the construction.

If no further nonzero output occurs in that orbit, keep $a$ inactive
and let $b$ traverse the same initial state sequence and perform its
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. If this violates $\mathrm{SRO}$, we are done.
Otherwise the robots are still distinct and both are now in state
$g(s)$, from which every subsequent normalized output is zero. Fair
alternating activations therefore leave the configuration stationary
forever, violating the perpetual-motion requirement of $\mathrm{SRO}$.
This specifies a fair infinite continuation rather than an infinite
solo execution.
<!-- end proof-103 -->
<!-- lemma-81: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-10-FC-A}
$\mathrm{RS}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-81 -->
<!-- proof-104: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Run fully synchronous cycles with identical normalized observations
until the first nonzero output.
Throughout this zero-Move prefix, the positions remain unchanged
and the colors remain equal.
If no nonzero output occurs, the resulting fair, time-divergent
execution violates both the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$
and the terminal rendezvous condition of $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$.

Otherwise, identify the plane with $\mathbb C$ using
orientation-preserving coordinates in which $a_0=0$ and $b_0=1$.
The outer exchange points are then $A=-1$ and $B=2$.
In the first round with a nonzero output, let both robots perform
their Looks before either performs its Compute, and then let both
complete their Computes.
Write $z=\lambda e^{\mathrm i\theta}\ne0$ for their common normalized
displacement coefficient and $\gamma'$ for their common updated color.
Their computed destinations are $z$ for $a$ and $1-z$ for $b$.

Delay the Move of $b$ until strictly after $a$ has landed,
and do not reactivate $a$ in the meantime.
There is therefore a joint stop with positions $(z,1)$,
whose relative-position vector is
\[
  d_1=1-z,\qquad d_0=1.
\]

\emph{Case $z\ne2$.}
The first nonzero Move of $a$ does not land at $B$.
Since its Look observed the initial configuration,
the first-move obstruction of Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}
applies, so no extension can satisfy the exchange phase of $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$.

If
\[
  d_1\notin\left\{-\mathrm i,\frac{1-\mathrm i}{2}\right\},
\]
then neither $\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$ holds at the first
transition, and $\mathrm{SRO}$ already fails.
Otherwise
\[
  z\in\left\{1+\mathrm i,\frac{1+\mathrm i}{2}\right\}.
\]
Let $b$ complete its stored Move while $a$ remains at rest.
The next joint-stop vector is $d_2=1-2z$, and
\[
  \frac{d_2}{d_1}=
  \begin{cases}
    2-\mathrm i, & z=1+\mathrm i,\\
    1-\mathrm i, & z=(1+\mathrm i)/2.
  \end{cases}
\]
Its modulus is respectively $\sqrt5$ or $\sqrt2$.
Thus the distance increases, whereas $\mathbf{C1}$ and
$\mathbf{C2}$ permit only factors $1$ and $1/\sqrt2$.
Hence $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails at this second transition.
Once the pending cycle of $b$ is complete, append an arbitrary
admissible fair, time-divergent continuation.
Both finite violations persist.

\emph{Case $z=2$.}
The first joint-stop vector is $d_1=-1$, which satisfies neither
$\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$.
Thus $\mathrm{SRO}$ has already failed.
Without reactivating $a$, let $b$ complete its stored Move.
The robots are now at $(B,A)=(2,-1)$, both have color $\gamma'$,
and neither has a pending cycle.

Let $\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$ have the same transition rule as
$\mathcal A$, but designated initial color $\gamma'$.
Apply the general impossibility of stable $\mathrm{RDV}$
in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A}$ used in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_fc_a}.
It gives a fair, time-divergent counterexecution of
$\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$ from distinct initial positions.
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-3-FC-A},
an orientation-preserving similarity and corresponding choices
of local frames reproduce this counterexecution from $(B,A)$.
The reached colors and absence of pending cycles make it
a valid continuation of our prefix.

This continuation violates the terminal rendezvous condition
of $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$, while preserving the earlier violation of
$\mathrm{SRO}$.
In every case, a single admissible fair, time-divergent execution
violates both predicates.
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-104 -->
<!-- lemma-82: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-11-FC-S}
$\mathrm{RZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-82 -->
<!-- proof-105: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
As above the colors follow a common eventually periodic sequence
$c_0,g(c_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) while both robots are
activated simultaneously, and the configuration stays at $\iota$.

If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, so the
sequence of configurations reduces to $C_0$ and the perpetuity
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails, while the robots remain at distinct
positions and the convergence condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fails. This
fair execution witnesses both liveness violations.

Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$ and
replace round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated $k$
times in a row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}, with $k$ large enough for what
follows). Since $b$ is not activated, the visible state of $a$ is
constantly $c_t$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) the rule is the
single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$ with $\lambda\neq0$, and $b$ is at rest
throughout.

For $\mathrm{SRO}$: if $c_1=0$ the robot $a$ lands on the position of
$b$ at the first activation, and $d_{i+1}=0$ satisfies neither
$\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$, so the second condition of
$\mathrm{SRO}$ fails. If $c_1\neq0$, taking $k\ge2$ makes $a$ perform
two nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations with its peer at rest, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$
fails. Either way this is a safety violation in the prefix.

For $\mathrm{ZCC}$: put $\sigma_1:=1-\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}$ and
$c_1:=|\sigma_1|$, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-4-FC-S}.
Under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$ every activation of $a$ is a complete cycle, so neither
robot has a pending operation at the end of any of them.
If $c_1=0$, end the solo interval after its first activation; the
robots then coincide. Use the coincidence continuation described in
the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}. This either keeps both
positions fixed forever, so that the zig-zag condition fails, or
produces a finite violation of the collision-freedom condition.
If $c_1\neq0$ and $\sigma_1\notin(0,1)$, the cases $\psi\not\equiv0$
and $\psi\equiv0$ with $c_1>1$ in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-4-FC-S} apply verbatim: for $k$ large enough the
collision-freedom condition fails at a finite time, and an arbitrary
fair, time-divergent continuation is appended.
In the remaining contraction case $\sigma_1\in(0,1)$, after the $k$
activations we have $a(k)=b(0)-\sigma_1^{\,k}\bigl(b(0)-a(0)\bigr)$
and $b$ is still at $b(0)$. Thus the robots still lie in the original
initial segment in their original order, and neither has a pending
operation. Apply the continuation property proved in
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}, keeping the original initial positions
fixed. It supplies a fair, time-divergent continuation violating
$\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, while preserving the safety violation of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ already obtained in the prefix.

The safety violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ occurs in the prefix and
precedes every continuation used above, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-105 -->
<!-- lemma-83: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-11-FS-AM}
$\mathrm{RZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-83 -->
<!-- proof-106: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $A_M$,
which admits synchronous activations of one robot at a time
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}). Begin with an interval in which $b$ is never
activated and $a$ alone is activated, one complete cycle at a time,
with normalized frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ at which the robots are
distinct. Since in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ activations that only update the color may be
interleaved, the length of this interval is measured in nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
operations and not in activations. Continue it until $a$ lands on the
position of $b$ or completes its second nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, whichever comes
first. As long as $a$ has not landed on $b$, every ${\mathit{Look}}$ of $a$
observes distinct positions, so its color follows
$c_0,g(c_0),g^2(c_0),\dots$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:pumpB2}).
 
If in this interval $a$ lands on the position of $b$, then
$d_{i+1}=0$ and neither $\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$ can hold, so
the second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails at that point, a safety
violation.
 
Suppose next that $a$ never lands on $b$ and performs at most one
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ along its whole solo orbit, which includes the case in
which no state produces a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$. Then the periodic part of the
orbit of $c_0$ contains no nonzero rule. Stop activating $a$ once its
color has entered that periodic part, and activate $b$ alone the same
number of times. The color of $b$ follows the same finite orbit as
long as its ${\mathit{Look}}$s observe distinct positions. If $b$ lands on the
position of $a$, the second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails as in
the previous case, and the prefix is ended there as described below.
Otherwise both robots now carry colors in the periodic part, at
distinct positions, and neither has a pending operation. Continue with
alternating singleton activations forever. Every ${\mathit{Look}}$ observes
distinct positions and every output is zero, so the positions remain
fixed. This fair, time-divergent execution contains only finitely many
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations, so the sequence $(C_i)$ is finite and the
perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails, while $f_r$ is eventually
constant and the zig-zag condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fails.
 
In the remaining case $a$ does not land on $b$ and performs two nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ operations with its peer at rest, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the rotation condition and
$\mathbf{C3}$ cannot both hold, whatever the internal states, and the
second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails.
 
In each case with a safety violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$, the
violation is produced by the last ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the prefix constructed so
far, and every ${\mathit{Look}}$ in that prefix observed distinct positions. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1), each robot that has been activated $k$ times
carries $g^{k}(c_0)$.
End the prefix at this joint stop, with no pending operation.
If the robots coincide, use the coincidence continuation
from Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}. Otherwise their colors lie on the
same normalized color orbit, so the continuation statement
proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fs_am} applies.
In either case it supplies a fair, time-divergent continuation
violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, with the original initial
positions kept fixed. The safety violation established
in the prefix persists.
 
All the blocks may be concatenated by Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2)(3),
and a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-106 -->
<!-- lemma-84: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-13-FC-S}
$\mathrm{RX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-84 -->
<!-- proof-107: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
The colors follow a common sequence $\gamma_0,g(\gamma_0),\dots$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) while both robots are activated
simultaneously, and the configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, so the
sequence of configurations reduces to $C_0$ and both the perpetuity
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ and the attainment condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$, which would require $d_0\perp d_0$, fail.
 
Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$, replace
round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated $k\ge3$ times
in a row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and append a fair tail. The visible
state of $a$ is constantly $c_t$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) it applies the same pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$, with $\lambda\neq0$, at every activation.
 
If $c_1=0$, the robot $a$ lands on the position of $b$ at the first
activation and $d_{i+1}=0$; both $\mathbf{C1}$, $\mathbf{C2}$ and all
the targets permitted by the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ are
nonzero, so the second conditions of both tasks fail simultaneously.
 
If $c_1\neq0$, the same robot performs two nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations with
its peer at rest, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails. For $\mathrm{VEC}$ the argument of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-6-FC-S} applies: the only single displacements
satisfying the transition condition rotate the segment clockwise by
$45^\circ$ or by $90^\circ$, so if $a$ departs from them the transition
condition fails, and otherwise $a$ reaches a configuration with
$d_i\perp d_0$ in at most two moves and then repeats the same
displacement, so the stopping condition fails. All of these are safety
violations.
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-107 -->
<!-- lemma-85: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-13-FS-A}
$\mathrm{RX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-85 -->
<!-- proof-108: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Define the execution by starting, as in the first stage of
Lemma~\ref{lem:dmsd_not_fs_a}, with a finite fully synchronous prefix
that freezes the common state of the two robots, which $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$ admits
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}), then placing an observation-during-movement
interval (Lemma~\ref{lem:mid}), and finally appending an arbitrary fair
tail.

If $\lambda_s=0$ for every state $s$, the configuration never changes,
so the sequence $(C_i)$ is finite and $d_0\not\perp d_0$; both the
perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ and the attainment condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$ fail.

Otherwise, in the round of the first common state $s$ with
$\lambda_s>0$, activate $a$ alone so that it performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$,
and let the robot $b$, in state $s$, observe a point $p_\mu$,
$\mu\in(0,1)$, of that movement segment (Lemma~\ref{lem:mid}, which is
admissible for $K=A$).
Delay the Move of $b$ until after $a$ has landed, so that the
landing configuration of $a$ is a joint stop.
Do not reactivate $a$ before $b$ completes this Move.
If this ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ is neither the clockwise
$90^\circ$ rotation about the peer ($\mathbf{C1}$) nor the clockwise
$90^\circ$ rotation about the midpoint ($\mathbf{C2}$), then by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second condition of
$\mathrm{SRO}$ already fails.
If it is one of them, the robot $b$ performs the displacement
it computes from $p_\mu$, and the distance at the time both robots
are at rest is a non-constant continuous function of $\mu$.
The distances permitted by $\mathrm{SRO}$ belong to the
countable set generated from $d$ by the ratios of $\mathbf{C1}$ and
$\mathbf{C2}$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:continuum} some $\mu$ avoids
that set and $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ fails.
                                                           
                                                                      
                                                              
                                                                       
                                                                    
                                                                     
                                                                
                                                         
                                                                  
                                                                        
                                                                       
                                                                  
                                                                    
                                                                     
                                          

In the same observation, an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot $b$ cannot consult the internal
state of its peer and retains no previously observed angle or distance,
so its displacement is determined by $p_\mu$ alone. The segment
obtained after both landings varies continuously and non-constantly
with $\mu$, whereas the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ admits
only finitely many targets, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:continuum} some
$\mu$ avoids them. Both excluded sets being countable, a single
$\mu\in(0,1)$ avoids both, and the transition condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$ fails in the same execution.

Both are safety violations, so they may be concatenated by
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-108 -->
<!-- lemma-86: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-14-FC-S}
$\mathrm{RC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-86 -->
<!-- proof-109: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
The colors follow a common sequence $\gamma_0,g(\gamma_0),\dots$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}) while both robots are activated
simultaneously, and the configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
If $\lambda_{c_j}=0$ for every $j$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, so
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=0\neq1$ and the single-move condition of $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace$
fails, while the sequence of configurations reduces to $C_0$ and the
perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails.
 
Otherwise let $t$ be the least $j$ with $\lambda_{c_j}\neq0$, replace
round $t$ by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated twice in a row
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), and append a fair tail. The visible state of
$a$ is constantly $c_t$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b) it
applies the same pair $(\lambda,\theta)$, with $\lambda\neq0$, at both
activations. If $c_1=0$, the robot $a$ lands on the position of $b$ at
the first activation, so $a(t)=b(t)$ at that time and the
collision-freedom condition of $\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace$ fails, while
$d_{i+1}=0$ satisfies neither $\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$ and the
second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails. If $c_1\neq0$, both
activations are nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations, so $\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2\neq1$ and
the single-move condition fails, while
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} makes the second condition of
$\mathrm{SRO}$ fail as well. All of these are safety violations
witnessed at a finite time, hence preserved by the fair tail
(Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)).
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-109 -->
<!-- lemma-87: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-8-FC-A}
$\mathrm{OS}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-87 -->
<!-- proof-110: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Use coordinates $A=0$, $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line.
Run fully synchronous cycles with identical normalized observations
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}). While every ${\mathit{Move}}$ is zero, the positions stay
fixed and the colors stay equal.

\emph{No nonzero output.} If no nonzero output occurs, continue
forever. The robots stay distinct at constant distance. So
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails (no rendezvous), and $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails
(no decreasing phase). This execution witnesses both liveness
violations.

\emph{A nonzero output occurs.} Otherwise let $\gamma$ be the common
color at the start of the first round with a nonzero output. Let
$(\lambda,\theta)$, with $\lambda>0$, be the normalized displacement
for the initial configuration with peer color $\gamma$. Since
$\mathcal A$ is deterministic, $(\lambda,\theta)$ is known before that
round is scheduled.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$.} Replace the round by two solo
activations of $a$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), followed by a fair tail. The
peer color stays $\gamma$, so $a$ applies $(\lambda,\theta)$ twice
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b)). The first of these ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations
observes $\iota$ and does not land at $B$. So the exchange phase of
$\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ is unsatisfiable (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}).

As in Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-2-FC-S}, either a collision occurs or
$m_a=2,m_b=0$; either way $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ is violated. All these
violations are safety violations.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.} Let both robots Look, and then
both Compute; their colors become a common $\gamma'$. Delay the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of
$b$ so that it begins strictly after the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ ends
(Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}). The robot $a$ moves from $d$ to $3d$ while
$b$ rests at $2d$, so they collide, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails.

Then let $b$ complete its ${\mathit{Move}}$ to $A$. The robots are now at $(B,A)$
with common color $\gamma'$, and neither has a pending operation. Let
$\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$ be $\mathcal A$ with initial color $\gamma'$. The
impossibility of stable $\mathrm{RDV}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A}$ used in
Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_fc_a} gives a counterexecution of
$\mathcal A_{\gamma'}$. Transport it to $(B,A)$ by an
orientation-preserving similarity, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-3-FC-A}, and
append it. This continuation violates the terminal rendezvous
condition of $\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace$ and witnesses that liveness violation. The safety
violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ precedes it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2)(3) is satisfied in every case, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-110 -->
<!-- lemma-88: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-8-FS-S}
$\mathrm{OS}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-88 -->
<!-- proof-111: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
Use coordinates $A=0$, $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line,
and normalized frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ at which the robots are distinct.
The next color and the displacement of a robot then depend only on its
own color.
 
\emph{First part.} Activate $\{a\},\{b\},\{a\},\dots$, which $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
admits. By the $\pi$-symmetry of $\iota$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:silent},
both robots follow $c_0,g(c_0),\dots$ until the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$.
 
If there is no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$, continue forever. The robots stay at
$\iota$, so they never meet; $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails because
$d$ is constant. This execution witnesses both liveness violations.
 
Otherwise let $k$ be least with $\lambda_{g^k(c_0)}\neq0$. The robot
$a$ performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ at its $(k+1)$-st activation; let
that ${\mathit{Move}}$ complete, whether or not the two robots meet during it.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If its landing point is not $B$, $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ is
  unsatisfiable (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}).
  \item If it is $B$, let $b$ be activated next; it lands at
  $4d\notin[A,B]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}), so $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$
  fails.
\end{itemize}
Either way $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ suffers a safety violation at a finite time.
This argument uses only the landing points, so it does not assume that
the two robots stay distinct.
 
If a collision has occurred in the prefix constructed so far,
the collision-freedom condition of $\mathrm{OSPO}$ has already
failed. Both predicates have then suffered safety violations,
so append an arbitrary fair, time-divergent continuation.
 
Otherwise the first move of $a$ did not land at $B$, since
a move from $d$ to $3d$ would pass through the stationary
robot at $2d$. The safety violation of $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ has
therefore already occurred, and $b$ has not yet performed
its $(k+1)$-st activation.
 
Activate $b$ once. If a collision occurs during this cycle,
both predicates again have safety violations and an arbitrary
fair tail completes the construction. Otherwise let $T$ be
the end of this cycle. Both robots have observed distinct
positions, so they now carry
$\gamma=g^{k+1}(c_0)$, neither has a pending operation,
and $m_a(T)=m_b(T)=1$.
 
Every execution satisfying $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ has
$m_a(t_j)=m_b(t_j)=j$ at its phase boundaries.
Consequently $|m_a-m_b|\le1$ at all times, and both counts
are unbounded.
 
Let $J_\gamma=\{i\ge0:\lambda_{g^i(\gamma)}\ne0\}$.
If $|J_\gamma|\ge2$, let $i'$ be its second element and
activate $a$ alone for $i'+1$ cycles, stopping this
construction at the first collision if one occurs.
A collision violates $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$; otherwise
the resulting counts are $m_a=3$, $m_b=1$, which also
violate it. Append an arbitrary fair tail.
 
If $|J_\gamma|\le1$, use a fully synchronous fair tail.
A collision again violates $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$.
If no collision occurs, each robot performs at most one
further nonzero move, contradicting the required
unboundedness of the counts.
 
Thus one fair infinite execution violates both predicates,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-111 -->
<!-- lemma-89: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-8-OB-F}
$\mathrm{OS}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-89 -->
<!-- proof-112: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace$.
Use coordinates $A=0$, $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line
and take the infinite fully synchronous execution of
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1} from this instance, with a normalized frame at
every ${\mathit{Look}}$. The visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot is unique, so the rule
is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)),
and by Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii) the distance at the end of round~$k$
is $d(k)=c_2^{\,k}d(0)$.
 
\emph{Violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$.}
If the two robots ever occupy the same point, the collision-freedom
condition fails at a finite time; this is a safety violation. It covers
$c_2=0$, where they coincide at the end of round~$1$ and the
coincidence is maintained by Lemma~\ref{lem:keep-coincident}, and also
the case in which they meet while travelling inside a round.
 
Otherwise $d(t)>0$ throughout. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1} every joint
stop of the execution carries one of the round-boundary distances
$d(k)$, so the restriction of $d$ to $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{ab}}$ is monotone. The turning
times required by $\mathrm{OSPO}$ are joint stops, so by the criterion
stated after Definition~\ref{def:osp} no strictly decreasing phase can
be followed by a strictly increasing one, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$
fails. This is a liveness violation, and the fully synchronous
execution is itself the fair infinite continuation along which it
persists.
 
\emph{Violation of $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$.}
If $\lambda=0$ no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, so the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
demanded by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null} does not exist. This is a
progress violation, witnessed by the same infinite fully synchronous
execution. If $\lambda\neq0$, both robots perform a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in
round~$1$, so an admissible exchange configuration must be
$(B,A)=(3d,0)$ with move counts $(1,1)$. When
$(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$ the landing of round~$1$ is not this
configuration, so the requirement of Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move} is
unmet. When $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$ round~$1$ does land at $(3d,0)$,
but round~$2$ applies the same rule and sends $a$ to $3d+2(0-3d)=-3d$
and $b$ to $0+2(3d-0)=6d$, both outside $[A,B]=[0,3d]$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:srdv_not_ob_f}). These are safety violations witnessed
at a finite time.
 
In each case a single execution violates both predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-112 -->
<!-- lemma-90: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-9-FS-S}
$\mathrm{OV}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-90 -->
<!-- proof-113: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
Use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-8-FS-S}. It violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$: in that proof the violation comes from a
collision up to $T$, from the move-count requirement $(\ast)$ in the
second part, or, if no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs, from the constancy of $d$,
and none of these refers to the exchange task. We show that the same
execution also violates $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace}$, where $P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$.

If no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs, $(\mathrm{P1})$ fails by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}; the execution of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-8-FS-S} itself is the fair continuation witnessing
this liveness violation.

Otherwise, as in that lemma, the two robots traverse the same states
until the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ and $a$ is activated first, so that ${\mathit{Move}}$
is performed by $a$ and its ${\mathit{Look}}$ observes $\iota$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If it lands outside $P$, $(\mathrm{P1\text{-}b})$ fails.
  \item If it lands in $P\setminus\{B\}$, $(\mathrm{P1\text{-}c})$ is
  unsatisfiable (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}).
  \item If it lands at $B$, then $b$ lands at $4d\notin P$
  (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}), and $(\mathrm{P1\text{-}b})$ fails.
\end{itemize}
In each case this is a safety violation at a finite time, whether or
not a collision occurs, since $\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace$ permits passing.

In either case a single execution violates both predicates;
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-113 -->
<!-- lemma-91: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-9-OB-F}
$\mathrm{OV}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{F})$.
<!-- end lemma-91 -->
<!-- proof-114: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Fsynch}}\xspace$.
Take the fully synchronous execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA1} with
normalized frames. By Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a), both robots apply
one and the same pair $(\lambda,\theta)$ in every round. Use $A=0$,
$a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ and $P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$.

\emph{OSPO.} If a collision occurs, $\Phi_{\mathrm{OSPO}}$ fails.
Otherwise the joint stops lie between rounds when $\lambda>0$, and the
distance there is $c_2^{\,k}d(0)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii)). This is
monotone, so no decreasing phase can be followed by an increasing one.
The execution itself witnesses this liveness violation.

\emph{VSS.} We distinguish three cases.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $\lambda=0$, $(\mathrm{P1})$ fails by
  Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}. This is a liveness violation of the same
  execution.
  \item If $\lambda>0$ and $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$, the round-$1$
  ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ completes earliest and does not land at $B$. So
  $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{VSS}}\xspace}$ is unsatisfiable (Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}).
  \item If $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$, round $1$ yields $(3d,0)$ and
  round $2$ yields $(-3d,6d)$. Neither point lies in $P$, so
  $(\mathrm{P1\text{-}b})$ fails.
\end{itemize}
The last two violations are safety violations.

Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-114 -->
<!-- lemma-92: body_md -->
\label{lem:A2-15-FC-A}
$\mathrm{SZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-92 -->
<!-- proof-115: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Use coordinates $A=0$, $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line.
Run fully synchronous cycles with identical normalized observations
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidA2}). While every Move is zero, the positions stay
fixed and the colors stay equal.
 
\emph{No nonzero output.} Continue forever. The robots stay at $\iota$,
so $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails, while $f_r\equiv0$ for both robots, so the
zig-zag condition admits no strictly increasing pair and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$ fails. This execution witnesses both liveness
violations.
 
\emph{A nonzero output occurs.} Let $\gamma$ be the common color at the
start of the first round with a nonzero output, and let
$(\lambda,\theta)$, with $\lambda>0$, be the normalized displacement
for the initial configuration with peer color $\gamma$. Since
$\mathcal A$ is deterministic, $(\lambda,\theta)$ is known before that
round is scheduled.
