<!-- lemma-128: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-9-FC-A}
$\mathrm{RSZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-128 -->
<!-- proof-151: body_md -->
Use the construction of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-15-FC-A}.
If no nonzero output occurs, the perpetuity condition
of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails as well.
 
If the first nonzero rule is $(2,0)$, the first solo move
of $a$ reverses the segment and satisfies neither
$\mathbf{C1}$ nor $\mathbf{C2}$.
Thus $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ has a safety violation before
the continuation used in Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-15-FC-A}.
 
Otherwise keep the peer inactive during the initial
solo interval of $a$. If the first move lands on the peer,
the resulting zero segment violates the rotation condition
of $\mathrm{SRO}$. If it does not, choose the interval
to contain at least two nonzero moves of $a$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} then gives a safety
violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$.
 
For the $\mathrm{ZCC}$ component, use the finite safety
violation or the continuation property of Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s},
as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-15-FC-A}.
In the contraction case $\sigma_1\in(0,1)$ the robots remain in the
original initial segment in their original order after any number of
solo activations of $a$, so the continuation property applies at the
end of the interval chosen above.
The earlier safety violations persist.
 
Thus one fair infinite execution violates all three
predicates, and Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure}
gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-151 -->
<!-- lemma-129: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-9-FS-AM}
$\mathrm{RSZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-129 -->
<!-- proof-152: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $A_M$
and modify the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-11-FS-AM} as follows.
 
If no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}, and the first condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$
and the third condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fail as shown in
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-11-FS-AM}.
 
If the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ does not land at the $B=3d$ required
by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, then
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails at that point, and the execution
of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-11-FS-AM} may be used unchanged, so
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$ fail as shown there.
 
If it does land at $B$, then $(\lambda_s,\theta_s)=(2,0)$, and this
displacement is neither the $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation about the
peer required by $\mathbf{C1}$ nor the one about the midpoint required
by $\mathbf{C2}$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails already at this move and no second
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ is needed. Insert, immediately after this move, a
solo activation interval of $b$: activating $b$ alone until it reaches
the state $s$ leaves the configuration unchanged, since in all earlier
states $\lambda=0$ and the state transition of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ robot depends
only on its own state; then $b$ in state $s$ observes a peer at
distance $d$ and, in the normalized frame, receives a local input
isomorphic to that of $a$, so it applies the same $(2,0)$ and, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}, lands at $4d\notin[A,B]$, which violates
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$. Moreover, the first move of $a$ alone takes it
from $d$ to $3d$ while $b$ rests at $b_0=2d$, so
\[
  \|a-a_0\|=2d>d=\|b-a_0\|
\]
and the collision-freedom condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ has already
failed. No additional delayed ${\mathit{Move}}$ is needed; append an arbitrary fair,
time-divergent tail.
 
In every case a single fair execution violates all three predicates,
and the safety violations established in its prefix persist
(Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)), so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-152 -->
<!-- lemma-130: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-9-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RSZ}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-130 -->
<!-- proof-153: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$.
No lemma of Appendix~\ref{app:cf-two-task-disjunctions} has $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S}$
as a boundary class, so we construct the execution directly. The
visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot is unique, so in a normalized frame the
rule is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)).
 
\emph{Case $\lambda=0$.} Since $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has no colors, the two robots do
not move under any schedule. Hence the sequence of configurations
reduces to $C_0$ and the perpetuity condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails,
the robots remain at distinct positions and the convergence condition
of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fails, and no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ exists, so
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}. All
three are independent of the schedule, hence persist along any fair
infinite continuation.
 
\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.} Define the execution by one solo
activation of $a$, then one solo activation of $b$, then alternating
singleton activations and an arbitrary fair tail, all admissible under
$\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$. The displacement of $a$ is neither the $90^\circ$ clockwise
rotation about the peer ($\mathbf{C1}$) nor the one about the midpoint
($\mathbf{C2}$), so by Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails at this move. Moreover
$\sigma_1=1-2=-1$, so $c_1=1$ and $\psi\equiv\pi$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(iii)), whence
$f_a(1)=d\,|1-e^{\mathrm i\pi}|=2d>d=\|b(0)-a(0)\|$ and the
collision-freedom condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fails. Finally $a$ has
landed at $B=3d$, so the robot $b$, activated immediately afterwards,
receives in the normalized frame an isomorphic local input, applies the
same $(2,0)$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}, lands at
$4d\notin[A,B]$, so $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails.
 
\emph{Case $\lambda\neq0$ and $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$.} Define the
execution by an interval in which $a$ alone is activated $k$ times in a
row (Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}, with $k$ large enough for what follows),
then alternating singleton activations and an arbitrary fair tail. The
first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ is not the landing at $B$ required by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, so
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails at that point. For
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$: if that move is neither of type $\mathbf{C1}$
nor of type $\mathbf{C2}$, the second condition fails at once, which
includes the case $c_1=0$, since then $d_{i+1}=0$ while both types
require a nonzero value; if it is of one of the two types, the second
solo nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ makes the second condition fail by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves}. For $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, put $\sigma_1:=1-\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}$
and regard $\mathcal A$ as an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ algorithm with a single color, so
that the constructions in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}
apply. Every activation is a complete cycle under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$, so no
operation is pending at the end of the solo interval. If $c_1=0$,
the robots coincide after the first activation; end the solo interval
there and use the coincidence continuation described in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s}. This either keeps both positions fixed
forever or produces a finite violation of the collision-freedom
condition. If $c_1\neq0$ and $\sigma_1\notin(0,1)$, the
collision-freedom condition fails at a finite time for $k$ large
enough, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-15-FC-A}. In the remaining
contraction case $\sigma_1\in(0,1)$, the robots still lie in the
original initial segment in their original order after the $k$
activations, and neither has a pending operation; the continuation
property proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:zcc_not_fc_s} supplies a fair,
time-divergent continuation violating $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$, while
preserving the safety violations already obtained in the prefix.
 
In every case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-153 -->
<!-- lemma-131: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-10-FC-A}
$\mathrm{RSX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-131 -->
<!-- proof-154: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-16-FC-A}, which violates
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$. We show that it also violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$, under the same case distinction.

\emph{No nonzero output.} No nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, so the sequence
of joint-stop configurations reduces to $C_0$ and the perpetuity
condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails. The same infinite execution
witnesses this, together with the two liveness violations of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-16-FC-A}.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$.} The landing of $a$ is a joint
stop realizing $C_1=(3d,2d)$, so $d_1=-d_0$. Neither $\mathbf{C1}$,
which requires $d_1=R_{-90^\circ}d_0$, nor $\mathbf{C2}$, which
requires $d_1=2^{-1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_0$, is satisfied by a rotation by
$180^\circ$ of the same norm. The second condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$
therefore fails, a safety violation in the prefix.

\emph{Case $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$.} In the solo activation
interval of $a$ the robot applies the same pair $(\lambda,\theta)$,
with $\lambda\neq0$, at every activation
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(b)). If $c_1=0$ then $a$ lands on the
position of $b$ at the first activation and $d_1=0$, while
$\mathbf{C1}$ preserves the norm and $\mathbf{C2}$ scales it by
$2^{-1/2}$, so neither can hold with $d_0\neq0$; the second condition
of $\mathrm{SRO}$ fails. If $c_1\neq0$, the interval has length
$k\ge3$, so $a$ performs two nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations with its peer at
rest, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the rotation condition
and $\mathbf{C3}$ cannot both hold, so the second condition fails
again. Either way this is a safety violation in the prefix.

In the first case all three violations are liveness violations of one
infinite execution. In the other two the violation of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ is finite and precedes the continuations
supplied by Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-16-FC-A}. In either case
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-154 -->
<!-- lemma-132: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-10-FS-A}
$\mathrm{RSX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-132 -->
<!-- proof-155: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-13-FS-A}, which violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$.
 
If $\lambda_s=0$ for every state $s$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs and
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null},
while $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$ fail in the first
case of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-13-FS-A}.
 
Otherwise the robot $a$ performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in the round of
the first common state $s$ with $\lambda_s>0$. If its landing is not
the $B=3d$ required by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, then
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails at that point. If it is, then
$(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$, which is neither the $\mathbf{C1}$ rotation
about the peer nor the $\mathbf{C2}$ rotation about the midpoint, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ fails at once.
In this case the points of the movement segment of $a$ are
$p_\mu=(1+2\mu)d$ with $\mu\in(0,1)$, and the robot $b$, observing
$p_\mu$ in state $s$, applies the same $(2,0)$ in the normalized frame
and lands at $2d+2\bigl((1+2\mu)d-2d\bigr)=4\mu d$. Taking
$\mu\in(3/4,1)$ gives $4\mu d>3d$, so the robots leave
$[A,B]=[0,3d]$ and $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ fails. The set of
parameters to be excluded for the $\mathrm{VEC}$ violation is
countable, so such a $\mu$ can be chosen inside $(3/4,1)$ and all three
violations occur in the same execution.
 
All three are safety violations, so they may be concatenated by
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-155 -->
<!-- lemma-133: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-10-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RSX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-133 -->
<!-- proof-156: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S}, in which $a$ alone
is activated and then $a$ and $b$ are activated alternately. The
violations of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ were shown there. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a) the rule is a single pair
$(\lambda,\theta)$.
 
If $\lambda=0$ the robots do not move, the sequence of configurations
reduces to $C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition
of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails. If $c_1=0$, the robot $a$ lands on the
position of $b$ at its first activation and $d_{i+1}=0$, while all the
targets permitted by the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ are
nonzero, so that condition fails. Otherwise the only single
displacements satisfying the transition condition rotate the segment
clockwise by $45^\circ$ or by $90^\circ$; if $a$ departs from them the
transition condition fails at that point, and otherwise $a$ reaches a
configuration with $d_i\perp d_0$ within its two activations, at which
moment both robots are at rest, but the same displacement is repeated
in the alternating singleton activations that follow, so the robots
move again and the stopping condition fails.
 
All of these are safety violations, and a single execution violates all
three predicates, so Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the
claim.
<!-- end proof-156 -->
<!-- lemma-134: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-11-FC-A}
$\mathrm{RSC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-134 -->
<!-- proof-157: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-17-FC-A}, which violates
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace}$ and $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$. The three cases are those of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-10-FC-A}, and the argument there applies verbatim,
the solo activation interval of $a$ now having length two, which still
supplies the two nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations required by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves}.

In the first case all three violations are liveness violations of one
infinite execution; in the other two the violation of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ is finite and precedes the continuations supplied
by Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-17-FC-A}. In either case
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(3) is satisfied, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-157 -->
<!-- lemma-135: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-11-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RSC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-135 -->
<!-- proof-158: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S}, where the
violations of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ were shown; $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace}$ fails
under the same case distinction.
 
If $\lambda=0$, the two robots do not move under any schedule, so
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=0\neq1$ and the single-move condition fails.
 
If $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$, then $c_1=\sqrt{1-4+4}=1\neq0$, so the
distance remains $d$ and $a$ performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ both in round~$1$
and at its second activation in the alternating singleton part; hence
$\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2\neq1$ and the single-move condition fails.
 
If $\lambda\neq0$ and $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$, then for $c_1=0$ the
robot $a$ lands on the position of $b$ at its first activation, so
$a(t)=b(t)$ and the collision-freedom condition fails, while for
$c_1\neq0$ both of its two consecutive solo activations are nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ operations and $\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2$ violates the single-move condition.
All of these are safety violations.
 
In each case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-158 -->
<!-- lemma-136: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-12-FS-AM}
$\mathrm{RZV}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-136 -->
<!-- proof-159: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $A_M$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-FS-AM} with
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{S-RDV}}\xspace}$ replaced by $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$.
 
If no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ ever occurs, condition $(\mathrm{P1})$ of
$\mathrm{VSS}$ fails, and the first condition of $\mathrm{SRO}$ and the
third condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ fail as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-11-FS-AM}.
 
If the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ does not land at the $B=3d$ required
by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, no valid $T_1$ exists and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails at that point; the execution of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-11-FS-AM} may then be used unchanged.
 
If it does land at $B$, then $(\lambda_s,\theta_s)=(2,0)$, which is
neither the $\mathbf{C1}$ rotation about the peer nor the
$\mathbf{C2}$ rotation about the midpoint, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cf-sro-two-moves} the second condition of
$\mathrm{SRO}$ fails at this move. Insert immediately afterwards a
solo activation interval of $b$: activating $b$ alone until it reaches
the state $s$ leaves the configuration unchanged, since
$\lambda=0$ in all earlier states, and then $b$ in state $s$ receives,
in the normalized frame, a local input isomorphic to that of $a$,
applies the same $(2,0)$ and by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay} lands at
$4d\notin P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails.
Moreover, the first move of $a$ alone takes it from $d$ to $3d$ while
$b$ rests at $b_0=2d$, so
\[
  \|a-a_0\|=2d>d=\|b-a_0\|
\]
and the collision-freedom condition of $\mathrm{ZCC}$ has already
failed. No additional delayed ${\mathit{Move}}$ is needed; append an arbitrary fair,
time-divergent tail.
 
In every case a single fair execution violates all three predicates,
and the safety violations established in its prefix persist
(Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)), so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-159 -->
<!-- lemma-137: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-12-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RZV}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-137 -->
<!-- proof-160: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S}, where the
violations of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ZCC}}$ were
shown; $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails under the same case distinction.
 
If $\lambda=0$, the two robots do not move, so no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ exists
and condition $(\mathrm{P1})$ of $\mathrm{VSS}$ fails.
 
If $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$, then in that execution $a$ is activated
alone in round~$1$ and $b$ in round~$2$, both under normalized frames.
The robot $a$ lands at $B=3d$, and $c_1=1\neq0$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay} applies and the robot $b$, activated
immediately afterwards, receives an isomorphic local input and lands at
$4d\notin P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails.
 
If $\lambda\neq0$ and $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$, the first nonzero
${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ is not the landing at $B$ required by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, so no valid $T_1$ exists and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails.
 
In each case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-160 -->
<!-- lemma-138: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-13-FS-A}
$\mathrm{RVX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-138 -->
<!-- proof-161: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-13-FS-A}, which violates
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$.
 
If $\lambda_s=0$ for every state $s$, no nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ occurs and
condition $(\mathrm{P1})$ of $\mathrm{VSS}$ fails, while
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$ fail in the first case
of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-13-FS-A}.
 
Otherwise the robot $a$ performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in the round of
the first common state $s$ with $\lambda_s>0$. If its landing is not
the $B=3d$ required by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, no valid $T_1$
exists and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails at that point. If it is, then
$(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$ and, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-10-FS-A}, the
points of the movement segment of $a$ are $p_\mu=(1+2\mu)d$ with
$\mu\in(0,1)$, and the robot $b$ observing $p_\mu$ in state $s$ applies
the same $(2,0)$ in the normalized frame and lands at $4\mu d$. The set
$P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$ being finite, only finitely many $\mu$ give
$4\mu d\in P$, so together with the countable set to be excluded for
the $\mathrm{VEC}$ violation a $\mu\in(0,1)$ avoiding all of them can
be chosen. For that $\mu$ we have $4\mu d\notin P$, so
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails, and all three violations occur in the same
execution.
 
All three are safety violations, so they may be concatenated by
Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-161 -->
<!-- lemma-139: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-13-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RVX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-139 -->
<!-- proof-162: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S} with the same case
distinction $\lambda=0$ / $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$ / otherwise. The
violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ is that of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S} and the violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ is
that of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-12-OB-S}.
 
For $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$: if $\lambda=0$ the robots do not move, the
sequence of configurations reduces to $C_0$, and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so
the attainment condition fails. If $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$ then
$d_{i+1}=-d_i$, which is none of $d_i$, $R_{-90^\circ}d_i$ and
$2^{\mp1/2}R_{-45^\circ}d_i$, so the transition condition fails.
Otherwise, if $c_1=0$ then $d_{i+1}=0$ while all the permitted targets
are nonzero and the transition condition fails, and if $c_1\neq0$ then,
as in Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-10-OB-S}, the only single displacements
satisfying the transition condition rotate the segment clockwise by
$45^\circ$ or by $90^\circ$; departing from them makes the transition
condition fail, and otherwise an orthogonal configuration is reached
within the two activations of $a$ and the same displacement is repeated
afterwards, so the stopping condition fails.
 
In each case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-162 -->
<!-- lemma-140: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-14-OB-S}
$\mathrm{RVC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{S})$.
<!-- end lemma-140 -->
<!-- proof-163: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Ssynch}}\xspace$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S}. All three
violations follow the same case distinction
$\lambda=0$ / $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$ / otherwise: the violation of
$\Phi_{\mathrm{SRO}}$ is that of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-9-OB-S}, the
violation of $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ is that of
Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-12-OB-S}, and the violation of
$\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace}$ is that of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-11-OB-S}. A single
execution violates all three predicates, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-163 -->
<!-- lemma-141: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-15-FS-A}
$\mathrm{MVX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A})$.
<!-- end lemma-141 -->
<!-- proof-164: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace$ under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
Use coordinates $A=0$, $a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line,
with $P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$, and normalized frames at every ${\mathit{Look}}$ at which
the robots are distinct. Activate both robots simultaneously while
every output is zero; they then carry the same state at every round
boundary and the configuration stays at $\iota$.
 
\emph{No nonzero output.} Continue forever. Condition $(\mathrm{P1})$
fails by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null}, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails;
the sequence of joint-stop configurations reduces to $C_0$ and
$d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$
fails; and the two robots remain at distinct positions, so the
convergence condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails as well. This execution
witnesses all three liveness violations.
 
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the common state at the start of the first
round with a nonzero output, let $(\lambda,\theta)$, with
$\lambda\neq0$, be the corresponding normalized displacement, and put
$c_1:=c_1(\sigma)$.
 
\emph{Case $c_1=0$, that is $(\lambda,\theta)=(1,0)$.} Activate both
robots in that round. Each moves to the position of its peer, so they
exchange positions and the distance returns to $d$ after passing
through $0$; the monotonicity condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails. The
cumulative nonzero-move counts are $(1,1)$, so an admissible exchange
configuration would have to be $(B,A)=(3d,0)$, whereas the landing is
$(2d,d)$; no valid $T_1$ exists and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}. Finally $C_1=(2d,d)$ gives $d_1=-d_0$,
which is neither the clockwise rotation by $45^\circ$ nor the one by
$90^\circ$, so the transition condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails at
$i=0$. All three are safety violations at a finite time; append an
arbitrary admissible fair, time-divergent tail.
 
\emph{Case $c_1\neq0$.} At the round boundary at which both robots
carry $\sigma$ the configuration is still $\iota$; from there continue
as in Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-22-FS-A}, activating $a$ first, so that $a$
performs the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ from $\sigma$ while $b$ is in $\sigma$
with no pending operation. Let $p_E$ be its landing point.
 
If $p_E=B$, then as in that lemma $d_1=-d_0$ violates the transition
condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$, and $b$ lands at $4d\notin P$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails. Moreover
the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $a$ from $d$ to $3d$ passes through $b_0=2d$, so the
distance to the stationary peer drops to $0$ and returns to $d$, and
the monotonicity condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails. All three are
safety violations; append an arbitrary fair tail.
 
If $p_E\neq B$, then as in that lemma $b$ observes $p_\mu$ and its
${\mathit{Move}}$ is delayed until $a$ has landed; $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, and the transition condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$ fails for all $\mu$ outside a finite set. The landing
point of $b$ is affine in $\mu$ with nonzero slope, so it equals $p_E$
for at most one $\mu$; excluding it as well, and since $c_1\neq0$
gives $p_E\neq b_0$, the robots are at distinct positions after both
landings. It remains to violate $\mathrm{MCv}$ in this case.
 
For $\mathrm{MCv}$ we use the following dichotomy, applied to every
nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ of the execution whose peer is at rest. Along such a ${\mathit{Move}}$
the distance to the stationary peer is the distance from a fixed point
to a point travelling along a segment, hence non-increasing and then
non-decreasing. If the landing point is not the point of that segment
closest to the peer, the distance strictly increases on a nonempty
final part of the ${\mathit{Move}}$, so the monotonicity condition of
$\mathrm{MCv}$ fails at a finite time and we are done. We may therefore
assume that every such ${\mathit{Move}}$ ends exactly at its closest approach, so
that the distance is non-increasing along the execution so far.
 
Both robots have now performed the same number of activations, and
every ${\mathit{Look}}$ so far has observed distinct positions (excluding also the
at most one $\mu$ with $p_\mu=b_0$), so by Lemma~\ref{lem:norm}(1)
they carry the same color.
At this point the robots occupy distinct positions, carry
the same internal color, and have no pending operation.
Apply the continuation statement proved in
Lemma~\ref{lem:mcv_not_fs_am}; its schedules are admissible under
$A_M$, hence under $\textnormal{\textsc{Asynch}}\xspace$.
It supplies a fair, time-divergent continuation violating
$\Phi_{\mathrm{MCv}}$, while all safety violations established
in the prefix persist.
 
In the case without nonzero output, all three liveness violations are
witnessed by the explicit fair execution given there. In the cases $c_1=0$ and $p_E=B$, and whenever the
dichotomy above yields a monotonicity violation, all three violations
are safety violations at a finite time. In the remaining case, the
companion predicates have already suffered safety violations. The continuation from Lemma~\ref{lem:mcv_not_fs_am} witnesses either
a finite monotonicity violation or a failure of convergence.
Thus all predicates fail on the same fair infinite execution.
Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}(1)(2)(3) is satisfied and
$\{\mathrm{MCv},\mathrm{VSS},\mathrm{VEC}\}$ has the common failure
property on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives
the claim.
<!-- end proof-164 -->
<!-- lemma-142: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-15-OB-AM}
$\mathrm{MVX}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-142 -->
<!-- proof-165: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $A_M$.
No lemma of Appendix~\ref{app:cf-two-task-disjunctions} has $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}$
as a boundary class, so we construct the execution directly, using the
two activation patterns recorded above. Use coordinates $A=0$,
$a_0=d$, $b_0=2d$, $B=3d$ on the initial line, with
$P=\{0,d,2d,3d\}$. The visible state of an $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ robot is unique, so in
a normalized frame the rule is a single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:single-rule}(a)). Put $c_1:=c_1(\lambda,\theta)$ and
$c_2:=c_2(\lambda,\theta)$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}.

\emph{Case $\lambda=0$.} Neither robot ever moves, under any schedule.
Hence $(\mathrm{P1})$ fails by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_no_null} and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails; the sequence of joint-stop configurations
reduces to $C_0$ and $d_0\not\perp d_0$, so the attainment condition of
$\mathrm{VEC}$ fails; and the robots remain at distinct positions, so
the convergence condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails. All three are
independent of the schedule and persist along any fair infinite
continuation.

\emph{Case $c_1=0$, that is $(\lambda,\theta)=(1,0)$.} Activate both
robots simultaneously in round~$1$, which $A_M$ permits. Each moves to
the position of its peer, so they exchange positions and the distance
returns to $d$ after passing through $0$; the monotonicity condition of
$\mathrm{MCv}$ therefore fails. The cumulative nonzero-move counts are
$(1,1)$, so an admissible exchange configuration would have to be
$(B,A)=(3d,0)$, whereas the landing is $(2d,d)$; no valid $T_1$ exists
and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}.
Finally $C_1=(2d,d)$ gives $d_1=-d_0$, which is neither the clockwise
rotation by $45^\circ$ nor the one by $90^\circ$, so the transition
condition of $\mathrm{VEC}$ fails at $i=0$. All three are safety
violations at a finite time; append an arbitrary admissible fair,
time-divergent tail, which preserves them.

\emph{Case $0<c_1<1$.} Define the execution by an interval of
alternating singleton activations of $a$ and $b$, carried up to the
round following the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ and given normalized frames
(Lemma~\ref{lem:solo}), followed by a delayed-${\mathit{Move}}$ interval of $b$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:stale}; the suspension is placed between
$t_C(b,i)$ and $t_B(b,i)$ and is therefore admissible under $A_M$),
followed by an arbitrary fair tail.

In the first interval, if the landing point of the first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
is not the point required by Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}, no valid
$T_1$ exists; and if it is that point, the robot activated in the next
round receives an isomorphic local input and lands at $4d\notin P$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_replay}. Either way $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ fails.
For $\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$ the argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:A2-6-OB-R}
applies verbatim: the only single displacements that the transition
condition admits while the peer stands still are the $45^\circ$ and
$90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of the segment, so if $a$ departs from
them that condition fails at that move, and if it does not, a
perpendicular configuration is reached within at most two moves, after
which the same displacement is applied again and the stopping condition
fails. Since $c_1\neq0$, neither of the two Move operations of this
interval lands on the peer, so the robots are at distinct positions at
its end.

In the second interval, if no robot performs a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ from that
point on, the two robots stay at these distinct positions and the
convergence condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails. Otherwise $b$ computes a
destination with displacement $v\neq0$ approaching $a$, suspends its
${\mathit{Move}}$, and in the meantime $a$ alone is activated repeatedly. Since
$\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ has no colors, every such activation applies the same
$(\lambda,\theta)$, so $d(j)=c_1^{\,j}d\to0$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(i) and the vector $w$ from $b$ to $a$ at the
release can be made to satisfy $\|w\|<\|v\|/2$. The distance
immediately before the ${\mathit{Move}}$ of $b$ is $\|w\|$, whereas at its
completion it satisfies
\[
  \|w-v\|\ \ge\ \|v\|-\|w\|\ >\ \|w\| ,
\]
so the monotonicity condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails
\cite[Lemma~4]{CP}.

\emph{Case $c_1\ge1$.} The solo activations of $a$ no longer bring the
distance below $\|v\|/2$, so define the execution to be an infinite
sequence of fully synchronous rounds. For $\lambda>0$ the inequality
$c_1\ge1$ is equivalent to $\lambda\ge2\cos\theta$, which implies
$\lambda\ge\cos\theta$, that is $c_2\ge1$. Hence
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratios}(ii) gives $d(k)=c_2^{\,k}d(0)\ge d(0)>0$ for
every $k$, so the two robots do not converge to a single point and the
convergence condition of $\mathrm{MCv}$ fails. For
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VEC}}$ the argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:vec_not_ob_f}
applies verbatim to this execution, since it uses only that both robots
are activated simultaneously in every round and that the displacement
rule is the single pair $(\lambda,\theta)$. For
$\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$: if $(\lambda,\theta)\neq(2,0)$, the nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$
of round~$1$ does not meet the requirement of
Lemma~\ref{lem:p1_first_move}; and if $(\lambda,\theta)=(2,0)$, then
round~$1$ takes $a$ to $3d$ and $b$ to $0$, so in round~$2$ the robot
$a$ lands at $-3d$ and $b$ at $6d$, both outside $P$, which violates
$(\mathrm{P1}\text{-}b)$.

In every case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
$\{\mathrm{MCv},\mathrm{VSS},\mathrm{VEC}\}$ has the common failure
property on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-165 -->
<!-- lemma-143: body_md -->
\label{lem:A3-16-OB-AM}
$\mathrm{MVC}\notin\mathsf{Sol}(\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M})$.
<!-- end lemma-143 -->
<!-- proof-166: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal A$ be any deterministic algorithm of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace$ under $A_M$
and use the execution of Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-15-OB-AM}, where the
violations of $\Phi_{\mathrm{MCv}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{VSS}}$ were
established. We show that $\Phi_{\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace}$ fails under the same case
distinction.

\emph{Case $\lambda=0$.} Neither robot ever moves, so
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=0\neq1$ and the single-move condition fails.

\emph{Case $c_1=0$.} The two robots exchange positions in round~$1$ and
therefore occupy the same point while they travel, so the
collision-freedom condition fails.

\emph{Case $0<c_1<1$.} The robot $a$ performs its first nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in
the interval of alternating singleton activations, and in the
delayed-${\mathit{Move}}$ interval of $b$ the distance stays positive, so each of
the repeated solo activations of $a$ is again a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$; hence
$\mathrm{moves}(a)\ge2\neq1$ and the single-move condition fails.

\emph{Case $c_1\ge1$.} The execution consists of fully synchronous
rounds, and $c_2\ge1$ gives $d(k)\ge d(0)>0$ for every $k$, as shown in
Lemma~\ref{lem:A3-15-OB-AM}. Since $\lambda\neq0$, the displacement of
each robot in round~$k$ has norm $\lambda\,d(k)>0$, so both robots
perform a nonzero ${\mathit{Move}}$ in every round, and these are counted as
distinct ${\mathit{Move}}$ operations because $t_E(r,i)<t_L(r,i+1)$. Hence
$\mathrm{moves}(a)=\infty\neq1$ and the single-move condition fails.

In every case a single execution violates all three predicates, so
$\{\mathrm{MCv},\mathrm{VSS},\textnormal{\text{CFSM}}\xspace\}$ has the common failure property
on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-common-failure} gives the
claim.
<!-- end proof-166 -->
<!-- lemma-144: body_md -->
\label{lem:computational-lattice}
The poset $\mathcal Q$ is a finite lattice with least element $\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^A$
and greatest element $\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F$. Its nonleast join-irreducible elements
are exactly
\[
  J(\mathcal Q)=\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S,\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A,\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A,\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}\}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-144 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:antichain-boundary-enumeration}
The antichain polynomial of $\mathcal Q$ is
\[
  \mathsf A_{\mathcal Q}(z)
  =\sum_{A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)}z^{|A|}
  =1+13z+24z^{2}+16z^{3},
\]
so $\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal Q)$ has $54$ elements, of which $53$ are nonempty.
For an antichain $A$ put
$U_A=\bigcup_{X\in A}\mathord{\uparrow} X$ and
$\mathcal N_A=\operatorname{Max}(\mathcal Q\setminus U_A)$. Then
\[
  \sum_{\substack{A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)\\|A|=2}}|\mathcal N_A|=47,
  \qquad
  \sum_{\substack{A\in\operatorname{Ant}(\mathcal Q)\\|A|=3}}|\mathcal N_A|=34.
\]
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-145: body_md -->
\label{lem:width-three}
The width of $\mathcal Q$ is three.
<!-- end lemma-145 -->
<!-- proof-167: body_md -->
The thirteen classes are partitioned into the three chains
\[
\begin{aligned}
  C_1&:\quad \ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^A<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^{A_M}<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^S<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^R<\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F<\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^F,\\
  C_2&:\quad \ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^A<\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^{A_M}<\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^S<\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R,\\
  C_3&:\quad \ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^A<\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S<\ensuremath{\mathcal{LUMI}}\xspace^R.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each $C_i$ is a chain in the order established by
Theorem~\ref{thm:six-signature-landscape}, and the three cover all
thirteen classes. An antichain meets each chain at most once, so its
size is at most three. Conversely $\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{OBLOT}}\xspace^F,\ensuremath{\mathcal{FST\!A}}\xspace^R,\ensuremath{\mathcal{FCOM}}\xspace^S\}$ is a
three-element antichain, since no two of its signatures are comparable.
Hence $\operatorname{width}(\mathcal Q)=3$.
<!-- end proof-167 -->
<!-- lemma-146: body_md -->
\label{lem:antichain-deletion-recurrence}
For a finite poset $P$ and $x\in P$, let
$\mathsf A_P(z)=\sum_{A\in\operatorname{Ant}(P)}z^{|A|}$. Then
\[
  \mathsf A_P(z)
  =\mathsf A_{P\setminus\{x\}}(z)
   +z\,\mathsf A_{P\setminus(\downarrow_Px\cup\mathord{\uparrow}_Px)}(z),
  \qquad \mathsf A_{\varnothing}(z)=1,
\]
where deletions carry the induced order.
<!-- end lemma-146 -->
<!-- proof-168: body_md -->
Antichains not containing $x$ are precisely those of
$P\setminus\{x\}$. If an antichain contains $x$, its other elements
must be incomparable with $x$, and form an antichain of
$P\setminus(\downarrow_Px\cup\mathord{\uparrow}_Px)$.
Conversely, adjoining $x$ to any such antichain is valid and increases
its size by one, accounting for the factor $z$.
<!-- end proof-168 -->
<!-- proof-169: body_md -->
There is one empty antichain and there are thirteen singleton
antichains. Lemma~\ref{lem:width-three} excludes antichains of size
four or more, and the columns $a_2$ and $a_3$ of
Table~\ref{tab:antichain-enumeration-certificate} give $24$ and $16$.
Thus $\mathsf A_{\mathcal Q}(z)=1+13z+24z^2+16z^3$, and by the
antichain--upset bijection of
Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-upset-decomposition} the number of
upsets is $1+13+24+16=54$. The columns $b_2$ and $b_3$ give the totals
$47$ and $34$ for the maximal-complement obligations.
<!-- end proof-169 -->
